or domiciled. Parent/Guardian's income should not exceed ₹ 2.5 lakh per annum. The objective

appreciably increase the Gross Enrollment Ratio of SC students in higher education with a focus 
on those from the poorest households. It is the endeavor of the Government to raise the GER of 
SCs in higher education from 23.0 % to the national average.

Enrolment Ratio of SC students in higher education when the actual expenditure and the

substantial increase in the number of beneficiaries and actual expenditure. The Committee 
would like the Department to take appropriate action so that the number of beneficiaries 
increase, such as, publicizing the Scheme, obtaining feedback from the students, etc. The 
Committee would like to be informed of the concrete measures taken by the Department to 
enhance the number of beneficiaries.

remains the same. The Committee are happy to be informed that the guidelines are under

timely and the revised guidelines will yield the desired results from the academic year 2026-
27.

in Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Odisha, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West

achieving the target particularly in the context when the population of the country is 
increasing. The Committee would especially like to draw the attention of the Department 
with regard to the States where the number of beneficiaries has gone down. The Committee 
are of the view that schemes meant for deprived sections of society cannot be left entirely 
at the mercy of the Implementing Agencies, Governments need to take control of the 
Schemes. The Central Government instead of making the State/UT Governments entirely 
responsible for implementing the Scheme, the Committee feel that the Department should 
also be held responsible in case the Schemes are not being implemented, meticulously. The 
Committee would therefore like the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment to take 
necessary action in this regard.

4.38 The Committee note that the Annual Expenditure under the National Fellowship for 
SC Scheme was more than the Budget Estimates in the years 2023-24 and 2024-25 and is

2005-06 has remained the same even in subsequent years. The Committee does not find 
any justification for not increasing the target for more than 20 years and thereby restricting 
students from availing the benefits of the scheme to undertake advanced studies and 

42  
research leading to PhD degrees. The Committee believe that increasing the number of 
fellowships under this scheme would provide greater opportunities to under-privileged 
candidates in addition to those qualifying the cut-off marks notified by UGC-CSIR for NET-
JRF. Even after the several evaluations of the scheme conducted over the year, the 
Committee are surprised that no recommendation for enhancement of fellowship numbers 
has been made till date. The Committee are of the view that the department should analyze 
the number of applications received under the scheme in the last three years. If the number 
of applications received each year is increasing then it justifies the need to increase the 
number of fellowships so that a larger number of applicants get an opportunity to avail the 
fellowship. It is also a fact that several students do not pursue advanced studies due to lack 
of financial assistance. Keeping in view the educational backwardness of a large section of 
the SC population, the Committee strongly believe that the number of fellowships need to 
be enhanced so that the scheme accommodates more aspiring students. The Committee 
would like to be informed of the action taken in this regard. 
 
4.39 The Committee are happy to note that the beneficiaries of the PM- CARES Children 
Scheme have been included in the free coaching scheme for SCs and OBCs from 2024-25. 
All beneficiaries of the PM- CARES Children Scheme are eligible to avail the benefits of the 
scheme irrespective of income whereas the ceiling of the total family income for SC and 
OBC students is ₹8 lakh per annum. The Committee find that the target fixed for 2023-24 
and 2024-25 could not be achieved even after the inclusion of PM-CARES Children Scheme. 
The requirement for coaching support is well recognized particularly among students 
belonging to the educationally disadvantaged sections of Scheduled Castes and Other 
Backward Classes. It is also well known that the coaching is an expensive affair and 
everybody cannot avail coaching due to its high cost, hence the candidates from Scheduled 
Castes and Other Backward Classes aspiring for coaching cannot avail this facility even if 
the annual income of family is more than ₹ 8 Lakh. The Committee strongly feel that the 
total family income criterion fixed for SC and OBC students may be one of the major hurdles 
preventing candidates from these categories from availing the benefits. The Committee also 
does not understand the reason for fixing a target of 7000, which is double the previous 
target, particularly when the target fixed earlier is not being achieved. The Committee desire 
that the family income ceiling should be re-examined so that a large number of candidates 
can avail the facility and scheme becomes more effective. 
 

43  
4.40 The Committee appreciate that the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment 
provide scholarships to meritorious SC students for pursuing studies beyond the 12th class 
in the selected 274 premier Institutions and Top 100 National Institutional Ranking 
Framework under the Top Class Education scheme. The Committee note that no target will 
be fixed from 2026-27 onwards and scholarships will be provided to all eligible SC students 
but subject to the availability of budget. The Committee feel that non-fixing of target become 
meaningless if the budget is not appropriately enhanced as the budget available for 2026-
2027 is ₹120 crore whereas actual expenditure incurred in 2024-2025 was ₹103.26 crore. The 
Committee are of the view, that the Scheme will give much benefit to the candidates if the 
Budget is  enhanced to accommodate all applicants getting admission in selected 
Institutions. Hence, the changes proposed, if implemented, may prove superfluous unless 
the budget is substantially enhanced, as the available budget can only accommodate a 
limited number of students and not all eligible candidates. The Committee also find that the 
family income ceiling of ₹8 lakh fixed in 2020-21 may also be one of the constraints for 
students intending to avail scholarship under the scheme. The Committee would also like 
to draw the attention to the fact that the Department is spending the allocated budget 
despite receiving less applications than the target fixed for previous years. This sufficiently 
indicates that the income eligibility criteria need to be revised to attract more applicants, as 
it has been more than five years since the ceiling was revised from ₹6 lakh to ₹8 lakh. The 
students with the income eligibility limit of ₹8 lakh may still not be in a position to bear the 
burden of the high fees charged by such institutions. The Committee are sure that the 
Department will understand and take substantive measures to enhance the income ceiling 
and annual budget to extend the benefits of the scheme to the maximum number of needy 
candidates securing admission in to premier selected Institutions.  
 
4.41 The Committee are happy to note that the slots of National Overseas Scholarships 
for SCs have been increased from 125 to 250 from the year 2026-27 based on the 
recommendations of this Committee’s report in march 2025. Simultaneously, it is surprising 
to note that the Budget Estimate for 2026-27 is same as 2025-26.  The Committee are unable 
to understand how the Department will provide scholarship to the students if the demand 
for 250 slots is received in 2026-27 in the limited Budget meant for 125 slots only. The 
Committee also find that the Overseas Scholarships offered by some States is more 
preferred over National Overseas Scholarship as these State Governments provides the 
facility of direct transfer of scholarship amounts to students’ bank accounts and there is no 

44  
restriction to return to India. The Committee believe that all efforts should be made to make 
the scheme more popular among students and necessary changes should be made in 
provisions that are becoming impediments in making the scheme attractive to candidates.  
   The Committee observed that the slots earmarked for Denotified, Nomadic and Semi-
Nomadic Tribes, Landless Agricultural Laborers and Traditional Artisans have remained 
unutilised over the years due to financial constraints. The Committee recommend that the 
government find out ways and means to fill the earmarked slots this year. 
The Committee are deeply concerned with the outcome of this Scheme as the Department 
may not find sufficient students to fill the available slots for 2026-27 unless the restrictions 
applicable are waived off and the income eligibility criteria is amended. The Committee 
strongly feel that the scheme needs to be exhaustively re-examined with respect to income 
ceiling limit, budgetary allocation, etc. and revised in the interest of the targeted sections 
of the society.  The Committee would like to be informed of the action taken in this regard. 
 
4.42 The Committee are concerned to note the poor physical and financial performance of 
the scheme of ‘Free Coaching for SCs and OBCs’ over the years. The objective of the 
scheme is to provide coaching of good quality for economically disadvantage SCs & OBCs 
to enable them to appear in competitive examination and/or for securing admission in 
reputed technical and professional higher education institution. Out of the BE of ₹ 47 cr in 
2023-24 AE was only ₹ 7.76 cr BE was reduced to ₹ 35 cr in 2024-25 still AE was ₹ 17.68 cr 
only. Similarly in 2025-26, BE was further downgraded to ₹ 20 cr & AE was only ₹ 7.11 cr. 
The physical performance has been equally poor as vis-à-vis the target of 3500 achievement 
has only been 223 in 2023-24, 2136 in 2024-25 & 431 in 2025-26. 
   The Committee are not satisfied with the explanation given by the department for this poor 
performance such as limited participation by the Central Universities and delayed 
proposals. The performance has remained poor inspite of changes introduced by the 
Department over the years such as making Dr. Ambedkar Foundation as the Central Nodal 
Agency. The Committee note that the proposal for 16th Finance Committee cycle includes 
inclusion of state Universities and introduction of student centric mode for wider coverage. 
The Committee desire that these changes be made effective at the earliest to ensure that 
the BE of ₹ 20 cr for this purpose for the year 2026-27 is fully utilized.

6.15 The Committee are pleased to find that the Scheme of Residential Education for 
Students in High School in Targeted Areas (SRESHTA) has been introduced to enable 
students from the SC community to receive better education. The Scheme runs under two 
modes. In mode 1 fee is reimbursed to private residential schools affiliated to CBSE/State 
Boards for providing high quality residential education to meritorious SC students. The 
Committee had observed during the study visit to some residential schools selected under 
this mode that the students are finding difficult to adjust in the schools located in States 
other than their domicile State due to linguistic and cultural difference. The Committee 
accordingly recommended Department of Social Justice and Empowerment during the 
Examination of Demand for Grants for the year 2025-26 to examine the issue and suitably 
revise the Scheme to accommodate the students selected in the Schools selected under the 
Scheme in their domicile State. The Committee, however, found during the Examination of

Central but by the State Governments as well to attract more students. The Committee

PRE-MATRIC SCHOLARSHIPS 
 
7.5 The objective of Pre-Matric Scholarship for OBC, EBC and DNT students (who are not 
covered under SC, ST or OBC) is welfare and motivation to the children of these categories by 
providing financial assistance at pre-matriculation or secondary stage. Scholarship under the 
Scheme will be available for studies in India only. The Salient Features of the scheme are as 
follows: 
 
(i) The scheme is implemented through respective State Governments/ UTs. 
(ii) The scholarship will be provided for students studying in class IXth and Xth on a full-
time basis in Government School only. 
(iii) Parents /guardians income from all sources does not exceed Rs.2,50,000/- per 
annum.  
(iv) The students shall be given a consolidated academic allowance of Rs. 4000/- per 
annum.  

62  
(v) The scheme will be implemented and administered in accordance with the procedure 
laid down by the State Govts. /UT Administration in this regard.  
(vi) The concerned State Governments and Union Territory Administrations will lay 
down   the detailed procedure for selection of students. 
(vii) The award once made will be payable until the student passes Class Xth, subject to 
satisfactory academic performance and attendance of 75% in every academic year.  
(viii) The scholarship portals would remain open throughout the year so that all eligible 
students can register for the Freeship Card and apply for the scholarships. 
(ix) The entire scholarship amount - both from the State and Central Government - 
including the academic allowance and disability allowance, if any, is paid directly into 
the account of the students or parents only through DBT preferably through an 
Aadhaar Based Payment System (Aadhaar Payment Bridge-AePS). 
(x) There is a 60: 40 sharing ratio between the Centre and States. For North Eastern 
States and for the states of Uttarakhand and Himanchal Pradesh the sharing ratio is 
90:10. For UTs without legislatures, 100% funds is provided by Centre. 
(xi) At least 5% students with disabilities should be covered for grant of the scholarships. 
(xii) 30% of the beneficiaries should be reserved for girl students.

Social Justice and Empowerment that:  
“An evaluation study of the Scheme has already been conducted by NITI Aayog to 
assess its design, implementation framework, and overall impact. Based on the 
findings and recommendations of the study, necessary modifications have been 
incorporated to strengthen delivery mechanisms and improve efficiency. The revised 
provisions and implementation changes have also been duly considered and 
supported through the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) process. Accordingly, 
the Scheme has been suitably revised, and the recommended reforms have been 
implemented to ensure better outcomes and streamlined execution from next financial 
cycle from 2026-27 to 2030-31.” 
 
CONSTRUCTION OF HOSTELS FOR OBC BOYS AND GIRLS 
7.22 The scheme aims at providing hostel facilities to students belonging to socially and 
educationally backward classes, especially from rural areas to enable them to pursue secondary 
and higher education in the Govt. schools, universities, institutions and institutes located at a 
reasonable distance in order to provide them greater access to high quality education. The 
scheme as such mainly targets the students hailing from remote areas and from poor families 
as well who generally discontinue their studies either because no secondary school and college 

70  
is available near their location or due to non-availability of adequate hostel facilities at a 
reasonable cost at places where such educational institutions are located. The Salient features 
of the Scheme are as follows: 
 
(i) The scheme is implemented through respective States/UTs in respect of State 
Universities. For Central University, the grant is given directly to the institution. 
(ii) Agencies eligible for financial assistance under the revised Scheme will be as follows:- 
a) State Government and UT Administrations; 
b) The institution of repute ranked in the latest NIRF rankings of Ministry of 
Education subject to following conditions:- 
- The institution shall provide free of cost land within the campus.  
- The institution shall undertake to complete construction within 24 
months.  
- The institution shall maintain the hostel after construction as per 
standards prescribed.  
- The institution shall agree to provide as many hostel seats to the new 
OBC students as per the sanction order of the hostel. However, this 
additional accommodation shall be regulated in other hostels as well 
to avoid the hostel being designated as 'OBC hostel' exclusively i.e. if 
a hostel with 100 capacity has been sanctioned under this scheme, 
the institution shall provide 100 additional seats to the OBC students, 
but it can be spread over in all other hostels. 
(iii) Agencies eligible for assistance under the Scheme should have clear title and 
possession over the land where the hostel is to be constructed, and will submit 
proposals in the prescribed formats. 
(iv) The cost of construction of hostels for boys has to be shared between the Centre 
and the State in 60:40 ratio (in case of Girls Hostels 90%   of cost will be borne by 
the Central Govt). In case of Union Territories, the Central Assistance shall be 100% 
and for North Eastern States and 02 Himalayan States (Himachal Pradesh and 
Uttarakhand), it shall be 90%.  
(v) For the Institution of repute ranked in the latest NIRF rankings of Ministry of 
Education, Govt. of India, the Central Assistance shall be 100% irrespective of 
regional States.   
(vi) The construction work of the Hostel has to be completed within eighteen months 
from award of work order or two years from the release of 1st installment of Central 
assistance, whichever is earlier. In no case the time will be extended beyond 2 
years.   
(vii)  The cost per hostel seat in different areas are as follows:-   
- North Eastern Region/Himalayan Regions  -   ₹3.50 lakh per seat 
- Rest of country  -    ₹3.00 lakh per seat, or as per the schedule of the rates 

71  
for the concerned State Government, whichever is lower.  
(ix) The amount of grant will be released in 3 installments in 50:45:5 ratio, of which 5% 
grant will be released after completion of the work and occupation of the rooms by 
the OBC Boys and Girls.  
(x) There will be a one-time non-recurring grant of ₹2500/- per seat for providing 
furniture/equipment to the hostels constructed under the Scheme.

7.25 On being asked, the purpose of having separate hostel for OBC students the Department 
of Social Justice and Empowerment submitted vide written reply that: 
 
“The provision of separate hostels for OBC students is primarily intended as a 
supportive measure to improve access to education for students from socially and 
educationally disadvantaged backgrounds, particularly those coming from remote or 
economically weaker families. If seats reserved for OBC remains vacant, it would be 
filled up in following preference:-  
 
(a) De-notified Tribes (DNT) students 
(b) Scheduled Tribes (ST) Students 
(c) Scheduled Caste (SC) Students 
(d) Economically Weaker Section (EWS) Students 
 
The objective is not segregation, but facilitation of safe, affordable accommodation 
where such facilities are otherwise inadequate. Care is taken to ensure that these 
hostels function as part of the larger campus ecosystem, with students participating 
fully in academic, cultural and extracurricular activities alongside their peers. 
Institutions are advised to promote inclusivity and equal opportunity so that no sense 

73  
of isolation or stigma arises. The overall approach is developmental and welfare-
oriented, aimed at strengthening educational participation without compromising 
social integration.” 
 
7.26 On being enquired with regard to assessment was conducted prior to launch of the 
Scheme, the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment stated in their written reply that: 
 
“Department of Social Justice and Empowerment undertook preliminary assessments 
of the need for hostel facilities based on the number of eligible students, gaps in 
existing infrastructure, and regional educational backwardness. These assessments 
drew on data from State Governments, enrolment statistics, and demand projections 
for residential facilities for OBC students. While the scheme originally aimed at 
constructing hostels in phases, the timeline for completion varied by project 
depending on availability of land, administrative approvals, tendering processes, and 
release of funds by both Central and State Governments.” 
 
 
 
7.27 On being asked about the norms laid down for constructions of hostels sanctioned along 
with the number of Hostels constructed within the stipulated period including reasons for delay 
and the action taken thereon, the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment stated in their 
written reply that: 
 
“Cost norms are prescribed per seat by region and funding is shared between Centre 
and States/UTs (60:40 for boys, 90:10 for girls; 100% for UTs; 90:10 for Central 
institutions), with a mandatory completion period of 18 months from award of work 
order or 2 years from release of central assistance whichever is earlier, and any cost 
escalation due to delay is to be borne by the State/Institute. It has been noted that 
significant delays have occurred in completing sanctioned hostels, with few 
completed within the stipulated timelines and many remaining incomplete due to 
funding flow issues, administrative/approval bottlenecks, land acquisition and 
procurement delays, tendering and contracting slowdowns, and late release of 
matching State share. Detailed State/Institution‑wise sanctioned vs constructed 
numbers and exact reasons for delay are not maintained by the Ministry; however, 
parliamentary responses and audit observations have highlighted delays in several 
State implementations and noted efforts to review progress and improve monitoring. 
States and implementing agencies have been encouraged through official 
communications to expedite execution, ensure timely release of matching share, 
adhere strictly to prescribed timelines, and improve project management to minimise 
further delays and ensure students benefit from the hostel infrastructure.”

TOP CLASS EDUCATION IN COLLEGE  
 
7.30 The objective of the scheme is to recognise and promote quality education amongst 
Students belonging to OBC, EBC and DNT categories by providing full financial support. The 
Scheme will cover OBC/EBC/DNT students for pursuing studies beyond class XII th. The salient 
features of the Scheme are as follows:  
(i) This Scheme is implemented w.e.f. 2023-24  
(ii) The Scheme will operate in all the institutions notified by the Ministry of Social 
Justice and Empowerment for every financial year.  
(iii) All the IIMs / IITs/ IIITs / AIIMSs/ NITs/NIFTs/ NIDs/ Indian Institutes of Hotel 
Management, National Law Universities and other Central Government Institutions 
will be eligible to be included in the Scheme.  
(iv) The list of the ‘Top Class’ Institutions to be covered under the Scheme    along with 
number of scholarship slots will be notified by the Department of Social Justice and

(v) The scholarship, once awarded, will continue till the completion of the course, 
subject to satisfactory performance of the student.  
(vi) The scholarship will be terminated if the student fails to get promoted to the next 
semester/class.  
(vii) The students, who secure admission in the notified institutions, will be awarded 
scholarship to meet the following requirements for  
(a) full tuition fee and non-refundable charges (there will be a ceiling of ₹ 2.00 
lakh per annum per student for private sector institutions and ₹ 3.72 lakhs 
per annum per student for the private sector flying clubs for Commercial 
Pilot Training and Type Rating Courses)  
(b) living expenses to the beneficiary @₹3000/-per month per student  
(c) books and stationery @ ₹ 5000/- per annum per student; and  
(d) a latest computer/laptop of reputed brand with accessories like UPS and 
printer limited to ₹ 45000/- per student as one time assistance during the 
course. 

75  
(viii) Thirty percent (30%) of slots allotted to the Institution shall be reserved for eligible 
girl students as per their inter-se merit. In the absence of sufficient number of girl 
students, the slots may be transferred to eligible boy students as per their inter-
se-merit.

7.38 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment has 
neither been able to exhaust the budgetary allocation nor achieve the targets fixed for 
2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 under various components of PM-YASASVI. The Committee 
find that certain procedural issues such as pending Aadhaar seeding, bank account 
validation, utilization certificates (UCs), etc., are challenges before the Department in 
optimizing the utilization of resources and maximizing the targets laid down under the 
Scheme. The Committee note that despite various measures such as periodic review, 
third party evaluation, awareness of Scheme, etc. taken by the Department to address the 
challenges in implementing the schemes these challenges continue to recur year after 
year. The Committee have no doubt about the sincerity of the Department, but it would 
appreciate if suitable steps are taken so that the issues hampering the Scheme dies down 
once and for all and the Scheme is  smoothly implemented. 
The Committee also note that the income eligibility has been enhanced from ₹2.5 
lakh to ₹4.5 lakh by the Department and has also introduced disability allowance of 
₹10,000 per annum from 2026-27. However, the Committee find that the Budgetary 
Estimate for 2025-26 has not increased for most of the sub-components of the Scheme 
for the year 2026-27. The Committee expect that the expenditure on the sub-components 
may multiply as the number of applicants may increase with the enhanced income 
eligibility and disability allowance.  The Committee would therefore, like the Department 
to timely assess the funds requirement for the year 2026-27 to meet the increased demand 
under each sub-component of the Scheme. The Committee believe that the Department 
will take all necessary measures to ensure that no applicant is deprived of the Scheme 
for want of funds. The Committee would like to be informed in this regard. 
7.39 The Committee note that the target fixed for 2024-25 under Post Matric Scholarship 
Scheme was not achieved and the same target was again fixed for 2025-26. The 
Committee are not sure about the status of achievement vis-a-vis the target fixed for 2025-
26 as the Committee have been informed that the details of Beneficiaries are not available

78  
it is better to bring down the goal so that you don’t have to face the failure. The Committee 
are not satisfied with the way the Scheme is being implemented by the Department as 
they strongly feel that the Scheme can be considered successful only if the target fixed 
are achieved and the target for next year are enhanced.  The Committee are of the opinion 
that the target fixed should increase every year so that the revised estimates also

 The Committee are happy to note that a proposal has been submitted for revision 
of the scheme to the Expenditure Finance Committee with regard to the income ceiling 
and scholarship rates. In view of the proposed revision, the Committee feel that the 
budgetary allocation made may not be sufficient as the number of beneficiaries is likely

7.40 The Committee note that the Top Class Education in School Scheme for

           CHAPTER-VIII 
 
ATAL VAYO ABHYUDAY YOJANA (AVYAY) 
The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (MoSJE) is the nodal Ministry for the 
welfare of senior citizens. In alignment with the principles of active and healthy ageing and to 
ensure dignified living for the elderly, the Ministry is implementing the umbrella scheme Atal 
Vayo Abhyudaya Yojana (AVYAY). AVYAY seeks to provide comprehensive and integrated 
services through the convergence of various interventions targeted at different aspects of elderly 
welfare ranging from shelter and medical care to assistive devices, helpline services and 
caregiver training. The components under AVYAY are as follows: - 
 
INTEGRATED PROGRAMME FOR SENIOR CITIZENS (IPSRC) 
 
8.2 The objective of the IPSrC is to enhance the quality of life of senior citizens, particularly 
indigent elderly persons, by providing essential amenities such as shelter, food, medical care 
and recreational facilities, while promoting productive and active ageing. Under the scheme, 
financial assistance in the form of grant-in-aid is provided to eligible implementing agencies, 
including NGOs and voluntary organizations, for the operation and maintenance of various 
facilities, including Senior Citizens’ Homes for 25 beneficiaries, Senior Citizens’ Homes for 50 
beneficiaries (male only or combined male and female), Senior Citizens’ Homes exclusively for 
50 elderly women, Continuous Care Homes and homes for senior citizens suffering from 
Alzheimer’s disease or dementia for a minimum of 20 beneficiaries, Regional Resource and 
Training Centers, and Mobile Medicare Units (MMUs) and Physiotherapy Clinics for senior 
citizens. 
 
STATE ACTION PLAN FOR SENIOR CITIZENS (SAPSRC) 
 
8.3 The State Action Plan for Senior Citizens (SAPSrC) is a component of the Atal Vayo 
Abhudaya Yojana (AVYAY) under which financial assistance is provided to States and Union 
Territories to implement state-specific initiatives for the welfare of senior citizens, with a primary 
focus on cataract surgeries for senior citizens, training of geriatric caregivers, awareness 
generation about the scheme, and any other activities considered appropriate by the States/UTs 
to improve the well-being of senior citizens. 
 
RASHTRIYA VAYOSHRI YOJANA (RVY) 
 
8.4 Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana (RVY) was first announced in the 2015-16 Union Budget 
speech by the finance minister and subsequently launched on 01st April, 2017. The objective of 
the scheme is to provide eligible senior citizens suffering from any of the age-related disability/ 
infirmity, with assisted living devices which can restore near normalcy in their bodily functions, 

81  
overcoming the disability/ infirmity manifested such as low vision, hearing impairment, loss of 
teeth and loco-motor disabilities. 
  
ELDERLINE: NATIONAL HELPLINE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS (NHSC) 
 
8.5 National Helpline for Senior Citizens was dedicated to the Nation on 01st October, 2021 
on the occasion of the International Day of Older Persons, with the toll-free number 14567. 
Elderline operates for 12 hours a day (8:00 AM to 8:00 PM) and provides free information, 
guidance, emotional support and field intervention in cases of abuse, neglect and rescue. The 
National Institute of Social Defence, an autonomous body under MoSJE, is the nodal agency for 
implementation of Elderline across the country. 
 
 
SENIOR CARE AGEING GROWTH ENGINE (SAGE) 
 
8.6 SAGE portal was dedicated to the Nation on 01 October 2021. The scheme aims to 
encourage entrepreneurs and start-ups to develop innovative solutions to address challenges 
faced by the elderly. Under the scheme, Government of India support is provided to start-ups 
through equity participation of up to 49%, with assistance up to ₹1 crore, to promote elder-care 
innovations. 
 
SYSTEM FOR PROVISION OF ELDERCARE IN-HOUSE AND ASSISTED LIVING (PM 
SPECIAL)/ TRAINING OF GERIATRIC CARE GIVERS 
 
8.7 The main objective of the PM Special (Training of Geriatric Care Givers) scheme is to 
bridge the gap in supply and increasing demand in the field of geriatric caregivers so as to 
provide more professional services to the senior citizens and also to create a cadre of 
professional caregivers in the field of geriatrics. The Scheme will ensure sufficient availability of 
dedicated, professionally trained manpower of geriatric caregivers who can attend to diverse 
and dynamic needs of elderly population relating to recreation and holistic well-being. So far, 
35,480 trainees have been imparted training under the scheme.

the Department has proposed to associate State/UT Governments in the implementation

citizens Division of the Department is not sufficient to cater to the requirement of the 
senior citizens. The Department has also received suggestions from various quarters for 
a separate dedicated Department for the welfare of senior citizens. The Department 
should examine the infrastructure available in the Department to manage the affairs of 
Senior Citizens. As is already known that the population of Senior Citizens in the country 
is projected to increase from 8.4% to 14.9% of the total population by 2036, and a small

senior citizens. The Committee would also like to draw the attention towards the creation 
of separate Department for Divyangjan in 2012 by the Government. The separate 
Department was created to manage the affairs of comparatively less population of 
Divyangjan in the country and is effectively catering to their needs. The Committee would 
also like to express that once the ‘Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior 
Citizens (Amendment) Bill, 2019 is enacted the responsibilities of the Division will 
multiply. In view of the large population of Senior Citizens which continues to increase 
every year, the Committee would like the Government to examine creation of a separate

NATIONAL ACTION FOR MECHANIZED SANITATION ECOSYSTEM (NAMASTE) 
 
NAMASTE, a joint initiative of the MoSJE and the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs 
(MoHUA), is being implemented since FY 2023-24. The scheme envisages safety and dignity of 
sanitation workers by creating an enabling ecosystem that recognizes sanitation workers as one 
of the key contributors in operations and maintenance of sanitation infrastructure thereby 
enhancing their occupational safety through capacity building and improved access to safety 
gear and machines. Components of erstwhile Self Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of 
Manual Scavengers (SRMS) have been subsumed in NAMASTE scheme from 2023-24. Further, 
waste pickers have been added as target group under NAMASTE in FY 2024-25. The Key 
Interventions of the scheme are as follows:- 
 
A. Sewer and Septic tank Workers (SSWs) 
Interventions  
(i) Profiling of Sewer/ Septic Tank workers. 
(ii) Distribution of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) kits to identified 
SSWs 
(iii) Distribution of safety devices to ERSUs 
(iv) Imparting occupational safety training to SSWs 
(v) Health insurance coverage of SSWs and manual scavengers and their 
dependents under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (after profiling of SSWs by 
ULBs) 
(vi) Upfront capital subsidy upto ₹7.50 Lakh for individual projects costing upto 
₹ 15.00 lakh for sanitation related projects and capital subsidy of ₹25.00 
Lakh for a group project of five sanitation workers including manual 
scavengers for a project costing ₹ 50.00 Lakh. 
(vii)Appointment of Responsible Sanitation Authority (RSA) in every District. 
(viii)Constitution of Emergency Response Sanitation Unit (ERSU) in larger 
Urban Local Bodies (ULB) of Districts to cover Urban and Rural areas.  
(ix) Operationalization of Helpline number (14420). 
(x) IEC Campaign: Targeting Safai Mitras, Operators/ Contractors and 
Citizensthrough RWAs etc. through print and digital media, innovative 
media interventions and by organizing workshops/webinars 
  

91  
B.  Waste pickers  
Waste Pickers have been included as an additional target group along with sewer 
septic tank workers under NAMASTE scheme. The identified waste pickers would 
later on be provided occupational/ up gradation training for waste value addition. The 
scheme has various components for welfare of waste pickers namely profiling, Health 
Insurance under AB-PMJAY, Social Security Benefits, Occupational Safety Training, 
PPE Kits, Capital Subsidy for Dry Waste Collection Centres (DWCCs) to procure 
Waste Collection Vehicles and other welfare measures. The waste pickers 
component of the Scheme intends to integrate waste pickers in the solid waste 
management by addressing challenges, difficulties faced by them by mainstreaming 
them in the society, recognizing and strengthening their contribution in waste 
collection, recovery & recycling, providing safe, dignified and sustainable livelihood 
by empowering them through various interventions. Department of Social Justice & 
Empowerment, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, National Health Authority, 
National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation, Ayushman 
Bharat Empanelled Hospitals and Waste Pickers are the major stakeholders. The 
core objective of the Scheme is to ensure that waste pickers live dignified lives and 
work in a safe environment by enabling their enumeration, recognition and integration 
into the solid waste management value chain, while ensuring access to social security 
and welfare schemes based on their occupational identity.

Scheme get the benefits of the Scheme in the fixed time frame, the Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment stated vide  their written reply that the following steps are being taken: 
 
(i) “Central Monitoring Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of the Minister 
of Social justice and Empowerment, monitor the progress of implementation of the 
‘Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 
2013” and NAMASTE Scheme.  
(ii) Various Committees have been constituted at State / District level and 
Commission for Safai Karmacharis at National and State level. 
(iii) Regular monitoring mechanisms, including weekly review meetings with ULBs, 
have been institutionalised to track progress and address delays. 
(iv) Active involvement of training partners and workshop partners has been ensured 
to expedite processes such as e-KYC and beneficiary on-boarding. 
(v) Phased and parallel dispatch of PPE and safety devices to ERSUs has been 
undertaken to avoid logistical delays and ensure timely distribution to validated 
workers. 
(vi) Field visits by SPMUs to ULBs have been conducted to resolve bottlenecks and 
accelerate implementation at the ground level.” 
9.12 The Department of Social Justice and Empowerment, informed the Committee that the 
following monitoring mechanism has been adopted by them: 
 
“It is monitored through a multi-tiered mechanism. At the national level, a 
Coordination Committee chaired by the Secretary, Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment oversees the scheme, supported by three Working Groups at 
the national, state, and district levels, chaired respectively by the Divisional Head 
of the Plan Division (DoSJE), the Principal Secretary/Secretary of Social Welfare, 
and the DM/ADM/CEO of Zila Parishad. At the state level, two State Nodal Officers 
(SNOs) are designated in each State/UT, with the SNO from the Urban 
Development Department responsible for implementation and the SNO from the 
Social Welfare Department responsible for monitoring. A dedicated Project 
Management Unit at NSKFDC, supported by a Technical Support Unit, facilitates 
implementation and conducts review meetings with SPMUs and ULB Nodal 
Officers to track progress. A dedicated Management Information System (MIS) 
portal captures critical data on implementation, beneficiary coverage, and scheme 
interventions. The Central Monitoring Committee, chaired by the Minister of Social 
Justice and Empowerment, also monitors implementation of the NAMASTE 
Scheme along with the “Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and 
their Rehabilitation Act, 2013,” with the last meeting held on 22.08.2025. 

97  
Additionally, video calling of training classes and workshops is conducted to ensure 
effective oversight and engagement.” 
 
 
 
9.13 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice s Empowerment, in a 
joint initiative with the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, has been implementing the 
‘NAMASTE’ scheme since 2023-24 for the safety and dignity of sanitation workers 
comprising Manual Scavengers, Sewer and Septic Tank Workers. The Department has 
also included waste pickers under the scheme since 2024-25. The Committee are happy 
to note that the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment has also proposed a new 
target group consisting of drain-cleaners, workers at Sewage Treatment Plants and 
Faecal Sludge Treatment Plants during the next financial cycle, i.e., 2026-27 to 2030-31. 
The Committee finds that 89,248 Sewer and Septic Tank Workers and 1,87,120 waste 
pickers have been validated, out of which 87,037 Sewer and Septic Tank Workers and 
7,499 waste pickers have been provided PPE kits. The Committee appreciate the 
measures such as occupational safety training, safety devices, workshops, health 
insurance coverage, etc., taken by the Department since the initiation of the scheme in 
2023-24. However, the Committee are of the opinion that profiling, distribution of PPE kits 
and provision of occupational safety training to all sanitation workers will require greater 
effort, time and funds. The Department of Social Justice and Empowerment should 
therefore expedite the process and lay down a time frame to complete all necessary steps 
for the economic and social welfare of sanitation workers.  
  The Committee also feel that the funds provided under the scheme need to be 
increased, as the Department has already spent 93% of the Revised Estimate for 2025-26, 
therefore, the allocation of ₹110.00 crore made for 2026-27 may not be sufficient to 
complete the tasks undertaken by the Department as a large number of workers are still 
to be provided PPE kits and other benefits. Further, after the inclusion of the new target 
group from 2026-27 under the scheme, the Department may face a shortage of funds. The 
Committee would therefore like the Department to take sufficient steps so that basic 
facilities such as PPE kits, training and health insurance are provided to all workers at 
the earliest, and budget constraints should not become a hurdle, especially when several 
deaths of sewer and septic tank workers are still being reported.

10.9 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment is 
the custodian of civic rights and is responsible for the prevention of atrocities against 
Scheduled Castes. Funds are allocated to the Department for strengthening of machinery 
for enforcement of protection of Civil Rights Act,1955 and Prevention of Atrocities Act 
,1989. The Department has accordingly taken measures over the years for the functioning 
and strengthening of Protection Cells and Special Police Stations as envisaged under 
these Acts. The Committee however find that though almost all States/UTs have set up 
Protection Cells but only 181 Special Police Stations have been established in only 7 
States/UTs. The Committee are shocked to know that even after more than three decades 
of enactment of PoA Act only 7 States/UTs have such police stations. The Committee are 
of the opinion that the setting up of Special Police Stations by the States/UTs is essential 
as victims first approach police station for protection at the time of atrocity and it is 
assumed these police stations would be able to address such situations more effectively.  
The Committee do not find any information regarding setting up of Special Courts also. 
The regular meetings with the State government over the years have also failed to yield 
the desired result. 
The Committee note that the Department has submitted a proposal before the 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) to enhance the relief amounts and provide 
financial support to States for setting up Special Police Stations and Special Courts. The 
Committee hope that the Department should have incorporated the expected increase in 
funds for the year 2026-27 so that there is no shortage of funds to meet the expenditure 
likely to increase with the approval of the proposal. The Committee accordingly desire 
that the Department should take necessary steps to ensure that the proposal is approved 
at the earliest so that it is implemented from 2026-27 itself and the machinery is 
adequately strengthened.

The regular meetings with the State government over the 
years have also failed to yield the desired result. 
The Committee note that the Department has 
submitted a proposal before the Expenditure Finance 
Committee (EFC) to enhance the relief amounts and 
provide financial support to States for setting up Special 
Police Stations and Special Courts. The Committee hope 
that the Department should have incorporated the 
expected increase in funds for the year 2026-27 so that 
there is no shortage of funds to meet the expenditure likely 
to increase with the approval of the proposal. The 
Committee accordingly desire that the Department should 
take necessary steps to ensure that the proposal is 
approved at the earliest so that it is implemented from 
2026-27 itself and the machinery is adequately 
strengthened.

CHAPTER – I 
INTRODUCTORY 
The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) was carved out 
of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on 12 May, 2012 with the objective 
of giving focused attention to policy issues and providing a meaningful thrust to 
activities aimed at the welfare and empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). 
Subsequently, on 8 December, 2014, the Department of Disability Affairs was renamed 
as the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. 
 
1.2 The Department acts as the nodal agency for matters relating to disability and 
persons with disabilities and is responsible for coordinating with various stakeholders 
including Central Ministries, State Governments, Union Territory Administrations and 
voluntary organizations working in the disability sector. The Department is primarily 
entrusted with the task of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. The subjects, 
allocated to the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) as 
per Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules are:- 
i) The following subjects which fall within List I-Union List of the Seventh Schedule 
to the Constitution: 
ii) Indo-US, Indo-UK, Indo-German, Indo-Swiss and Indo-Swedish Agreements for 
Duty-free import of donated relief goods/supplies and matters connected with 
the distribution of such supplies. 
iii)  The following subjects which fall within List-III - Concurrent List of the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution (as regards Legislation only): 
iv)  "Social Security and Social Insurance, save to the extent, allotted to any other 
Department"  
v) For the Union territories, the following subjects which fall in List II -State List or 
List III Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, in so far as 
they exist in regard to such territories:  

2 
 
vi)  "Relief of the Disabled and the unemployable; Social Security and Social 
Insurance, save to the extent allotted to any other Department". 
vii)  To act as the nodal Department for matters pertaining to Disability and Persons 
with Disabilities.  
1.3 The Department also administers important legislations governing different 
aspects of disability for the welfare and empowerment of persons with disabilities. 
These include the following: 
i. The Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 
ii. The National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, 
Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999 
iii. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 
1.4 To discharge its mandate effectively, the Department operates through a network 
of Statutory Bodies, National Institutes, and Public Sector Undertakings: 
Statutory Bodies 
 Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI): Established to regulate and oversee training 
programs for professionals in rehabilitation and special education, maintaining 
the Central Rehabilitation Register (CRR). 
 The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities (CCPD): Set up under 
Section 74(1) of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, to safeguard 
the rights of PwDs and look into complaints regarding the deprivation of such 
rights. 
 The National Trust: An autonomous body discharging legal duties through Local 
Level Committees (LLC) and welfare duties through various schemes for persons 
with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation, and Multiple Disabilities.  
 
 

3 
 
National Institutes (NIs) 
The Department oversees several specialized National Institutes located across the 
country, namely: 
i. Ali Yavar Jung National Institute of Speech and Hearing Disabilities (Divyangjan) 
(AYNISHD), Mumbai 
ii. National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (NIEPID), Secunderabad 
iii. National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Visual Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (NIEPVD), Dehradun 
iv. National Institute of Mental Health Rehabilitation (NIMHR), Sehore, Madhya 
Pradesh 
v. Swami Vivekanand National Institute of Rehabilitation Training and Research 
(SVNIRTAR), Cuttack 
vi. National Institute for Locomotor Disabilities (Divyangjan) (NILD), Kolkata 
vii. Pt. Deendayal Upadhyaya National Institute for Persons with Physical Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (PDUNIPPD), New Delhi 
viii. National Institute for Empowerment of Persons with Multiple Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (NIEPMD), Chennai 
ix. Atal Bihari Vajpayee Center for Disability Sports (CDS), Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh 
x. Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre (ISLRTC), New Delhi. 
 
1.5 In addition to its statutory and research frameworks, the Department exercises 
administrative control over the following Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), 
which are tasked with providing financial assistance and manufacturing high-quality 
rehabilitative aids: 
i. National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corporation (NDFDC) 
ii. Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO), Kanpur

1.7 The Committee sought to ascertain from the Department whether there exists an 
updated and reliable estimate of the population of persons with disabilities in the 
country, particularly in view of the fact that the currently available figures are based on 
the Census of 2011 which is estimated at 2.68 crores and that the scope of recognized 
disabilities has since been expanded under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 

5 
 
(RPwD) Act, 2016. The Department, during the course of evidence before the 
Committee, deposed as under: 
“When we talk about the exact population, the most common data to be harped 
upon is the 2011 census data. At that point in time, the 2011 census data it was 
2.68 cr. But now there are lot many caveats regarding these figures. Firstly, when 
the 2011 census was done, we had PWD Act 1995 in vogue. Our present RPWD 
Act came in vogue in 2016. In 2011, it was PWD Act, 1995 which was 
operational, and that Act mentioned only seven disabilities. Whereas right now, 
since 2016, we are legally recognizing 21 disabilities. That is the first point, there 
are 21 number of disabilities. ******** Now we have again requested the 
Registrar General of India to take into account 21 types of disabilities and to 
consult us whenever they feel like, so that the forthcoming census, whenever the 
results are out, we can rely upon those figures”.  
1.8 The Committee sought to know the mechanism adopted by the Department for 
preparing Budget Estimates in the absence of updated or latest data on the population 
of persons with disabilities. The Committee also desired to know whether the 
Government has any interim mechanism to estimate and track the changing 
demographics of persons with disabilities in the absence of updated census data. In 
reply, the Department submitted as under: 
"The Central Sector schemes being implemented by this Department namely 
SIPDA, DDRS, ADIP and Scholarship are demand driven and funds are disbursed 
based on the proposals received from States/UTs/Institutions/NGOs and 
individuals. The budget estimates are therefore prepared on the basis of previous 
years’ performance and expected demands rather than the population of persons 
with disabilities."  
 
1.9 The Committee note that the presently available estimate of persons 
with disabilities in the country is based on the Census of 2011, which 

6 
 
recorded the number at 2.68 crore. The Committee further note the 
submission made by the representative of the Department during the course 
of evidence that while around 1.35 crore Unique Disability Identity (UDID) 
cards have been issued so far, the Department has also requested the 
Registrar General of India to take into account all the 21 categories of 
disabilities recognized under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) 
Act, 2016 while conducting the forthcoming Census. In this context, the 
Committee recommend that the Department may impress upon the Registrar 
General of India the need to ensure accurate and comprehensive 
enumeration of all categories of disabilities, particularly those disabilities 
which may not visible or have physical symptoms. The Committee are of the 
view that a robust and reliable database, supplemented by the UDID 
framework, would greatly assist in evidence-based policy formulation and 
more effective targeting of welfare schemes for persons with disabilities.

2.3 The Committee sought to know the details of the Budget Estimates proposed by

2.4 On being asked how the Department proposes to meet the gap between the 
estimates, proposed and allocated, the DEPwD submitted as below:-  
“Although the allocation is lower than the proposal submitted by the 
Department, it represents an overall increase of 30.95% over the BE of 2025–26. 
Therefore, in comparison with the BE 2025–26, the Department has received an 
enhanced budget allocation for FY 2026–27. 
The reduction in the proposed BE may be attributed to overall fiscal 
prioritization and resource constraints. The scheme-wise allocations are 
provisional at this stage, as the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) proposals 
for 16th Finance Commission Cycle in respect of the schemes of the Department 
are currently under process. The final scheme-wise allocation will be determined 
after the completion of the EFC appraisal and approval process. 
The Department proposes to meet any shortfall between the proposed 
and approved estimates through the phased implementation of activities, 
wherever feasible; and submission of proposal to the Ministry of Finance at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage for seeking additional funds, if required, based on 
the pace of implementation and actual fund requirement”.  
2.5 The Committee further sought to know whether the enhanced Budget Estimates 
(BE) for the year 2026–27 adequately meet the financial requirements for the effective 
implementation of various schemes of the Department. In their written replies the 
Department has submitted that: 

12 
 
“The Budget Estimate (BE) 2026–27 has been enhanced by 30.95% as compared 
to the previous year, keeping in view the expanding scope of activities, 
introduction of new schemes, and the need for strengthening implementation of 
ongoing schemes. Further the enhanced BE has been formulated after Review of 
past expenditure trends (including BE/RE 2025–26), Assessment of committed 
liabilities and spill-over components, Projection of physical and financial targets 
under each scheme, Provision for newly announced schemes and expansion of 
coverage. The enhanced allocation is assessed to be adequate for effective 
implementation of the Department’s programmes during 2026–27”.  
2.6 On being enquired as to what specific steps are proposed by the Department to 
improve the lives of persons with disability during the year 2026–27. In response, the 
Department submitted as under: 
a) Strengthened Financial Planning & Monitoring: Preparation of Quarterly 
Expenditure Plans (QEPs) and Monthly Expenditure Plans (MEPs). 
b) Regular review meetings with States/UTs/Organizations to monitor 
physical and financial progress. 
c) Close monitoring of pending utilization certificates (UCs) to ensure timely 
release of subsequent installments. 
d) Timely sanction and release of funds to implementing agencies. 
e) Digital Monitoring & Transparency through UDID portal, NSP Portal, 
ARJUN MIS Portal etc. 
f) Focused monitoring of implementation of schemes in North-Eastern 
Region (NER) and aspirational districts.  
2.7 Regarding the thrust areas of the Annual Plan for the year 2026–27 and the 
roadmap for the implementation of the said Annual Plan, the Department submitted the 
following details: 
“The thrust areas of the Annual Plan 2026–27 of the Department of 
Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities are focused on strengthening 

13 
 
inclusion, accessibility, rehabilitation, skill development and social 
empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). The major priority 
areas include continuation and expansion of ongoing flagship programmes 
and infrastructure development initiatives. 
The Department is implementing various Central Sector schemes such as 
SIPDA, DDRS, ADIP and Scholarship Schemes, which are demand-driven 
in nature. Funds are released to implementing agencies based on 
proposals received from States/UTs, institutions, NGOs and individual 
beneficiaries. The roadmap includes: 
a) Strengthening coordination with States/UTs/ implementing 
agencies/NGOs/other bodies for timely submission and approval of 
proposals; 
b) Regular review meetings with States/UTs and stakeholders to monitor 
progress and resolve bottlenecks; 
c) Capacity building and awareness programmes for effective outreach; and 
d) Periodic evaluation and outcome-based monitoring of schemes”.  
 
2.8 In response to a query regarding the criteria adopted by the Department for 
allocation of funds across various schemes under its purview and the methodology 
followed for fixing physical targets for implementation of these schemes so as to ensure 
effective utilization of resources and achievement of intended objectives, the 
Department submitted as under: 
“The Budget Estimates in respect of the Central Sector Schemes of the 
Department namely ADIP, SIPDA, DDRS and Scholarship have been broadly 
recommended by the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) upto 31.03.2026. All 
the four schemes are appraised and approved with financial allocation and 
physical targets for the entire period of the ongoing 15th Finance Commission’s 
recommendations. Along with EFC recommendation, past expenditure trends are 

14 
 
also taken into consideration while allocating budget outlays under these 
schemes. 
Based on the previous year’s actual expenditure, achievement of physical targets 
and EFC approved allocations, the physical targets are fixed for individual 
schemes. However, in case of additional demands under schemes, the targets 
are revised on the basis of demand for aids and assistive devices, camp requests 
of VIPs, number of scholarship claims received on NSP Portal and proposals from 
Statement Government/ training partners”.  
2.9 On observing that the Actual Expenditure in the past several years fell short of 
the Revised Estimates, which themselves had been reduced from the Budget Estimates, 
the Committee sought to know whether any assessment of past shortcomings had been 
undertaken by the Department to ensure more effective utilization of funds and 
improved outcomes under its schemes. In reply, the Department submitted as under:  
The key shortcomings identified in previous years include: 
a) Under-utilization of funds in initial quarters leading to expenditure 
concentration in the last quarter. 
b) Delay in submission of Utilization Certificates (UCs) by 
States/UTs/implementing agencies, affecting timely release of subsequent 
instalments. 
c) Late receipt of proposals from States/UTs/other implementing agencies 
d) Procedural delays in release of funds due to issues concerning onboarding 
of States/UTs/ organization to TSA-Hybrid Model. 
2.10 The Department has informed that the following the ameliorative steps or new 
initiatives are being taken by the Department to improve the utilization of fund 
allocations and program execution during the year 2026–27. In reply, the Department 
submitted as under: 

15 
 
(a)   The department regularly reviews the schemes guidelines to simply the 
procedure for release of funds. 
(b)   Regular Review Meetings with States/UTs/ implementing agencies 
(c)   All the Schemes of the Department onboarded on TSA-Hybrid Model”. 
2.11 The Committee find that in the past few years the Actual Expenditure 
of the Department has consistently fallen short of the Revised Estimates. In 
2023–24, against the Revised Estimates of ₹1225.01 crore, the Actual 
Expenditure stood at ₹1143.89 crore (about 93.37 per cent). Similarly, in 
2024–25, against the Revised Estimates of ₹1167.27 crore, the Actual 
Expenditure was ₹1112.61 crore (about 95.32 per cent). In the current 
financial year 2025–26, the Actual Expenditure as on 26.02.2026 is ₹1008.49 
crore against the Revised Estimates of ₹1291.60 crore, which is only about 
78 per cent of the Revised Estimates. The Committee are of the view that 
such gaps between allocations and actual expenditure point to structural 
issues in planning, timely receipt of proposals, and coordination with 
implementing agencies. While the Department has indicated certain 
administrative constraints such as delay in submission of Utilization 
Certificates and late receipt of proposals from States/UTs, the Committee 
feel that these issues require a more systematic and proactive approach.   
 The Committee therefore recommend that the Department strengthen 
its expenditure management framework by instituting a more rigorous 
system of quarterly expenditure targets, real-time monitoring of fund 
utilisation, and advance identification of implementable proposals from 
States/UTs and implementing agencies. The Committee also urge the 
Department to establish strict timelines for submission of Utilization 
Certificates and proposals, and to introduce digital tracking mechanisms and 
periodic review meetings with States/UTs to ensure that procedural delays 
do not hinder timely release and utilisation of funds. The Committee are of 

16 
 
the firm view that such measures would help prevent concentration of 
expenditure in the last quarter of the financial year and ensure that the 
funds allocated translate into tangible and timely benefits for persons with 
disabilities. 
2.12 The Committee note that the major share of the Department’s scheme 
expenditure is concentrated in a few key demand-driven schemes such as 
ADIP, SIPDA, DDRS and the Scholarship Schemes, which together accounted 
for ₹741.80 crore in BE 2025–26 and have been allocated ₹1117.00 crore in 
BE 2026–27. The Committee observe that the effectiveness of these schemes 
depends significantly on timely submission of proposals, completion of 
documentation and submission of Utilization Certificates by States/UTs and 
implementing agencies. However, delays in these processes have been cited 
by the Department itself as major reasons for under-utilisation of funds in 
previous years The Committee therefore recommend that the Department 
put in place a structured mechanism for advance planning of proposals, 
periodic engagement with State Governments and implementing agencies, 
and a streamlined process for verification of documentation so that funds 
earmarked under these major schemes are released and utilised in a timely 
manner. The Committee further recommend that the Department may 
strengthen the monitoring system for tracking proposals, approvals and fund 
releases under each scheme, thereby ensuring greater transparency and 
efficiency in implementation. 
2.13 The Committee note that the Budget Estimates for the year 2026–27 
have been significantly enhanced to ₹1669.72 crore, reflecting an increase of 
about 30.96 per cent over the Budget Estimates of ₹1275.00 crore for the 
year 2025–26. While welcoming the enhanced allocation, the Committee 
emphasise that the increased outlay must lead to measurable improvements 
in service delivery and outreach to persons with disabilities. The Committee 
therefore recommend that the Department adopt a more outcome-oriented 

17 
 
approach in implementation of its schemes, with clearly defined physical 
targets, periodic evaluation of progress and stronger monitoring of 
implementation across States and Union Territories. The Committee also 
urge the Department to prioritise expansion of assistive device distribution, 
rehabilitation services, scholarships and skill development programmes, 
particularly in the North-Eastern Region and aspirational districts. The 
Committee are of the view that such targeted and outcome-focused 
utilisation of the enhanced allocation will ensure that the increased 
budgetary support translates into meaningful and tangible benefits for 
persons with disabilities across the country.

CHAPTER-III 
 
ASSISTANCE TO PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES FOR PURCHASE/FITTING  
OF AIDS/APPLIANCES (ADIP) 
 
 The Scheme of Assistance to Persons with Disabilities for Purchase/Fitting of Aids 
/Appliances (ADIP Scheme), launched in 1981 by the Government of India, aims to 
empower persons with disabilities (PwDs) by supplying scientifically manufactured, 
durable, modern, and cost effective aids and assistive devices that promote their 
physical, social and psychological rehabilitation, reduce the effects of disabilities, and 
enhance beneficiaries’ educational and economic potential. The Scheme was last revised 
w.e.f. 26.09.2024 and the major modifications undertaken are as under: 
a) “Since, ADIP is 100% central Sector Scheme, the requirement of State 
Government recommendations has been removed for receiving proposals. 
b) Data of assessment of beneficiaries and distribution of aids & assistive 
devices has been made mandatory through ARJUN Portal. Also beneficiaries 
can register themselves on the ARJUN Portal for requisite aids and appliance. 
ARJUN Portal is developed and maintained by ALIMCO, a CPSE under this 
Department ensures proper implementation and monitoring of the Scheme. 
c) The Department has taken a major step of opening Pradhan Mantri Divyasha 
Kendra (PMDK) of ALIMCO. These PMDKs are the walk-in centres where 
eligible beneficiary can directly avail required aids and appliances free of cost 
by visiting these centers.  
d) Eligibility of high-end Prosthesis has been reduced from 80% disability to 
40% disability. 
e) Under ADIP SSA eligibility for Motorized Tricycle has been relaxed 80% 
disability to 40% disability. 

19 
 
f) Benefits of ADIP SSA has also been extended to students studying through 
home Schooling and Special Schools. 
g) Age of Children criteria for availing aids and assistive devices every one year 
has been increased from 12 years to 18 years for customized items. 
h) Provision for self-certification of income by beneficiaries themselves has been 
introduced. 
i) In case of amputees without any disability certificate may also be provided 
with the benefit of Artificial Limbs only after the recommendation of P&O 
officials of ALIMCO/NIs/CRCs and enrolment for UDID Card. 
j) Inclusion of Motorized Tricycle with Li-Iron-Phosphate batteries in ADIP 
scheme with subsidy up to Rs 50,000.00 in line with recent advancement and 
towards green environment.  
k) Inclusion of Folding Joystick wheelchair in ADIP scheme with subsidy up to 
₹50,000/- 
l) Inclusion of Active Folding Wheelchair in ADIP scheme for high activity 
Divyangjan.”  
3.2 The Committee desired to know the thrust areas under the ADIP Scheme and the 
action plan proposed for the year 2026–27, particularly when the proposed 
modifications to the Scheme are awaiting approval of the Expenditure Finance 
Committee (EFC). In reply, the Department submitted as under: 
“Implementation of the ADIP Scheme shall continue as per the existing approved 
guidelines until the proposed modifications receive approval from the 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) for next cycle. The thrust areas of the 
Scheme include strengthening outreach and service delivery through 
establishment of Pradhan Mantri Divyasha-Vayoshri Kendra (PMD-VK Centres) 
across districts in coordination with Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of 
India (ALIMCO) to provide aids and assistive devices to walk-in Divyangjan, 
thereby enhancing last-mile delivery. The Scheme also focuses on organizing 
identification and distribution camps in remote regions, Aspirational Blocks, and 

20 
 
other unserved or underserved areas to ensure wider and equitable coverage. 
Further, emphasis is being placed on inclusion of modern, technologically 
advanced and high-end assistive devices to improve functionality and overall 
quality of life of beneficiaries. Transparency and accountability are being 
reinforced through beneficiary authentication and real-time monitoring via the 
ARJUN Portal.”  
3.3 The Committee further sought to know the reasons for revision of the Scheme in 
2022 and 2024 and the extent to which these revisions have been effective in serving 
the interests of Divyangjan. In reply, the Department submitted as under: 
“The 14th Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) cycle was completed in 2020. 
With the objective of expanding outreach, enhancing user-friendliness, and 
ensuring distribution of improved quality aids and assistive devices, the ADIP 
Scheme was subsequently revised in 2022 and again in 2024. 
The impact of these revisions has been significant. Since simplification of the 
Scheme w.e.f. 26.09.2024, a total of 3,92,638 beneficiaries have been covered. 
Out of these, 4,457 Divyangjan have been provided high-end prostheses. 
Additionally, advanced mobility devices such as motorized tricycles, motorized 
tricycles with Li-Ion batteries, joystick-operated wheelchairs (including non-
folding variants) have been provided to 40,081 Divyangjan under the ADIP 
Scheme. Out of these, 568 Motorized Tricycles has been distributed under ADIP-
SSA (Sarva Siksha Abhiyan). These measures have enhanced accessibility, 
expanded coverage of advanced assistive devices, and strengthened service 
delivery in the interest of Divyangjan.”  
3.4 The Department has implemented significant policy revisions in 2022 and 2024 
and the Budget Estimates for the Scheme have remained largely stagnant. 
Consequently, on being sought to provide a detailed clarification on the fiscal 
mechanisms employed by the Department to accommodate the resultant financial 

21 
 
implications within these existing budgetary constraints, the Department submitted as 
under: 
“The changes introduced in 2022 were necessitated by factors such as escalation 
in the cost of raw materials, recommendations of the Standing Committee 
regarding providing 100% subsidy for Motorized Tricycles, and the need to 
incorporate high-end devices to keep pace with evolving assistive technologies. 
These revisions, which had financial implications, were considered and 
accommodated during the 15th Finance Commission (EFC) cycle i.e. from 
01.04.2021 to 2025-26. 
However, the subsequent modifications carried out in 2024 were primarily 
procedural and aimed at simplifying the Scheme and improving ease of access 
and implementation. These changes did not entail any additional financial 
implications and were managed within the existing Budget Estimates.”

3.16 The Committee find that while the financial allocation under the 
Assistance to Persons with Disabilities for Purchase/Fitting of Aids and

₹375.00 crore in BE 2026–27, the physical coverage of beneficiaries has

against a target of 2.15 lakh in 2023–24, the achievement declined to 2.51 
lakh against a target of 3.15 lakh in 2024–25, and 1.91 lakh beneficiaries 
have been covered so far in 2025–26 against a target of 2.05 lakh. The 
Committee note that the increasing provision of technologically advanced 
assistive devices has led to higher per-unit costs, which has moderated 
overall coverage. While appreciating the emphasis on improved quality of 
assistive devices, the Committee recommend that the Department maintain 
an appropriate balance between provision of advanced technologies and 
wider beneficiary coverage. The Committee further note that with 21 
categories of disabilities recognised under the RPwD Act, 2016, the demand 
for assistive technologies is likely to increase. Accordingly, as the 
Department enters the 16th Finance Commission cycle (2026–2031), the 
Committee recommend that the Department must present a realistic and 
adequately assessed fiscal requirement before the Ministry of Finance so that 
eligible Divyangjan are not deprived of assistive aids due to financial 
constraints. 
3.17 The Committee further recommend that the Department undertake 
periodic assessment of device-wise demand and cost structures and 
rationalise the mix of assistive devices provided under the Scheme so as to 
optimise utilisation of available resources and ensure wider outreach of 
essential assistive aids while facilitating access to advanced devices where 
required. The Department may also explore additional funding avenues, 
including leveraging the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds of 
CPSUs and private entities, specifically to bridge the funding gap for 

28 
 
expensive devices so that the primary budgetary outlay can maintain a wider 
net of beneficiaries. 
3.18 The Committee take note of the Department’s major initiative to 
establish Pradhan Mantri Divyasha Kendras (PMDKs) as permanent walk-in 
centers to facilitate direct access to aids and appliances. The Committee 
welcome this move to supplement the traditional camp-based model, and 
further recommend that the Department should also prioritize the expansion 
of PMDKs in Aspirational Blocks, remote regions and under-served areas to 
ensure that "walk-in" access is not a privilege limited to urban centers 
Furthermore, these Kendras should be equipped to provide minor repair and 
maintenance services for sophisticated devices, ensuring the long-term 
functionality of the equipment provided. The Committee suggest that the 
Department set a clear timeline for the conversion of all temporary 
distribution points into permanent, full-service PMDKs to ensure sustained 
last-mile delivery. 
3.19 The Committee note that the requirement of obtaining 
recommendations from the State Governments for proposals submitted by 
implementing agencies has been removed with a view to simplifying 
procedures and reducing delays in release of assistance under the Scheme. 
While the Committee appreciate the objective of expediting implementation, 
they are of the view that the removal of this layer of scrutiny may require 
stronger institutional safeguards to ensure transparency and accountability 
in the selection and functioning of implementing agencies. The Committee, 
therefore, recommend that the Department strengthen its due diligence, 
monitoring and audit mechanisms, including periodic review of implementing 
agencies and greater reliance on digital platforms such as the ARJUN portal, 
so that timely delivery of assistive devices is ensured without compromising 
oversight and accountability. 
 

29 
 
3.20  The Committee note that awareness activities are being undertaken 
under the Awareness Generation and Publicity (AGP) component as well as 
through initiatives such as Purple Fest and Divya Kala Melas. The Committee 
recommend that the Department further strengthen its outreach through 
greater use of digital platforms, social media and targeted publicity 
campaigns, so that information about schemes and services for Divyangjan 
reaches a wider section of potential beneficiaries across the country.
