CHAPTER-IV 
DEENDAYAL DIVYANGJAN REHABILITATION SCHEME (DDRS) 
 
  The Deendayal Divyangjan Rehabilitation Scheme is a central sector scheme of 
the Department to provide grant-in-aid to non-governmental organizations (NGOs) for 
projects relating to rehabilitation of persons with disabilities aimed at enabling them to 
reach and maintain their optimal, physical, sensory, intellectual, psychiatric or socio-
functional levels.  
4.2  The Grant-in-aid is provided to Implementing agencies (IAs) which are registered 
with NGO-Darpan Portal of NITI Aayog and have obtained unique ID of NITI Aayog. 
The Grant-in-Aid (GIA) is provided through e-Anudaan portal of the Department. All 
financial assistance is provided to the Implementing agencies through Public Financial 
Management System (PFMS).  
There are eight model projects under the DDRS Scheme.  
i. Cross Disability Pre-Schools and Early Intervention with option for Home 
Based Rehabilitation & Community-Based Rehabilitation Project  
ii. Special School for the Children with Hearing Disability with option for 
Home Based Rehabilitation & Community-Based Rehabilitation Project  
iii. Special School for the children with Visual Disability (including Deaf 
blindness) with option for Home Based Rehabilitation and Community 
Based Rehabilitation Project and Low Vision Centre Project. 
iv. Special School for the children with other disabilities (ID/CP/ASD/MD/ 
Muscular Dystrophy, Deaf blindness etc.) with option for Home Based 
Rehabilitation and Community-Based Rehabilitation Project. 
v. Rehabilitation of Leprosy Cured Persons with option for Home-Based 
Rehabilitation & Community-Based Rehabilitation Project. 

31 
 
vi. Half Way Home for Psycho-Social Rehabilitation of Treated and Controlled 
individuals with Mental Illness with option for Home-Based Rehabilitation 
& Community-Based Rehabilitation Project vii. Preparatory / Remediation 
Centre for Children with Specific Learning Disabilities to continue Inclusive 
Education Project. 
vii. Cross-Disability Therapy and Counseling Centre Project. 
Activities/components admissible for grant under DDRS include:  
Honorarium to staff, Transportation of beneficiaries, Stipend for 
beneficiaries/hostel maintenance Cost of raw materials, and Contingencies to 
meet office expenses, electricity & water charges, rent, furniture, equipment etc.  
The eligibility conditions for Grants under DDRS are as under:  
Organizations registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (XXI of 1860) 
or any relevant Act of the State/Union Territory; or A Trust registered under the 
Indian Trust Act, 1882 or any other similar Act for the time being in force; or, A 
Not-for-Profit company registered under Companies Act, 2013 or any relevant Act 
for the time being in force. 
Registration should have been in force for at least 2 years at the time of applying 
for grant under this scheme.  
a. Must be registered in the NITI Aayog Portal (NGO-Darpan) Portal and 
obtain Unique ID of NGO-Darpan before applying for Grant under the 
scheme.  
b. Must be registered either under erstwhile Persons with Disabilities Act, 
1995 or Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
 4.3  The scheme has been revised and is effective from 1st October 2024, with no 
changes to the cost norms. The key highlights of the revised scheme, in comparison to 
the previous version, are as follows:-  

32 
 
a. If the organization has not received the full and final GIA of the previous year 
due to pending proposal at the end of the Department and an advance 
proposal of the current year has been received, then the GIA up to 25 % of 
amount released for the previous to previous year may be released to the 
PIAs as advance GIA, so that the functioning of the organization does not 
come to a standstill. 
b.  In case of projects being run by the institutions/Autonomous bodies of the 
Government or Armed forces, the proposal can be submitted by the 
concerned Head of the Institution directly to the DEPwD. 
c. PIAs can avail additional grants from any sources like state governments, CSR 
etc as supplementary to the funding given by the GoI in order to provide 
basic minimum wages or additional services/activities or additional 
equipments, so that PIAs can provide the rehabilitation services to PwDs 
smoothly. This will be over and above the funding norms of the GoI.  
4.4  District Disability Rehabilitation Centre (DDRC)  
The DDRC Scheme is a sub-component of the DDRS scheme. Main functions of DDRCs 
include Early Identification and Intervention, awareness generation, assessment of 
need/provision/fitment of assistive devices, therapeutic services e.g. Physiotherapy, 
Occupational Therapy, Speech Therapy, etc., referral and arrangement of surgical 
correction, assistance in providing scholarships, skill training, arrangement of loans for 
self-employment, survey & identification of persons with disabilities through camp 
approach, assisting in the issue of UDID Cards, and to act as outreach centres for the 
services provided by the National Institutes and for promoting barrier free environment. 
Revised scheme is effect from 01.04.2023.  
Regarding the steps taken for better implementation of the scheme, the DEPwD have

information and communication ecosystems and upholds their independence and 
dignity.

The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) is 
implementing the Central Sector Umbrella Scheme of Scholarship for Students with 
Disabilities.  The main objectives of these scholarship schemes are to 
empower students with disabilities to study further in order to prepare themselves for 
earning their livelihood and  find a dignified place for themselves in the society, as they 
face several barriers-physical, financial, psychological in pursuing studies and living a 
dignified life. 
7.2  The scheme consists of the following six components :- 
a) Pre-matric (for classes IX and X). 
b)  Post-matric (for classes XI to postgraduate degree/diploma). 
c) Higher education (for undergraduate and postgraduate degree/diploma in 
notified institutions of excellence in education). 
d) National Fellowship (for M.Phil and Ph.D. in Indian universities). 
e) National Overseas Scholarship (for postgraduate degree/doctorate from foreign 
universities). 
f) Free coaching (for government recruitment examinations and entrance 
examinations to technical and professional courses).  
7.3  Regarding the eligibility criteria for scholarship it has been stated as under : 
a) The scholarships are open only to Indian nationals.  
b) All the components of scholarships are open to students with benchmark 
disability i.e. 40% or more disability as defined in ‘Rights of Persons with 
Disabilities Act, 2016

entitled to receive benefits of the scheme. In case the second child is a twin,

d) Scholarship for studying in any class will be available for only one year.  If a 
student has to repeat a class, she/he would not get scholarship for that class

7.10  The Committee find that the financial allocation under the Scholarship 
Scheme for Students with Disabilities has remained largely stable during the 
period under review, with the Budget Estimates ranging between ₹142.68 
crore and ₹155.00 crore during 2023–24 to 2026–27. However, the 
Committee observe that the physical achievement under the Scheme has 
consistently fallen short of the prescribed targets. Against a target of 43,520 
beneficiaries, only 29,374 beneficiaries were covered in 2023–24 (about 67.5 
per cent) and 23,085 beneficiaries in 2024–25 (about 53 per cent). Similarly, 
17,378 beneficiaries have been covered so far in 2025–26, indicating a 
continuing gap between the intended outreach and actual coverage. The 
Committee note the Department’s explanation that stricter verification 

65 
 
through e-KYC authentication, UDID linkage and the National Scholarship 
Portal has led to elimination of duplicate or ineligible applications. While 
appreciating the steps taken to improve transparency in the system, the 
Committee recommend that the Department intensify awareness campaigns, 
coordination with States/UTs and monitoring of pendency at the State Nodal 
Officer level, so that a larger number of eligible students with disabilities are 
able to access the benefits of the Scheme. 
7.11  The Committee note the Department’s proposal to introduce a uniform 
lump-sum scholarship structure for certain components of the Scheme from 
the next EFC cycle (2026–27 onwards) with the objective of simplifying 
calculations and expediting disbursement. The Committee also note that 
delays in verification and processing at various stages, particularly due to 
pendency of applications and prolonged scrutiny at the level of State Nodal 
Officers, have adversely affected the timely release of scholarships in several 
cases. The Committee are of the view that scholarships constitute a critical 
support mechanism enabling students with disabilities to pursue education 
without financial hardship. The Committee therefore recommend that while 
finalising the revised framework, the Department ensure that the scholarship 
amounts remain adequate to meet actual educational expenses and that 
appropriate mechanisms are put in place to minimise processing delays at 
the State level, so that the simplified disbursement system results in faster 
and more predictable release of funds to eligible beneficiaries.

9.9  The Committee note that the National Institutes and Composite Regional 
Centres (CRCs) play a crucial role in human resource development, research

being extended through the SIPDA component on priority areas of disability.

increasingly function as centres of excellence in research, innovation and 
assistive technology development. The Committee therefore recommend that

that indigenous assistive technologies, rehabilitation tools and evidence-

CHAPTER-X 
NEW SCHEMES INTRODUCED IN THE YEAR 2026–27 
 
The Department has introduced two new schemes during the year 2026–27, namely 
Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana and Divyangjan Sahara Yojana, with allocations of ₹200 
crore and ₹100 crore respectively.  
Objectives of the Schemes 
The Department in their written have stated that Divyangjan Sahara Yojana is a newly 
introduced scheme during FY 2026-27 aimed at strengthening the assistive device 
ecosystem for Persons with Disabilities (Divyangjan) through enhanced provisioning of 
high-quality assistive aids and appliances, including modern and advanced assistive 
technologies. The Scheme will be implemented through ALIMCO a CPSE under this 
Department. The proposal is under consultation stage with Stakeholders However, the 
objective proposed by ALIMCO is as under: 
(i) Scaling up ALIMCO Manufacturing and R&D Capacity: With the 
increased demand for high-end assistive devices under the scheme, 
scaling up ALIMCO’s manufacturing capacity is essential to ensure timely 
production and supply.

CHAPTER-XI 
 
MONITORING MECHANISM 
The Department implements a number of schemes involving substantial financial 
outlays for the welfare and empowerment of persons with disabilities. In this context, 
effective monitoring and oversight mechanisms assume importance to ensure that funds 
released under various schemes are properly utilized and that the intended objectives of 
the schemes are achieved. 
11.2  In this regard, the Committee sought to know the monitoring mechanism put in 
place by the Department to prevent misuse of funds and to ensure optimal utilization of 
financial resources under its various schemes. The Committee also sought to know how 
effective these mechanisms have been in actual practice. In reply, the Department 
submitted as under: 
 The monitoring mechanism in the Department to prevent misuse of funds and to 
ensure optimal utilization of financial resources to achieve the intended objectives of 
various schemes  
is given below: 
a. Monitoring of the Scheme is undertaken regularly at the level of the Secretary 
(DEPwD). 
b. The organizations have to furnish an audited utilization certificate in time in 
respect of the previous grant (s).   
c. Implementing agencies are required to maintain an updated official website and 
upload complete details of beneficiaries, including particulars of aids and assistive 
devices distributed, on their website as well as on the ARJUN Portal. 
d. Proposals of NGOs are being received and processed online on e-Anudaan Portal. 
e. Mandatory Registration of NGOs on NITI Aayog Portal (NGO Darpan). 

81 
 
f. ‘Arjun Portal facilitates near real-time Monitoring of beneficiary data and also 
prevent & check duplication of beneficiaries. The Implementing Agencies have to 
mandatorily upload the data of beneficiaries on ARJUN Portal. Further, duplicacy is 
also checked through UDID card which has been mandatory for beneficiary. 
g. Sample checking of beneficiaries against the utilisation of Grant-in-Aid released 
to Implementing Agencies by nearest NI/CRC/ALIMCO or by the Department of 
Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities if required. Sample Checking covers at 
least 2% of aids & assistive devices provided to the beneficiaries. 
i. Periodic field inspections and sample checks by the Central Monitoring Unit(CPMU) 
team are conducted to verify distribution of aids and appliances and beneficiary 
coverage. 
j. The regular follow ups are made with States/UTs for submission of pending 
utilization certificates (UCs) by writing letters, Video Conferencing (VCs) and 
telephonic correspondences so that any proposal with complete documents might 
not be kept on hold for want of pending UCs. Due to these efforts, the pending UCs 
have been reduced. 
k. Under Pre Matric, Post Matric & Top class Education, the Department monitors the 
times lines of verification of applications, application status and through the NSP 
portal on regular basis for proactive intervention if bottlenecks are identified. 
l. National Fellowship for PwDs in implemented through DEPwD and disbursement 
through Canara Bank on DBT Mode. NDFDC has been nominated as Implementing 
Agency and CNA for smooth implementation of NFPwD Scheme. Further, 
m. National Overseas Scholarship, the scheme is implemented by DEPwD and 
disbursement through MEA and the Department ensures that scholarship funds are 
disbursed in a timely manner and effectively utilized, enabling PwD students to 
pursue their education abroad without financial barriers or delays.  

82 
 
 11.3  Replying to the queries on the challenges faced in the execution and monitoring 
of the schemes implemented through State Governments/UT Administrations, Non-
Governmental Organizations and other agencies, and the measures being adopted to 
overcome these constraints the Department has furnished the following details: 
ADIP Scheme: Under the ADIP Scheme, certain operational challenges are 
experienced due to its implementation through multiple agencies such as 
NGOs/National Institutes/CRCs and ALIMCO. These include delays in 
submission of proposal for grants in aid, Utilization Certificates, difficulty in 
organizing distribution camps in remote areas/hilly areas, and ensuring 
timely and accurate uploading of beneficiary data due to high-speed 
internet facility. 
To address these issues, the Department has strengthened digital 
monitoring through UDID card, the ARJUN and e-Anudaan portals, 
mandated NGO Darpan registration, enforced submission of audited UCs 
before release of further grants, and undertaken periodic reviews and 
sample verifications through NIs/CRCs/ALIMCO. These measures have 
improved transparency, streamlined fund flow, and enhanced accountability 
in execution of the Scheme. 
SIPDA Scheme: Owing to the demand driven nature of the Creation of 
Barrier Free Environment (CBFE) component, fund disbursement is 
constrained by the actual demand from State Governments, the timely 
submission of appropriate proposals and documentation, and the receipt of 
Utilization Certificates from implementing agencies. This demand-driven 
nature presents a distinctive challenge in target-setting and budgetary 
projections, as allocations cannot be pre-determined independent of 
demonstrated state engagement and proposal quality. Estimates and 
targets for the CBFE/AIC component shall be recalibrated at the beginning 
of each financial year based on historical expenditure trends and 

83 
 
demonstrated state absorptive capacity recognizing the inherent constraints 
of demand-driven disbursement. The Department recognizes that rigid 
allocation and fixed target-setting methodologies have created persistent 
mismatches between budgetary projections and actual utilization; 
consequently, Revised Estimates shall be arrived based on the 
implementable commitments within the financial year, ensuring alignment 
between allocations and achievable outcomes given the demand-driven 
nature of the scheme. The Department commits to demonstrating sustained 
improvement in fund utilization through reduced proposal-to-sanction 
timelines, timely UC submissions, accelerated project completion rates, and 
enhanced state participation, with measurable progress being periodically 
reviewed to ensure accountability in advancing accessibility objectives 
across all government buildings in all states and UTs under the increasingly 
integrated and data-driven implementation framework. 
Scholarships: The Department is not facing any challenges/constraints in 
execution and monitoring of the Schemes. However, the scholarship scheme 
is a Central Sector Scheme and implemented pan India basis and is a 
demand-driven scheme. To cover all area across the country, the 
Department publishes advertisements in leading Newspapers across the 
country twice to increase awareness of these schemes amongst students 
and other stakeholders All other types of media and social media platforms 
are also used for spreading awareness. The Chief Secretaries/Principal 
Secretaries of the States are also addressed to spread awareness of the 
schemes through various mediums of communication in their respective 
States/UTs. Also, the department is actively organizing meetings with State 
Nodal Officers (SNOs) to ensure effective implementation of the schemes. 
 
 

84 
 
11.4 The Committee find that the Department has put in place several 
monitoring mechanisms such as ARJUN Portal, e-Anudaan, UDID integration, 
NGO-Darpan registration, field inspections and periodic review at the level of 
Secretary (DEPwD) to ensure transparency and proper utilisation of funds. 
However, the Committee also note that implementation of several schemes 
continue to face operational challenges such as delays in submission of 
proposals and utilisation certificates by implementing agencies, gaps in 
timely uploading of beneficiary data and logistical constraints in conducting 
camps and outreach activities in remote and hilly areas. The Committee are 
of the view that such procedural bottlenecks weaken the efficiency of 
otherwise well-designed monitoring systems. The Committee therefore 
recommend that the Department institutionalise a time-bound compliance 
framework for implementing agencies, strengthen digital integration of 
monitoring platforms such as ARJUN, UDID and e-Anudaan, and establish a 
structured follow-up mechanism with States/UTs and implementing agencies 
so that delays in documentation, reporting and fund utilisation are minimized 
and scheme benefits reach beneficiaries in a timely manner. 
11.5  The Committee note that several schemes of the Department, 
particularly ADIP and SIPDA, are implemented through a large network of 
States/UTs, NGOs, National Institutes, CRCs and other agencies, which poses 
inherent challenges in ensuring uniform standards of implementation and 
monitoring. The Committee further observe that issues such as delayed 
proposals, weak absorptive capacity at the State level, pending utilisation 
certificates and infrastructure or connectivity constraints in certain regions 
continue to affect the pace of scheme implementation. The Committee are of 
the view that addressing these structural constraints requires stronger 
institutional coordination and capacity building. The Committee therefore 
recommend that the Department develop a comprehensive monitoring and 
capacity-building framework for implementing agencies, including regular 

85 
 
performance reviews, targeted training for State and NGO partners, and a 
robust data-driven dashboard for real-time tracking of scheme 
implementation. Such measures would help improve accountability, 
strengthen implementation capacity across States/UTs and ensure that 
public funds allocated for the welfare of persons with disabilities are utilised 
efficiently and deliver measurable outcomes.

agencies. While the Department has indicated certain 
administrative constraints such as delay in submission

streamline processing through the e-Anudaan portal 
and digital verification mechanisms, the Committee 
recommend that the Department further simplify 
procedural requirements and strengthen coordination 
with implementing agencies so that proposals are 
submitted in a timely manner and funds are released 
without avoidable delays, thereby ensuring smoother 
utilisation of funds and more effective delivery of 

97 
 
rehabilitation services to persons with disabilities. 
11. 4.19 The Committee are concerned to find that several 
States and Union Territories currently do not have 
projects under the DDRS or functioning District 
Disability Rehabilitation Centres (DDRCs). The 
Committee are of the view that the absence of such 
facilities may limit access to rehabilitation services for 
persons with disabilities in these regions. The 
Committee therefore recommend that the Department 
take proactive steps, in coordination with State 
Governments, local bodies and credible voluntary 
organisations, to promote establishment of DDRS 
projects and DDRCs in such underserved areas. The 
peoples representatives should also be involved to 
generate awareness and better implementation of the 
scheme. Focused outreach and facilitation in these 
regions would help ensure more equitable availability 
of rehabilitation services across the country and 
enable a larger number of Divyangjan to benefit from 
the Scheme. 
12. 5.7 The Committee note that the budgetary allocation and 
expenditure under the Scheme for Implementation of 
the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 
(SIPDA) have shown significant volatility during the 
last 3 financial years While the Budget Estimates of 
₹150.00 crore in 2023–24 were reduced sharply to 
₹67.00 crore at the Revised Estimates stage, in 2025–
26 the allocation was enhanced from ₹115.10 crore to 
₹200.00 crore, indicating considerable fluctuation in 
financial planning. The Committee further note that in 
2024–25 the Actual Expenditure stood at ₹44.16 crore 
against the Revised Estimates of ₹111.00 crore, 
reflecting utilisation of less than 40 per cent of the 
available allocation. The Committee are of the view 
that such instability and under-utilisation under an 
umbrella scheme meant for implementing statutory 
obligations under the RPwD Act, 2016 may adversely 

98 
 
affect the continuity of key interventions relating to 
accessibility, skill development and UDID 
implementation. The Committee therefore recommend 
that the Department adopt more realistic budgeting 
and stronger advance appraisal of proposals, along 
with closer monitoring of utilisation certificates and 
project readiness at the State/UT level, so that 
allocations under SIPDA are utilised in a timely and 
effective manner. 
13. 5.8 The Committee observe that actual expenditure under 
SIPDA has frequently fallen short of the allocated 
funds, with the Department attributing these shortfalls 
to transitions in the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) and 
Treasury Single Account (TSA) models, as well as 
delays in the submission of Utilization Certificates 
(UCs) by States/UTs. While appreciating the corrective 
measures taken by the Department, including revised 
proformas and digital processing of proposals, the 
Committee recommend that the Department 
strengthen its coordination with States/UTs and 
implementing agencies through regular reviews and 
advance identification of projects. This should also 
include providing dedicated technical support to States 
and implementing agencies to ensure their financial 
systems are fully integrated with the TSA/CNA 
framework. This would help ensure timely submission 
of proposals and more effective utilisation of funds for 
improving accessibility, rehabilitation services and 
overall empowerment of persons with disabilities. 
14. 6.6 The Committee observe with concern that the physical 
achievements under the National Action Plan for Skill 
Development of Persons with Disabilities (NAP-SDP) 
have remained significantly below the set targets over 
the last three years The performance data reveals a 
widening gap: against a target of 17,000 in 2023–24, 
the Department trained 9,333 beneficiaries; this fell 
sharply to 836 trainees against a target of 15,000 in 
2024–25, and further to only 2,264 beneficiaries 

99 
 
against a target of 10,000 in 2025–26 (as of January 
2026). While the Committee acknowledge the 
administrative challenges posed by the transition to 
the PM-DAKSH-DEPwD portal and the Hybrid Treasury 
Single Account (TSA) model, the continued shortfall in 
achieving even 25% of the set targets is a matter of 
serious concern. With the newly announced 
Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana, the Committee 
recommend that the Department adopt a more robust, 
industry-linked approach to bridge the gap between 
training and gainful employment. It is essential that 
the Department prioritize the placement of certified 
trainees by strengthening partnerships with private 
employers and ensuring that training modules remain 
aligned with current market demands. The Committee 
further suggest that the targets for the 2026–27 fiscal 
year be monitored quarterly to ensure that the 
transition to the new Yojana results in a measurable 
improvement in both the number of beneficiaries 
trained and their subsequent placement in sustainable 
employment. 
15. 7.11 The Committee find that the financial allocation under 
the Scholarship Scheme for Students with Disabilities 
has remained largely stable during the period under 
review, with the Budget Estimates ranging between 
₹142.68 crore and ₹155.00 crore during 2023–24 to 
2026–27. However, the Committee observe that the 
physical achievement under the Scheme has 
consistently fallen short of the prescribed targets. 
Against a target of 43,520 beneficiaries, only 29,374 
beneficiaries were covered in 2023–24 (about 67.5 per 
cent) and 23,085 beneficiaries in 2024–25 (about 53 
per cent). Similarly, 17,378 beneficiaries have been 
covered so far in 2025–26, indicating a continuing gap 
between the intended outreach and actual coverage. 
The Committee note the Department’s explanation 
that stricter verification through e-KYC authentication, 
UDID linkage and the National Scholarship Portal has 

100 
 
led to elimination of duplicate or ineligible 
applications. While appreciating the steps taken to 
improve transparency in the system, the Committee 
recommend that the Department intensify awareness 
campaigns, coordination with States/UTs and 
monitoring of pendency at the State Nodal Officer 
level, so that a larger number of eligible students with 
disabilities are able to access the benefits of the 
Scheme. 
16. 
 
7.12 The Committee note the Department’s proposal to 
introduce a uniform lump-sum scholarship structure 
for certain components of the Scheme from the next 
EFC cycle (2026–27 onwards) with the objective of 
simplifying calculations and expediting disbursement. 
The Committee also note that delays in verification and 
processing at various stages, particularly due to 
pendency of applications and prolonged scrutiny at the 
level of State Nodal Officers, have adversely affected 
the timely release of scholarships in several cases. The 
Committee are of the view that scholarships constitute 
a critical support mechanism enabling students with 
disabilities to pursue education without financial 
hardship. The Committee therefore recommend that 
while finalising the revised framework, the 
Department ensure that the scholarship amounts 
remain adequate to meet actual educational expenses 
and that appropriate mechanisms are put in place to 
minimise processing delays at the State level, so that 
the simplified disbursement system results in faster 
and more predictable release of funds to eligible 
beneficiaries. 
17. 8.5 The Committee express their displeasure with the 
financial performance of the scheme.  The Department 
has been able to utilize only 50% of the funds 
allocated in the year 2023-24 & 2024-25. The 
Committee note that the Centre for Disability Sports 
currently operates through training camps and talent 

101 
 
identification initiatives for Divyang athletes. The 
Committee are of the view that the impact of the 
Centre can be further strengthened through closer 
coordination with existing national sports 
programmes. The Committee therefore recommend 
that the Department explore collaboration with the 
Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, particularly under 
the Khelo India framework, so that talent scouting for 
Divyang athletes is integrated with existing sports 
infrastructure across the country. Such an approach 
would help identify promising athletes at the 
grassroots level and enable them to access structured 
training opportunities at the Centre for Disability 
Sports, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness of 
the facility at Gwalior. 
18. 9.9 The Committee note that the National Institutes and 
Composite Regional Centres (CRCs) play a crucial role 
in human resource development, research and 
rehabilitation services in the disability sector. 
However, the Committee observe that a significant gap 
exists between the sanctioned strength and the 
present staff strength in many of the Institutes and 
CRCs. For instance, institutions such as SVNIRTAR, 
Cuttack (115 against 197 sanctioned posts) and 
AYJNISHD, Mumbai (121 against 173 sanctioned 
posts) are functioning with substantial vacancies. 
Similarly, several CRCs are operating with limited 
manpower and in some cases posts remain entirely 
vacant. The Committee are of the view that such 
shortages may affect the quality of training, research 
and rehabilitation services being provided by these 
institutions. The Committee therefore recommend that 
the Department pursue the matter with the Ministry of 
Finance for early approval of creation and revival of 
posts and simultaneously take steps to expedite 
recruitment to existing vacancies, so that the National 
Institutes and CRCs are adequately staffed to 
effectively discharge their expanding mandate under 

102 
 
the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
19. 9.10 The Committee appreciate that the National Institutes 
are undertaking several important research initiatives 
in the disability sector, including the development of 
tools such as the NIEPID Indian Test of Intelligence 
(NITI), assistive technologies and innovations in 
rehabilitation sciences. The Committee also note that 
financial support for research and development is 
being extended through the SIPDA component on 
priority areas of disability. The Committee are of the 
view that the National Institutes should increasingly 
function as centres of excellence in research, 
innovation and assistive technology development. The 
Committee therefore recommend that the Department 
encourage greater collaboration of the National 
Institutes with premier scientific institutions, 
universities and technology agencies, so that 
indigenous assistive technologies, rehabilitation tools 
and evidence-based practices are developed and 
widely disseminated for the benefit of persons with 
disabilities. 
20. 10.5 The Committee welcome the introduction of the two 
new schemes during 2026–27, namely Divyangjan 
Kaushal Yojana and Divyangjan Sahara Yojana, with 
allocations of ₹200 crore and ₹100 crore respectively, 
aimed at strengthening skill development and the 
assistive device ecosystem for persons with 
disabilities. However, the Committee note that the 
detailed modalities of implementation, including 
operational guidelines and physical targets, are still 
under formulation. The Committee are of the view that 
early finalisation of the scheme framework is essential 
to ensure that the budgetary allocations translate into 
tangible outcomes. The Committee therefore 
recommend that the Department expedite the 
finalisation of guidelines and put in place a clear 
implementation framework with measurable targets 

103 
 
relating to skill training, employment opportunities 
and assistive device distribution, so that the schemes 
are operationalised effectively and deliver meaningful 
benefits to Divyangjan. 
21. 11.4 The Committee find that the Department has put in 
place several monitoring mechanisms such as ARJUN 
Portal, e-Anudaan, UDID integration, NGO-Darpan 
registration, field inspections and periodic review at 
the level of Secretary (DEPwD) to ensure transparency 
and proper utilisation of funds. However, the 
Committee also note that implementation of several 
schemes continue to face operational challenges such 
as delays in submission of proposals and utilisation 
certificates by implementing agencies, gaps in timely 
uploading of beneficiary data and logistical constraints 
in conducting camps and outreach activities in remote 
and hilly areas. The Committee are of the view that 
such procedural bottlenecks weaken the efficiency of 
otherwise well-designed monitoring systems. The 
Committee therefore recommend that the Department 
institutionalise a time-bound compliance framework 
for implementing agencies, strengthen digital 
integration of monitoring platforms such as ARJUN, 
UDID and e-Anudaan, and establish a structured 
follow-up mechanism with States/UTs and 
implementing agencies so that delays in 
documentation, reporting and fund utilisation are 
minimized and scheme benefits reach beneficiaries in a 
timely manner. 
22. 
 
11.5 The Committee note that several schemes of the 
Department, particularly ADIP and SIPDA, are 
implemented through a large network of States/UTs, 
NGOs, National Institutes, CRCs and other agencies, 
which poses inherent challenges in ensuring uniform 
standards of implementation and monitoring. The 
Committee further observe that issues such as delayed 
proposals, weak absorptive capacity at the State level, 

104 
 
pending utilisation certificates and infrastructure or 
connectivity constraints in certain regions continue to 
affect the pace of scheme implementation. The 
Committee are of the view that addressing these 
structural constraints requires stronger institutional 
coordination and capacity building. The Committee 
therefore recommend that the Department develop a 
comprehensive monitoring and capacity-building 
framework for implementing agencies, including 
regular performance reviews, targeted training for 
State and NGO partners, and a robust data-driven 
dashboard for real-time tracking of scheme 
implementation. Such measures would help improve 
accountability, strengthen implementation capacity 
across States/UTs and ensure that public funds 
allocated for the welfare of persons with disabilities 
are utilised efficiently and deliver measurable 
outcomes.

            (vii) Grants under Article 275(1) of the Constitution. 
  
1.5 An overview in respect of some of the important schemes, institutions of 
the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and relevant Acts is as under:- 
 
1.6 The Scheme of Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRSs), as a Central 
Sector Scheme, was started in the year 2018-19 to provide quality education to 
the tribal children (from class VI to XII) in their own environment. Earlier EMRS 
was a component under Article 275(1) of the Constitution. However, under the  
 

4 
 
 
 
new scheme, Government have decided to establish one EMRS in every block 
having more than 50% ST population and at least 20000 tribal persons. 
Accordingly, the Ministry have set-up the target to set-up 728 EMRSs.  
 
1.7  Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN) was 
launched on November, 15, 2023 with financial outlay of around ₹24,000 crores 
with the aim for socio-economic development of 75 PVTG communities residing in 
18 States and one UT by 9 line-Ministries and Departments.  
 
1.8   Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan envisions saturation of 
critical gaps in social infrastructure, health, education, livelihood, through 25 
interventions implemented by 17-line ministries of Govt of India by convergence 
and outreach to ensures holistic and sustainable development of tribal areas and 
communities.  
 
1.9 The Centrally sponsored ‘Support to TRI’ is meant to preserve and 
promote tribal culture and dissemination of information including research and 
documentation, maintenance, and preservation of art and artifacts, setting up of 
tribal museum, exchange visits for the tribals to other parts of the State, 
organizing tribal festivals etc. The Ministry also supports construction of tribal 
museums within the premises of the TRIs to preserve the tribal art, craft and 
culture. The National Tribal Research Institute (NTRI), a national-level institute, 
was inaugurated on 7th June 2022 with a broad objective for addressing tribal 
concerns, issues and better co-ordination and management of TRIs. In addition to 
activities/project sanctioned under the ‘Support to TRI Scheme’, there are 
dedicated portals ‘National Tribal Research Portal’, ‘Adi Prashikshan Portal’, ‘Adi 
Parsaran’ and ‘Tribal Repository’ which are repositories of the work done by the 
TRIs in the past few years.  
 

5 
 
 
 
1.10 Under proviso to Grants under Article 275 (1) of the Constitution of 
India, financial assistance is provided to the State Governments with notified STs,

CHAPTER-III 
TRIBAL RESEARCH INSTITUTES (TRIs) 
 
Ministry extend support to State and UT Governments through the sponsored 
scheme ‘Support to Tribal Research Institutes’. There are 29 Tribal Research 
Institutes across Country which are supported and administered by State 
Governments. The TRIs are primarily institutions under the State 
Governments/UT Administrations engaged in the work of conducting research 
and evaluation studies, collection of data, identification of challenges in the field 
of socio-economic developments in tribals and understanding, promoting and 
preserving their culture through various studies and other kind of 
interventions.  The Ministry extends support to the State Governments to 
strengthen Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs) in their infrastructural needs, 
research & documentation activities and training & capacity building 
programmes, Organization of tribal festivals/ yatras for promotion of unique 
cultural heritage and for promoting tourism and organization of "exchange visits 
by tribal’s", so that the tribal cultural practices, languages and rituals are 
preserved and disseminated. As part of the research activities of the TRIs, the 
Ministry also support construction of tribal museums within the premises of 
TRIs to preserve the tribal art, craft and culture. Also, The National Tribal 
Research Institute (NTRI), Delhi, is a national-level institute with a broad 
objective for addressing tribal concerns, issues and better co-ordination and 
management of TRIs.

3.6 On being asked about the assessment study conducted on the functioning 
of TRIs in the country, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs vide their written reply 
stated that the NITI Aayog on the basis of an evaluation study conducted in 
2025 submitted the following recommendations/observations:  
 
(i)  Greater emphasis should be on redesigning the objective of TRIs as think-
tanks, ensuring greater convergence with other tribal schemes as well as 
NGOs, eminent institutions and line departments. 
(ii) It is also important to ensure good quality research as well as greater 
community participation.  
(iii)  The scheme OOMF needs to be annually tracked and monitored by the 
Ministry. 
(iv) The scheme should introduce the following modifications for its 
rationalization and higher impact –  
 
 Higher emphasis on quality of the research activities as well as greater 
involvement of research experts.

 Overall improvement of fund flow systems in terms of fund availability 
and utilization timelines by addressing human resource availability. 
 Strengthening institutional structure at state TRIs and investing in their 
capacity building. 
 Improving the monitoring and results framework by undertaking periodic 
monitoring and evaluation of scheme interventions and their effect on 
end beneficiaries. 
 More interaction of researchers with Government. 
 
(v) Strengthen institutional capacity of TRIs through targeted resource 
allocation and standardization of research guidelines across states. 
(vi) Fill vacant research and administrative positions; develop a national-level 
repository for tribal research outputs that are accessible to government and 
academia. 
(vii) Institute annual work plans linked with a “fund release–monitoring–
utilization” framework to enhance accountability and timely project completion. 
(viii) Encourage collaborations with universities and international development 
agencies for co-funded research; introduce revenue-generating cultural 
documentation projects. 
(ix) Develop mechanisms for translating TRI studies into actionable inputs for 
tribal policy formulation and monitoring. 
(x) Introduce targeted research fellowships for tribal youth and women

(xi) Map national and state-level research overlaps; establish convergence 
mechanisms through MoTA’s Knowledge Management Division.

3.9 The Committee are happy to note that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs 
under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme ‘Support to Tribal Research 
Institutes (TRIs)’ provide financial assistance to 29 Tribal Research 
Institutes (TRIs) for execution and implementation of the sanctioned 
projects and activities. The Committee, however, find that budget 
estimates for 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 were revised downward at 
RE stage from ₹118.64 crore to ₹50.00 crore, ₹111.00 crore to ₹90.00 
crore and again ₹111.00 crore to ₹90.00 respectively. The revised 
estimate could also not be spent fully during 2023-24 and for the 
financial year 2025-26, only a meager 29.93% of RE the Ministry has been 
able to spend till 19.02.26. The Committee, therefore, believe that mere 
allocations of funds would not ensure effective implementation of TRI 
Scheme. The Committee note with concern the inability of State 
treasuries in transferring funds allocated by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, 
timely submission of Annual Action Plans and Utilization Certificates 
(UCs), clearance of SNA balances, submission of progress report/DPR etc 
by the State Authorities etc. The Committee, therefore, recommend the 
Ministry that they should endeavor to devise a specific mechanism, sound 
in technical knowhow and procedural matters, in consultation with 
States/UTs, to remove technical and procedural bottlenecks, 
administrative delays, capacity building issues etc. The Committee would 
also like the Ministry to consider the suggestions received from NITI 
Aayog for effective implementation of the scheme. The Committee would 
like to be informed of the action taken by the Ministry in this regard.

4.5 The Committee are happy to note that Budget allocation of ₹25 Cr for 
the scheme for 2023-24 was augmented to ₹45 Cr at the RE stage and the 
Ministry could spend ₹32.04 Cr during the financial year, which far 
exceeded the initial Budget allocation. The Committee would have been 
ever happier, had the Ministry been able to utilize the entire Revised

a reduction of ₹3.71 Cr in actual expenditure in 2024-25 vis-à-vis 2023-

CHAPTER-V 
EKLAVYA MODEL RESIDENTIAL SCHOOL (EMRS) 
 
 Ministry is implementing the Central Sector Scheme of Eklavya Model 
Residential School (EMRS) to provide quality education to the tribal children 
(from class VI to XII) in their own environment from the year 2018-19 in 
remote areas to enable them to access the best opportunities in education and 
to bring them at par with the general population. Earlier EMRS was a 
component under Article 275(1) of the Constitution. Under the new scheme, 
Government decided to establish one EMRS in every block having more than 
50% ST population and at least 20,000 tribal persons (as per census 2011). 
Accordingly, Ministry has set the target to set up 728 EMRSs benefitting 
around 3.5 lakh ST students across the country.  
 
5.2 As on date, a total number of 723 EMRSs have been sanctioned across 
the country, out of which 499 schools are reported to be functional. 
Additionally, to encourage tribal students in sports and provide them with a 
platform to enhance their capabilities, Ministry has decided to set up 15 
Centre of Excellence for Sports (CoE for Sports) in EMRSs.  
 
5.3  National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS), an autonomous 
organization, has been created to manage and implement the scheme of 
EMRS. Ministry releases funds to NESTS and NESTS further releases funds to 
States/ UTs/ PSUs/ Construction Agencies/ State Societies as per their 
requirements for construction of EMRSs and recurring cost for running of the 
schools. Construction of an EMRS requires provision of 15 acres land and has 
a capacity to accommodate 480 students including equal number of boys and 
girls studying in class VI to XII. The recurring cost is ₹1.46 lakhs per student 
per annum and the capital cost for construction of an EMRS is ₹37.80 cr in 
plain areas and ₹48 cr in North East/ hilly/ LWE affected areas.

introduced flexibility: earlier, passing Hindi was mandatory for evaluation. 
We have now allowed combined qualifying in Hindi and English, thereby 
enabling greater participation of local candidates. We expect increased 
local representation as a result. Out of 52 sanctioned posts, we have

5.12  723 Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) have been 
sanctioned out of 728 targeted to be set up in the country to provide 
quality education to the tribal children from class VI to XII in their own 
environment from the year 2018-19 to enable them to get access to the 
best opportunities in education. An allocation of ₹7150.01 crore has been 
made for the year 2026-27 for EMRS Scheme which is 46.67 percent of 
the total budget of the Ministry. The Committee note that under the 
Scheme, out of budgetary allocation of ₹6,399.00 crore and ₹7,088.60 
crore in the years 2024-25 and 2025-26, ₹4,716.29 crore and ₹4,011.25 
crore (till 19.01.2025) were utilized respectively. The Committee find that 
despite concerted efforts made by the Ministry to overcome the hurdles 
in implementation of scheme, the Ministry have been able to achieve a 
very limited success as BE of ₹7,088.60 Cr. for 2025-26 was reduced to             
₹4,900.00 Cr at RE stage and the Ministry have been able to utilize only 
₹4,011.25 Cr till 19.01.2026. Since the Ministry have not been able to 
address the problems and the problems still persist, the Committee urge 
the Ministry to persuade the implementing agencies to comply with the 
norms so that the hurdles are taken care of and the EMRS are established 
within the given timeline.  
 
5.13 The Committee have noted from the replies of the Ministry that out 
of 499 functional schools as on date, 377 schools are functioning from the 
permanent buildings, 111 from other Government Buildings and 11 from 
rented premises. The Committee in previous years highlighted the need 
that all the EMRS should be made functional from their own buildings and 
should not run from rented or other Government buildings as these 
buildings may be lacking required infrastructure for a school. Considering 
the fact that there is no scarcity of resources at the disposal of the 
Ministry, the Committee still consider this as an essential prerequisite for 
the comprehensive development of  EMRS infrastructure with a keen eye 
on the wholesome growth of tribal students. The Committee also believe 
that rented premises may not cater to the needs of present day 

27 
 
educational needs like technological and AI labs, smart-classrooms, 
sporting arenas etc. Therefore, the Committee desire that a 
comprehensive action plan should be chalked out to make all the 
remaining EMRS schools functional from their own buildings and the 
construction work of each EMRS is completed in a stipulated period of 2-3 
years. The Committee would like to be informed of steps taken in this 
regard.  
5.14 The Committee are happy to note that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs 
have made several proposals to the EFC for approvals such as increase in 
the annual expenditure for students, recruitment of teachers, zonal offices 
for NESTS etc for the functioning of EMRS. The Committee expect that the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs would get approval at the earliest and they would 
be able to implement them from next academic year.  The Committee 
would like to be informed about the further developments made in this 
regard.

6.5 On being enquired about the reasons for low utilization of funds in all 
these years, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs vide their written reply submitted 
that :-  
 
    “The release of funds under PM-JANMAN is subject to compliance of 
Ministry of Finance’s instructions regarding release of funds under the 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) and monitoring utilization of funds 
released. As per the erstwhile SNA instructions, the maximum funds which 
could be considered for release is 50% of amount earmarked for a State 
during the particular financial year (earmarking of funds among States can 
be maximum to the limit of BE under the scheme for the particular FY) and 
funds can be released on utilization of at least 75% of the funds released 
earlier. Hence, in case a State has not utilized funds to the extent of 75% of 
earlier releases, no funds can be released during the FY. Further, during 
2025-26, MoF has covered PM JANMAN (MPCs) scheme under SNA SPARSH 
procedure under which ‘mother sanctions’ are issued to State Governments 
which define State wise drawing limits and actual release funds are subject 
to claims made by State Government on PFMS for release of Central Share”

7.5 On being asked about the reasons due to which the budgetary allocation 
of FY 2025-26 was reduced to one-fourth of BE at RE stage along with the 
reasons due to which that only 12.5% of BE could be utilized till 19.01.2026, 
the Ministry of Tribal Affairs vide their written reply submitted that:-  
 
 

36 
 
 
     “The primary reason for the reduction in Budgetary allocation at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage is attributable to the transition in the fund 
disbursal mechanism under the Public Financial Management System 
(PFMS) from the Single Nodal Agency (SNA) framework to the SNA-SPARSH 
system. During the relevant period, States/UTs were in the process of 
opening SNA accounts for implementation of DAJGUA in compliance with 
the instructions issued by the Ministry of Finance. However, before the 
operationalisation of these accounts could be fully stabilized, the SNA-
SPARSH system was introduced. Consequently, States/UTs encountered 
practical and procedural challenges in on-boarding and migrating their 
functional accounts from the existing SNA framework to SNA-SPARSH. This 
transition necessitated additional approvals, technical validations, and 
system-level configurations, which resulted in delays in the seamless flow 
and utilisation of funds. Further, the transition of financial control and 
operational responsibility from the State/UT Finance Departments to the 
designated implementing Departments also required time for alignment of 
workflows, and familiarisation with the revised PFMS processes. These 
transitional issues cumulatively impacted the pace of fund utilization during 
the financial year, leading to lower expenditure at the RE stage. It is, 
however, pertinent to mention that the transition process has since largely 
stabilized. States/UTs have now been on-boarded on the SNA-SPARSH 
platform, and the fund flow mechanism under PFMS is in the process of 
smooth and efficient utilisation. With the system now streamlined, improved 
expenditure performance is expected in the subsequent period” 
7.6 As regards the focus areas conceived by the Ministry for utilization of 
funds in FY 2026-27 and the steps being taken to ensure that the funds for FY 
2026-27 could be utilized in full across the areas of utilization, the Ministry have 
replied as under:-  
 
“Regular review meetings with in-line Ministries, States/ UTs under DAJGUA 
has been started to ensure that the funds are fully utilized during the 
Financial Year 2026-27. Also, States/UTs have now been on-boarded on the 
SNA-SPARSH platform, and the fund flow mechanism under PFMS is in the 
process of smooth and efficient utilization. With the system now streamlined, 
improved expenditure performance is expected in the subsequent period. 
Now, all States/UTs are being supported and made  

37 
 
 
aware of the funding provisions through SNA. Further all States/UTs have 
been advised to submit project proposals for the remaining allocation in 
line with the scheme guidelines in April 2026 itself. Periodic meetings are 
being held to resolve the practical difficulties faced by the States/UTs and 
to facilitate the smooth implementation of approved projects at various 
levels, as required” 
7.7 On being enquired about the constraints faced by the line Ministries in 
executing, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs submitted vide their written reply that: 
  
 “the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan adopts a convergence-
based, "whole-of government" approach, bringing together multiple 
ministries to working close collaboration to ensure impactful, cost-effective, 
and sustainable outcomes for tribal communities. Periodic meetings are 
held by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs-being the nodal Ministry to address the 
constraints faced by the Line Ministries, if any. These issues are resolved 
through a dialogue based approach in collaboration with the State 
Governments, ensuring smooth implementation and strengthened inter 
ministerial co-ordination. However, delays in uploading utilization details 
and physical progress on the various channels have affected timely review, 
corrective action, and subsequent releases, thereby impacting pending 
works”  
 
7.8 As regards to the role of State Governments in the execution of work, the 
Ministry submitted vide their written replies as under:-  
   “The State Governments are the implementing agencies to execute 
interventions under the Abhiyan efficiently on the ground through robust 
state, district, and block-level mechanisms. At the state level, the Chief 
Secretaries of the respective states leads the mission, with the Principal 
Secretary of Tribal Welfare serving as the convener. Senior officers from 
sectoral departments act as Nodal Officers, responsible for supervising, 
ensuring convergence, and monitoring the implementation of the mission. 
At the district level, District Collectors are designated as Nodal Officers,  

38 
 
 
tasked with overseeing, coordinating, and monitoring mission execution. At 
the block level, the Block Development Officer, or a similarly designated 
official (such as ITDP/ MADA), assumes the role of Nodal Officer, ensuring 
the effective implementation of the mission’s objectives within specific 
blocks or regions. A Project Management Unit (PMU) will be established 
within the Department of Tribal Welfare of the State Government to facilitate 
coordination and monitoring between Government of India (GOI) 
departments, state level departments, and across various ministries and 
states. The multiple and decentralized levels do help in tackling the hurdles 
being faced by the Line Ministries from State/UT   and timely execution of 
the targeted works. State/UT Governments are responsible for identifying 
and verifying eligible beneficiaries and villages, preparing and submitting 
DPRs/proposals and utilisation certificates across interventions, ensuring 
land readiness and facilitating statutory clearances (forest, environment, 
security) for civil works and digital connectivity AND coordinating among 
State line departments and Tribal Welfare Departments for convergence. 
These roles are embedded in the DAJGUA Guidelines under the 
implementation plan and the Monitoring & Evaluation Framework, which 
emphasize state-led execution with central coordination” 
 
7.9 The Committee note that Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh 
Abhiyan (DAJGUA) was launched on 2nd October, 2024 to saturate critical 
gaps in social infrastructure, health, education, livelihood etc. through 25 
interventions implemented by 17-line Ministries of Govt. of India by 
convergence and outreach to ensure holistic and sustainable development 
of tribal areas and communities.  The Abhiyan will cover 63, 843 villages 
in 549 districts and 2911 blocks spread across all tribal majority villages 
and aspirational block in 30 States/UTS during FY 2024-25 to FY 2028-
29. Since multiple Ministries are involved and the Abhyan is stipulated to 
be completed by 2028-29, the Committee feel that in the prevailing 
circumstances the role of Ministry of Tribal Affairs becomes 
extraordinarily important as they have to effectively coordinate and 

39 
 
monitor the pace of work so that the objectives of the Scheme are 
achieved in the given time period. The Committee, however, find that 
during the financial year 2025-26, BE of ₹2,000 Cr. was reduced to ₹500 
Cr at RE stage and only ₹250.02 Cr. has so far been utilized by the 
Ministry till 19.01.26. The Committee are made to understand that the 
initial hurdles such as transition of financial control and operation 
responsibility from the State/UT Departments, familiarization with PFMS 
system have largely been now streamlined, hence the improved 
expenditure performance is expected in the subsequent period. The 
Committee have no doubt with regard to the expenditure performance as 
the hurdles have been taken care of but the concern of the Committee is 
with regard to the performance of the line Ministries as it does not appear 
to be at the required pace because the progress of the work is very tardy 
and far behind the target fixed upto March, 2026. The Ministry of Rural 
Development, Ministry of Jal Shakti and Ministry of New and Renewable 
Energy are yet to start work and several Ministries are yet to complete 
task assigned for completion by March, 2026. This directly points to the 
deep mismanagement in the execution of the scheme, the Committee are, 
therefore, of the view that the Ministry should take capacity building 
measures and provide technical support to implementing agencies, 
including local bodies and field-level officials so that the momentum picks 
up. The Committee would appreciate if the Ministry conducts 
comprehensive implementation audit across all participating states and 
implementing agencies so that the bottlenecks are identified and the 
necessary action is taken to plug them. The Committee also recommend 
the establishment of a dedicated monitoring and coordination mechanism 
at both the Central and State levels and creation of a digital dashboard 
with real-time progress indicators to track physical and financial 
performance, enabling early detection of delays and deviations. The 
Committee would like to be apprised of the measures taken by the 
Ministry in this regard.

scheme, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs submitted vide written reply that:- 
“As per scheme guidelines for the program of Grants under proviso to Article 
275 (1) of the Constitution, an Executive Committee (EC) is chaired by Chief

approval of perspective document, Monitoring and Evaluation. Provision of 
similar committee at District Level under Chairpersonship of District 
Collector has been made at District Level also. In addition to above, State 
furnishes Utilization certificate and physical progress report of the projects 
with approval of competent authority of concerned States. The proposals are 
submitted by the States on the basis of Perspective Plan Document to the 
Ministry for consideration under Article 275(1) by PAC constituted for the 
purpose. The funds are then disbursed for approved projects after thorough 
analysis of the progress of earlier approved projects.  The PAC, thus, also 
acts as oversight committee to monitor the funds utilization”  
 
9.7 The Committee note that under proviso to Grants under Article 275 
(1) of the Constitution of India, financial assistance is provided to the 
State Governments with notified STs based upon proposals received from 
them. The Committee note that a significant percentage of Budgetary 
allocation is earmarked for the grants. However, the Committee have 

48 
 
found that for the financial year 2025-26 ₹1,541.47 Cr. was allocated at 
BE stage which was reduced to ₹1,171.00 Cr. at the RE stage and the 
Ministry have been able to utilize only ₹327.29 Cr. till 19.01.26 of the 
financial year.  In this regard, the Committee firmly believe that grants 
under Article 275(1) of the Constitution of India represent a vital 
constitutional commitment to tribal welfare and strengthening the 
disbursal of funds, institutional capacity and oversight functions of the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs vis-à-vis the grants are of utmost importance for 
meaningful and measurable improvements in the socio-economic 
conditions of Scheduled Tribes. The Committee, therefore, recommend 
the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to take suitable measures to improve co-
ordination with States, creation of standardized project frameworks and 
outcome-based monitoring mechanism for better utilization of grants. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to apprise the Committee of the 
initiatives taken in this regard.

23.02.2026.  Therefore, the Committee strongly 
recommend that the Ministry should take concrete 
steps to utilize the unspent portion of RE for 2025-
26 within the remaining period left of the present 
financial year and ensure that the target fixed under 

55 
 
each of the schemes are achieved. The Committee 
also expect that the Ministry will address troubling 
issues once and for all to clear the deck for better 
usage of budgetary allocation in future. The 
Committee also hope that the Ministry would make 
a concerted effort to ensure that at least 50% of the 
allocated fund for 2026-27 are put to use by the 
month of September, 2026, so that the Budget 
allocation for 2026-27 is not reduced at RE stage by 
the Ministry of Finance.  
2. 3.9 The Committee are happy to note that the Ministry 
of Tribal Affairs under the Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme ‘Support to Tribal Research Institutes 
(TRIs)’ provide financial assistance to 29 Tribal 
Research Institutes (TRIs) for execution and 
implementation of the sanctioned projects and 
activities. The Committee, however, find that budget 
estimates for 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 were 
revised downward at RE stage from ₹118.64 crore to 
₹50.00 crore, ₹111.00 crore to ₹90.00 crore and 
again ₹111.00 crore to ₹90.00 respectively. The 
revised estimate could also not be spent fully during 
2023-24 and for the financial year 2025-26, only a 
meager 29.93% of RE the Ministry has been able to 
spend till 19.02.26. The Committee, therefore, 
believe that mere allocations of funds would not 
ensure effective implementation of TRI Scheme. The 
Committee note with concern the inability of State 
treasuries in transferring funds allocated by the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs, timely submission of 
Annual Action Plans and Utilization Certificates 
(UCs), clearance of SNA balances, submission of 

56 
 
progress report/DPR etc by the State Authorities 
etc. The Committee, therefore, recommend the 
Ministry that they should endeavor to devise a 
specific mechanism, sound in technical knowhow 
and procedural matters, in consultation with 
States/UTs, to remove technical and procedural 
bottlenecks, administrative delays, capacity building 
issues etc. The Committee would also like the 
Ministry to consider the suggestions received from 
NITI Aayog for effective implementation of the 
scheme. The Committee would like to be informed of 
the action taken by the Ministry in this regard. 
3. 3.10 The Committee note that out of 11 Tribal Freedom 
Fighters’ Museum sanctioned by the Ministry, only 4 
Museums have been inaugurated till date and rest of 
the Museums are either under the different stages of 
construction or curation development. Since very 
little progress has been achieved in last one year, 
the Committee once again convey their discontent 
at the delayed progress of work on this front. The 
Committee, therefore, desire to underscore the fact 
that the construction and inauguration delays of 
such museums defeats the objective for which 
Museum are being established.  The Ministry, while 
accepting the onus for the delays, conveyed that 
necessary measures have been taken to expedite the 
construction of Tribal Freedom Fighters Museums in 
the country. The Committee are of the view that the 
Ministry must take concrete measures and take an 
holistic approach to include in its ambit all factors 
that have long been hindering the progress of the 
scheme. The Committee urge the Ministry to upscale 

57 
 
their ongoing endeavors so that all sanctioned 
Museums are completed by March, 2027 as informed 
to the Committee. 
4. 4.5 The Committee are happy to note that Budget 
allocation of ₹25 Cr for the scheme for 2023-24 was 
augmented to ₹45 Cr at the RE stage and the 
Ministry could spend ₹32.04 Cr during the financial 
year, which far exceeded the initial Budget 
allocation. The Committee would have been ever 
happier, had the Ministry been able to utilize the 
entire Revised Allocation of ₹45 Cr. The Committee 
are rather disappointed to find that the Ministry 
could utilize only ₹28.33 Cr. for 2024-25, thereby 
indicating a reduction of ₹3.71 Cr in actual 
expenditure in 2024-25 vis-à-vis 2023-24. This 
under-utilization also underlines year-on-year 
fluctuation in performance of the TRI-ECE scheme. 
The Committee have been informed that for the year 
2025-26, the Ministry have forwarded a re-
appropriation file of ₹5 Cr. for seeking additional 
allocation from the Ministry of Finance to meet up 
committed expenses under the scheme. Therefore, 
the Committee expect that the additional allocation 
will be provided to the Ministry and fruitfully 
utilized till the end of financial year 2025-26. The 
Committee are hopeful that budget allocation of ₹32 
Cr. for 2026-27 will not be downsized at the RE 
stage and the Ministry will be able to spend the 
entire corpus across the desired areas, including, 
organization of National and State-level events, 
Integrated Media activities, Outreach and Branding, 
strengthening of Centers of Excellences etc. In 

58 
 
respect of planning of expenditure, the Committee 
would strongly recommend the Ministry to include 
more State-level Institutes and Research Institutes/ 
Organizations and State-Universities under the 
provision of grants, thereby broadening and 
expanding the horizon and scope of the scheme. The 
Committee would like to be informed of steps taken 
in this regard.  
5. 5.12 723 Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) have 
been sanctioned out of 728 targeted to be set up in 
the country to provide quality education to the 
tribal children from class VI to XII in their own 
environment from the year 2018-19 to enable them 
to get access to the best opportunities in education. 
An allocation of ₹7150.01 crore has been made for 
the year 2026-27 for EMRS Scheme which is 46.67 
percent of the total budget of the Ministry. The 
Committee note that under the Scheme, out of 
budgetary allocation of ₹6,399.00 crore and 
₹7,088.60 crore in the years 2024-25 and 2025-26, 
₹4,716.29 crore and ₹4,011.25 crore (till 19.01.2025) 
were utilized respectively. The Committee find that 
despite concerted efforts made by the Ministry to 
overcome the hurdles in implementation of scheme, 
the Ministry have been able to achieve a very limited 
success as BE of ₹7,088.60 Cr. for 2025-26 was 
reduced to ₹4,900.00 Cr at RE stage and the 
Ministry have been able to utilize only ₹4,011.25 Cr 
till 19.01.2026. Since the Ministry have not been 
able to address the problems and the problems still 
persist, the Committee urge the Ministry to 
persuade the implementing agencies to comply with 

59 
 
the norms so that the hurdles are taken care of and 
the EMRS are established within the given timeline.  
 
6. 5.13 The Committee have noted from the replies of the 
Ministry that out of 499 functional schools as on 
date, 377 schools are functioning from the 
permanent buildings, 111 from other Government 
Buildings and 11 from rented premises. The 
Committee in previous years highlighted the need 
that all the EMRS should be made functional from 
their own buildings and should not run from rented 
or other Government buildings as these buildings 
may be lacking required infrastructure for a school. 
Considering the fact that there is no scarcity of 
resources at the disposal of the Ministry, the 
Committee still consider this as an essential 
prerequisite for the comprehensive development of  
EMRS infrastructure with a keen eye on the 
wholesome growth of tribal students. The Committee 
also believe that rented premises may not cater to 
the needs of present day educational needs like 
technological and AI labs, smart-classrooms, 
sporting arenas etc. Therefore, the Committee desire 
that a comprehensive action plan should be chalked 
out to make all the remaining EMRS schools 
functional from their own buildings and the 
construction work of each EMRS is completed in a 
stipulated period of 2-3 years. The Committee would 
like to be informed of steps taken in this regard.  
7. 5.14 The Committee are happy to note that the Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs have made several proposals to the EFC 
for approvals such as increase in the annual 

60 
 
expenditure for students, recruitment of teachers, 
zonal offices for NESTS etc for the functioning of 
EMRS. The Committee expect that the Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs would get approval at the earliest and 
they would be able to implement them from next 
academic year.  The Committee would like to be 
informed about the further developments made in this 
regard. 
8. 6.8 The Committee note that Pradhan Mantri Janjati 
Adivasi Naya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN) is an 
ambitious scheme of Govt. of India for the holistic 
development of Tribal Communities of the Country 
with a view to saturate 29000 tribal dominated 
villages by 2025-26 with an total dedicated corpus of 
₹24,000 Cr. The Scheme is spread across 9-line 
Ministries/Departments over 11 interventions 
across health, education, nutrition, road and 
connectivity, construction of Multi-purpose Centers 
and Anganwadis, installation of solar panels, 
electrification and sanitation etc. The Committee 
also note that RE for 2025-26 was reduced to            
₹184.99 Cr. from ₹300 Cr. allocated at BE stage and 
the Ministry could utilize only ₹113.70 Cr. till 
19.01.26.  The Committee find that there is slow 
and tardy progress in execution of works by the 
several Ministries as the work done by the Ministries 
like, M/o Rural Development, M/o Education and 
M/o Jal Shakti, is lagging far behind the target. The 
Committee, therefore, again emphasize that the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs, as the nodal Ministry, 
must dovetail a well thought out mechanism and 
system of timely execution with PM-JANMAN in 

61 
 
order to complete the pending work of the line-
Ministries within the extended period, i.e, one year 
beyond its initial date of completion on 31st March, 
2026. 
9. 7.9 The Committee note that Dharti Aaba Janjatiya 
Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DAJGUA) was launched on 
2nd October, 2024 to saturate critical gaps in social 
infrastructure, health, education, livelihood etc. 
through 25 interventions implemented by 17-line 
Ministries of Govt. of India by convergence and 
outreach to ensure holistic and sustainable 
development of tribal areas and communities.  The 
Abhiyan will cover 63, 843 villages in 549 districts 
and 2911 blocks spread across all tribal majority 
villages and aspirational block in 30 States/UTS 
during FY 2024-25 to FY 2028-29. Since multiple 
Ministries are involved and the Abhyan is stipulated 
to be completed by 2028-29, the Committee feel 
that in the prevailing circumstances the role of 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs becomes extraordinarily 
important as they have to effectively coordinate and 
monitor the pace of work so that the objectives of 
the Scheme are achieved in the given time period. 
The Committee, however, find that during the 
financial year 2025-26, BE of ₹2,000 Cr. was reduced 
to ₹500 Cr at RE stage and only ₹250.02 Cr. has so 
far been utilized by the Ministry till 19.01.26. The 
Committee are made to understand that the initial 
hurdles such as transition of financial control and 
operation responsibility from the State/UT 
Departments, familiarization with PFMS system 
have largely been now streamlined, hence the 

62 
 
improved expenditure performance is expected in 
the subsequent period. The Committee have no 
doubt with regard to the expenditure performance as 
the hurdles have been taken care of but the concern 
of the Committee is with regard to the performance 
of the line Ministries as it does not appear to be at 
the required pace because the progress of the work 
is very tardy and far behind the target fixed upto 
March, 2026. The Ministry of Rural Development, 
Ministry of Jal Shakti and Ministry of New and 
Renewable Energy are yet to start work and several 
Ministries are yet to complete task assigned for 
completion by March, 2026. This directly points to 
the deep mismanagement in the execution of the 
scheme, the Committee are, therefore of the view 
that the Ministry should take capacity building 
measures and provide technical support to 
implementing agencies, including local bodies and 
field-level officials so that the momentum picks up. 
The Committee would appreciate if the Ministry 
conducts comprehensive implementation audit 
across all participating states and implementing 
agencies so that the bottlenecks are identified and 
the necessary action is taken to plug them. The 
Committee also recommend the establishment of a 
dedicated monitoring and coordination mechanism 
at both the Central and State levels and creation of a 
digital dashboard with real-time progress indicators 
to track physical and financial performance, 
enabling early detection of delays and deviations. 
The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
measures taken by the Ministry in this regard. 

63 
 
10. 8.7 The Committee appreciate that overseas scholarship 
scheme, namely, the National Overseas Scholarship 
Scheme, a Central Sector Scheme of Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs, under which scholarships are given to 
the meritorious Schedule Tribe (ST) students for 
pursuing higher education in top 1000 ranked 
Institutes/Universities abroad. The Scheme is 
implemented through the Indian 
Embassies/Missions abroad, Ministry of External 
Affairs. The Committee have also been informed that 
ST students with annual family income not 
exceeding ₹6.0 lakhs are eligible to apply for the 
Scholarship under the Scheme. The Committee are 
content to note that from the forthcoming EFC cycle 
the number of annual slots have been proposed to be 
enhanced from 20 to 50 and the Annual 
Maintenance Allowance from USD 15,400 to USD 
19,250. The Committee consider both the changes 
to be a positive step towards ensuring the welfare of 
meritorious ST students pursuing their academic 
dreams abroad. However, the Committee cannot but 
underscore a long-pending desire from ST 
communities to increase the eligibility criterion with 
regard to annual family income not exceeding ₹6.0 
lakhs applicable in scholarship under the scheme. 
The Committee genuinely feel that the annual 
income ceiling of ₹6.00 lakhs ought to be augmented 
and brought in parity to the need of the time. The 
Committee are happy that during the deliberation, 
Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, as well, 
recognized this need and assured the Committee to 
take necessary steps to raise annual family income 

64 
 
ceiling of ₹6.00 lakh under National Overseas 
Scholarship Scheme for ST students to bring it at 
least to the level of Gross annual family income 
ceiling followed under National Overseas Scholarship 
for SCs. The Committee would like to be informed 
about the steps taken by the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs in this regard.  
11. 9.7 The Committee note that under proviso to Grants 
under Article 275 (1) of the Constitution of India, 
financial assistance is provided to the State 
Governments with notified STs based upon proposals 
received from them. The Committee note that a 
significant percentage of Budgetary allocation is 
earmarked for the grants. However, the Committee 
have found that for the financial year 2025-26 
₹1,541.47 Cr. was allocated at BE stage which was 
reduced to ₹1,171.00 Cr. at the RE stage and the 
Ministry have been able to utilize only ₹327.29 Cr. 
till 19.01.26 of the financial year.  In this regard, 
the Committee firmly believe that grants under 
Article 275(1) of the Constitution of India represent 
a vital constitutional commitment to tribal welfare 
and strengthening the disbursal of funds, 
institutional capacity and oversight functions of the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs vis-à-vis the grants are of 
utmost importance for meaningful and measurable 
improvements in the socio-economic conditions of 
Scheduled Tribes. The Committee, therefore, 
recommend the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to take 
suitable measures to improve co-ordination with 
States, creation of standardized project frameworks 
and outcome-based monitoring mechanism for better 

65 
 
utilization of grants. The Committee would like the 
Ministry to apprise the Committee of the initiatives 
taken in this regard.
