CHAPTER-VIII 
 
 
SCHEME OF RESIDENTIAL EDUCATION FOR STUDENTS IN  
HIGH SCHOOL IN TARGETED AREA (SHRESHTA) FOR SCs 
 
8.1 The objective of the SHRESHTA scheme is to enhance the reach of development 
interventions of the Government and fill the gap in service deficient SCs population 
dominant areas, in the sector of education through the efforts of Voluntary Organizations 
and other organizations and to provide environment for socio-economic upliftment and 
overall development of the Scheduled Castes (SCs).   
8.2 The Scheme is operated under two Modes. Under Mode-I of the Scheme, every 
year a specified number of meritorious SC students in States/UTs are selected through a 
nation-wide entrance test conducted by National Testing Agency (NTA) for providing 
quality residential education in top-class CBSE / State Board affiliated Residential High 
Schools.  Under Mode II, financial assistance is provided to NGOs for running and 
maintenance of projects related to education for Scheduled Caste students. The Scheme 
broadly covers 3 types of projects namely (i) Residential Schools (ii) Non Residential 
Schools (iii)Hostels for both for Primary and Secondary Students. Under the SHRESHTA 
scheme, in mode-1, during the F.Y. 2023-24, fee was reimbursed to private schools for 
providing school and hostel facility to 4168 SC students. Under the SHRESHTA scheme, 
in mode-2, during the F.Y. 2023-24, approximately 11681 number of beneficiaries 
benefitted under the scheme.

“The scheme was started in 1953 and known as Grant-in-Aid to Voluntarily Organizations 
working for SCs till 2020-21. The scheme was revised in 2021-22 and renamed as 
Scheme for Residential Education for Students in High Schools in Targeted Areas 
(SHRESHTA). The scheme has been revised in 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24. During 
the 2021-22, one more mode was introduced under the scheme and presently the scheme 
is being run in following 2 modes.  
 Under mode-1, every year 3000 meritorious SC students are selected through NTA exam for admission in class 9th and 11th(1500 students in each class) for admission in best private residential schools affiliated to CBSE/State Boards for completing education till class 12th.

8.22 The Committee note that under SHRESHTA Scheme, the Residential 
Schools are selected from across the States/UTs on the recommendations of 
CBSE and State Boards to provide high quality residential education from 
class IX to XII  to meritorious  students form Scheduled Caste communities. 
The Committee find that 144 Private residential schools were selected to 
accommodate 3000 students on the basis of NTA examination during the 
year 2023-24 and 2024-25 under the scheme. The Committee note that an 
annual fee between ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,35,000 is granted to schools for each 
student taking admission in the Residential Schools. The Committee were 
informed that the students are getting admission in schools across the 
country as per their performance in NTA examination and preference made 
by the students. The Committee find that the students selected for admission 
are provided bridge course of 3 months to cover the study missed due to the 
time consumed in completion of the admission process. The Committee 
desire that the admission process should be completed in each school by 
the time academic session begins  so that the students do not undergo any 
pressure due to delay in admission.  The Committee feel that the fee fixed for 
each student is not sufficient to meet boarding, tuition fee expenses and 
other infrastructure required to provide top class education to the students. 
Therefore, there is a need to have inbuilt mechanism for review and revision 
of the fee in order to maintain standards of top class education.  The 
Committee during the study visit to one of the schools under SHRESHTA, 

65 
 
while interacting with the students who are coming from other States, 
observed that it is difficult for a school student to cope up with different 
socio-cultural and linguistic environment.  The Committee, therefore, desire 
that the Department may examine the entire process to explore the 
possibility that a student get admission in their domicile State. Hence, the 
Department should evolve a mechanism where a student is provided 
admission in a Top Class Residential Schools selected in their domicile 
State. In view of the foregoing, the Committee recommend that the 
Department would revise  the Scheme at the earliest and apprise the 
Committee in this regard.

1. 2.11 The Committee find that the Department of Social Justice and 
Empowerment spent ₹6,410.09 crore and ₹7,830.26 crore on 
various Scholarships and other educational schemes in 2022-
23 and 2023-24 respectively. Similarly, in the year 2024-25, the

Scholarship Schemes till February, 2025. The Committee

accessible to the deprived sections of the Society through 
various Schemes. The Committee believe that for the success 
of any educational scheme, other factors are also significant 
such as cost of education, availability of good Government

implementation. The Committee are of the opinion that the

schemes of the Department. The Committee would like to 
recommend that the quantum of Scholarship granted to a

to contain the inflation so that the Scheme is more fruitful.

Empowerment is utilized on the Scholarships and other

huge mandate of the Department to cater the needs of various 
marginalized sections including Scheduled Castes, Other 
Backward Classes, Denotified and Nomadic Tribes, 
Economically Weaker sections, Senior Citizens, 
Transgenders, victims of substance abuse through various 
welfare schemes, the Committee urge that the Department of 
Social Justice and Empowerment should focus on other 
schemes also. For this purpose, if additional funds are

the Committee find that there are frequent changes in the 
guidelines of various Schemes such as PM-AJAY, 
SHRESHTA, NAMASTE, PM-VISVAS etc. The Committee are of 
the view that the guidelines of any Scheme should be properly

that the Department will find out the solution by taking into 
confidence the State Governments and also consider 
stepping up the budgetary allocation in future so that the 
Schemes other than educational schemes become meaningful 
for the targeted sections of the society.. 
3. 2.13 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice and 
Empowerment has been able to implement the SNA system 
for flow of funds across the country. The Committee find that 
the Department is organizing ‘Chintan Shivir’, meetings with 
the State Governments and other Implementing Agencies so 
that the complete proposals and Utilization Certificates are 
timely submitted to the Department of Social Justice and 
Empowerment for timely release of funds. The Department 
has also been able to persuade some State Governments to 
return the unspent funds lying with their SNA Accounts. 
However, there are certain States such as Madhya Pradesh, 
Odisha, Assam, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar 

73 
 
Pradesh, etc. have failed in returning the unspent balance in 
their SNA Accounts. The Committee are satisfied with the 
provisions contained in the SNA System and expect that the 
system will certainly help the Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment in maximizing the use of funds allocated to 
the Department. Since some of the State Governments are yet 
to surrender the unutilized amount, they may be asked to 
surrender it immediately so that the next installment is 
released to them and the marginalized people for whom these 
Schemes have been framed  do not suffer for the failure of the 
State Government in completing the formalities required from 
them. The Committee would also like the Department of Social 
Justice and Empowerment to consider incentivizing those 
State Governments that are completing all the formalities in 
time so that the defaulting States also make sincere efforts to 
implement the Schemes of the Government of India.  
4. 2.14 The Committee are well aware that the Department of Social 
Justice and Empowerment is spending large amount of 
budgetary allocation in Scholarship Schemes. The Committee 
have found that year after year the scholarship amount 
released to the eligible students spills over to the next 
academic year as the applications from State Governments 
are received up to the months of February and March. The 
Committee are of the view that current system is required to 
be reviewed as the students should get scholarship within the 
same academic year so that the education of the student is 
not disrupted for want of money. The Committee would like 
the Department to give all the handholding support to the 
State Governments to start the process early so that the 
requisite formalities are completed in time.  The Committee 
expect that the Department should make all out efforts to 
sensitize the State Governments and Other Implementing 
agencies on this aspect and get the issue of last-minute 

74 
 
spending resolved.

livelihood activities for marginalized SC and OBC with a 5 per 
cent interest subvention on income-generating loans upto ₹ 2 
lakhs for individuals and ₹4 lakhs for Self-Help Groups(SHGs). 
However, the actual expenditure was ‘nil’ in 2022-23 and 2023-
24 as the Scheme was not approved for 2022-23. Since the

be made out of allocated funds of ₹11.49 crore and ₹11.95

not able to comprehend the reasons due to which the Scheme 
could not take off till 2024-25 and the Department took almost 
two years in finalizing the guidelines even after the third-party 
evaluation report was submitted in February, 2022. The 
Committee are of the opinion that any new Scheme should be 
launched after exhaustive consultations with all the State 
Governments, stakeholders, banks and other implementing 
agencies. The Committee desire that some mechanism should 
be evolved for the periodic review of Schemes so that the 
flaws are noticed and the requisite changes are made in the 
guidelines to plug the loopholes found during the 
implementation. The Committee would like to be informed of 
the instructions issued in this regard.

2025-26 under the Scheme. The Committee also find from the 
figures given by the Department of Social Justice and 
Empowerment that financial assistance of only  ₹3.00 crore 

75 
 
benefitting 47,809 OBC individuals and ₹4.452 crore 
benefitting 44,006 SC individuals have been provided in 2024-
25.  The Committee find that even after the issuance of 
revised guidelines, the Scheme is not attracting targeted 
beneficiaries. The Committee believe that the target of 15 lakh 
beneficiary fixed for 2024-25 and 2025-26 is very difficult to be 
achieved. The Committee, therefore, desire that the reasons 
due to which Scheme is not picking up should be identified. 
The initiatives taken by the Department to promote the 
Scheme may yield desired results if concerted efforts by the 
Department including NSFDC, NBCFDC, NSKFDC and Banks 
are made to make the Scheme successful. Since the Scheme 
is to be initially implemented in 2024-25 and 2025-26, the 
Committee are  concerned about the tenure of the Scheme 
and desire that the Department should consider extending the 
tenure of the Scheme as the tenure of two years is too less for 
any Scheme to be successful.

for SCs and OBCs were launched in 2015 and 2019 
respectively with a Corpus of ͅ₹750 crore and ₹180.92 crore. 
The Committee find that ͅ₹571.60 crore to 234 companies 
belonging to Scheduled Caste Entrepreneurs and ₹112.35 
crore to 22 companies belonging to Backward Classes have 
been sanctioned. The Committee find that the Scheme will be 
discontinued by 31st March, 2025. The Committee also find 
from the Report of the evaluation study conducted by IIPA 
that the VCF-SC is a distinct Scheme and needs continuation. 
The Committee feel that the suggestions made in the 
Evaluation study such as, delays in security clearances, 
better post loan support, dissemination about the Scheme, 
grievance redressal mechanism, etc should have been 
addressed instead of discontinuing the Scheme. Since the 
Scheme is proposed to be discontinued by 31st March, 2025, 

76 
 
the Committee expect that the sanctioned loan will be 
disbursed to the entrepreneurs in full as out of ₹558.09 crore 
sanctioned to 143 companies upto December, 2024 under 
VCF-SC only ₹393.87 crore has been sanctioned. Similarly, 
under VCF-BC out of ₹94.08 crore sanctioned to 18 companies 
upto December, 2024 only ₹51.50 crore has been disbursed. 
The Committee would also like to be informed of the 
proposals received after December, 2024 upto 31st March, 
2025 and the action taken on these proposals. 
8. 4.15 The Venture Capital Fund for SCs and OBC will be 
discontinued after 31st March, 2025 and the Department is in 
the process of formulating a new Venture Capital Fund for 
deprived and marginalized sections. The Committee hope that 
the observations made by IIPA in the evaluation study may 
also be considered before finalizing the new Scheme and take 
all the necessary steps to make it effective so that it is not 
required to revise the Scheme frequently. The Committee 
would like the Department to take requisite action for early 
finalization of the new Scheme with detailed guidelines for all 
the implementing agencies.  The Committee may like to be 
apprised of the current status and the time by which the new 
Scheme is likely to be launched.

Empowerment is implementing Pradhan Mantri Dakshata Aur 
Kushalata Sampana Hitgrahi (PM-DAKSH) for SC, OBC and 
others since 2020-21. It is found that during the year 2022-23 
and 2023-24, the Department was able to spend ₹14.94 crore 
out of RE of ₹84.00 crore, ₹58.34 crore out of RE of ₹140.00 
crore respectively. Further, the Department has not been able 
to spend even a single rupee in 2024-25 till February, 2025 out 
of Revised Estimate of ₹80.00 crore as empanelment of 
Training Institutes was delayed. The Committee are 

77 
 
concerned with the socio-economic development of SC, OBC 
and others, hence, believe that any slackness on behalf of the 
concerned authorities would defeat the purpose of the 
Scheme. The Committee are of the opinion that the Schemes 
instituted with the noble objectives cannot be left at the mercy 
of the concerned authorities, particularly when the 
Government of India is making all efforts for the socio-
economic development of the targeted communities by 
allocating huge funds. The Committee would therefore, like to 
recommend that in future all necessary steps are taken to 
ensure that the empanelment of Training Institutes, etc. is not 
delayed and the necessary formalities are timely completed.  
The Committee would like the Department to take necessary 
measures so that the targets fixed are achieved. The 
Committee would also like the Department to enhance the 
targets keeping into consideration the population of these 
categories i.e., SC, OBC and others so that the maximum 
people can take benefit of the Scheme.   
10. 5.13  The Committee have found that the Department of Social 
Justice and Empowerment has sent a proposal to Ministry of 
Skill Development & Entrepreneurship to merge the PM-
DAKSH Scheme with the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas 
Yojana (PMKVY) Scheme in order to improve efficiency and 
optimize public expenditure as the PM-DAKSH Scheme largely 
overlaps with the objectives and structure of PMKVY. The

78

Umbrella Scheme of SHREYAS consisting of 4 sub-
schemes viz. National fellowship for SCs, National 
Overseas Scholarship for SCs, Top Class Education for

Overseas Scholarship Scheme and ₹55.00 crore under

₹93.00 crore under various sub-schemes   are expected

to the Institutions/ Organisations to submit the complete 
proposals within the given time frame to avoid any delay

pending with the Department for approval and also the 
proposals expected by 31 March 2025, the Department 
may take necessary action for early approval so that 
funds allocated under this Scheme is utilized fully in this 
Financial Year. The Committee would like to be apprised 
in this regard.

due to late commencement of courses in the academic 
year 2023-24 and some proposals are also expected to

Committee also note that the Department have revised 
the guidelines from the selection year 2023-24 to 
achieve the target. However, the Memorandum of 
Understanding required to be signed with Dr. Ambedkar 
Foundation by all the Central Universities to become 

79 
 
part of the Scheme has been signed by 19 out of 55

availing benefits of the Scheme. The Committee also

the number of 125 slots fixed under the Scholarship 
Scheme each year. The Committee are of the strong 
opinion that the income eligibility criteria fixed for the 
Scholarship Schemes deprives many meritorious 
candidates from availing the benefits of the Scheme. 
The Committee, therefore, desire that the income fixed 
for making candidate eligible for scholarship needs to 
be reviewed so that more candidates are covered under 
the Scheme.

80 
 
for SC and in 2019-20 for National Overseas Scholarship

like the Department to take suggestions from all the 
stakeholders while evaluating all the Schemes so that 
the difficulties faced by them in implementing the 
Scheme are taken care of while framing the new

necessary measures may be taken for timely completion

fully during these years as the Department did not either

82

Schools. The Committee were informed that the 
students are getting admission in schools across the 
country as per their performance in NTA examination 
and preference made by the students. The Committee 
find that the students selected for admission are 
provided bridge course of 3 months to cover the study

admission process. The Committee desire that the 

83

students do not undergo any pressure due to delay in 
admission.  The Committee feel that the fee fixed for 
each student is not sufficient to meet boarding, tuition 
fee expenses and other infrastructure required to 
provide top class education to the students. Therefore,

revision of the fee in order to maintain standards of top

recommend that the Department would revise the

regard.

  I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment (2024-25) having been authorized by the Committee do 
present on their behalf this Sixth Report on 'Demands for Grants for the year

2. The Committee considered the ‘Demands for Grants (2025-26)’ of the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities which were laid on 
the Table of the House on 11 February, 2025. After obtaining the Budget 
Documents, Explanatory Notes, etc., the Committee took evidence of the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities on 20 February, 
2025. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at the sitting held 
on 12.03.2025. 
3. The Committee wish to express their thanks to the Officers of the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities for tendering oral 
evidence and placing before them the detailed written notes and post 
evidence information as desired by the Committee in connection with the 
examination of the ‘Demands for Grants (2025-26)’. 
4. For ease of reference observations/ recommendations/ comments of 
the Committee have been printed in bold in the body of the Report.

REPORT 
CHAPTER I 
The Department of Disability Affairs was carved out of the Ministry of Social 
Justice and Empowerment on May 12, 2012 in order to give focused attention to policy 
issues and meaningful thrust to the activities aimed at welfare and empowerment of the 
Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). It was subsequently renamed as Department of 
Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities on 8 December, 2014 and acts as a nodal 
agency for matters pertaining to disability and persons with disabilities including 
effecting closer coordination among different stakeholders. 
1.2 Empowerment of persons with disabilities is an inter-disciplinary process, 
covering various aspects namely, prevention, early detection, intervention, education, 
health, vocational training, rehabilitation and social integration. Thus the vision of the 
Department is to build an inclusive society in which equal opportunities are provided for 
the growth and development of persons with disabilities so that they can lead 
productive, safe and dignified lives. 
1.3 The Objectives of the Department are enumerated as under : 
(i) Physical rehabilitation, which includes early detection and intervention, 
counseling and medical rehabilitation and assistance in procuring 
appropriate aids and appliances for reducing the effect of disabilities; 
(ii) Educational rehabilitation including vocational education; 
(iii) Economic empowerment; 
(iv) Developing rehabilitation professionals/personnel; 
(v) Improving internal efficiency/responsiveness/service delivery; and 
(vi) Advocating empowerment of persons with disabilities through awareness 
generation among different sections of the society such as cultural, 
recreational and sports activities. 
1.4 The scope of the Department is enumerated as under:- 

2 
 
(i) Special schemes aimed at rehabilitation and social, educational and economic 
empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, e.g. supply of aids and appliances, 
scholarships, residential schools, skill training, concessional loans and subsidy for 
self-employment, etc.  
(ii) Education and Training of Rehabilitation Professionals. 
(iii) International Conventions and Agreements on matters dealt within the Department 
e.g. United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. 
(iv) Awareness generation, research, evaluation and training in regard to subjects 
allocated to the Department.

2.15 From a thorough examination of the Demands for Grants (DFG) over 
the past three years, the Committee observe a persistent trend of 
underutilization of funds across key schemes such as ADIP, SIPDA, DDRS, 
and Scholarships, with actual expenditures consistently falling short of 
Revised Estimates (RE) and Budget Estimates (BE). The BE allocations were 
invariably reduced at the RE stage in 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25, yet 
the Department was unable to fully utilize even the reduced funds. The 
Department utilized 97.38 percent of RE in 2022-23 and 93.39 percent in 
2023-24. However, as of 03.03.2025, only ₹892.68 crore of ₹1167.27 crore 
(76.48 percent) has been spent. This shortfall was primarily due to 
disruptions from the introduction of the CNA and TSA models. Delays in 
receiving Utilization Certificates (UCs) from State Governments under SIPDA 
and a lack of adequate proposals from North-Eastern States further hindered 
funds utilization. While the Committee were assured by the Department’s 
representatives that the remaining 2024-25 funds would be fully utilized by 
31.03.2025, the Committee strongly urge the Department to adopt targeted 
remedial measures and strategic interventions to ensure efficient fund 
utilization in 2025-26. Proactive engagement with State Governments, NGOs, 
and implementing agencies is essential to streamline proposal submissions 
and disbursement process, particularly for skill training programs and capital 
expenditure. Furthermore, given the challenges in meeting fixed targets for 
schemes like SIPDA and DDRS, the Department should reassess target-
setting methodologies to ensure that they are realistic, flexible, and aligned 
with performance trends. The Committee recommend decisive action to 
improve fund utilization and program execution in the remaining year of the 
2024-26 financial cycle, ensuring that allocated resources effectively 
advance the welfare of persons with disabilities and that the Department 
successfully meets its commitments under various schemes.

CHAPTER-III 
ASSISTANCE TO PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES FOR PURCHASE/FITTING OF 
AIDS/APPLIANCES (ADIP) 
 The main objective of the Scheme is to provide grants-in-aid to the various 
implementing agencies (National Institutes/ Composite Regional Centres /Artificial 
Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO)/District Disability Rehabilitation 
Centres/State Handicapped Development Corporations/other local bodies/ NGOs)   to 
assist  needy persons with disabilities in procuring durable, scientifically manufactured 
standard aids and appliances to promote physical, social and psychological rehabilitation 
of Persons with Disabilities through reducing the effects of disabilities and at the same 
time enhancing their economic potential.  Assistive devices are given to Persons with 
Disabilities with the aim of improving their independent functioning, and arresting the 
extent of disability and occurrence of secondary disability. The Scheme also envisages 
conduct of corrective surgeries, whenever required, before providing an assistive 
device. The Scheme has been revised/modified w.e.f  26.09.2024. 
3.2 The Eligibility criteria under the ADIP Scheme is as below: 
 Holding a UDID card issued by the Ministry with at least 40per cent 
disability. 
 Monthly income from all sources not to exceed ₹22,500/ per month for 
100per cent assistance ₹22,501/- to ₹30,000/- per month for 50 
percent assistance. 
 New assistive devices are provided after 3 years. However, for children 
below 18 years of age, the minimum time of assistance is one year for 
customized items.

and Camp activity for distribution of aids and assistive devices. Apart from this, 
ADIP Scheme in convergence with Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) i.e. ADIP SSA 
,aids and assistive devices are distributed to children with special needs (CWSN) 
in collaboration with Ministry of Education in 60:40 ratio of cost of aids and

CHAPTER IV 
DEENDAYAL DIVYANGJAN  REHABILITATION SCHEME (DDRS) 
  Deendayal Divyangjan Rehabilitation Scheme is a Central Sector scheme of the 
Department to provide grant-in-aid to non-governmental organizations (NGOs) for 
projects relating to rehabilitation of persons with disabilities aimed at enabling them to 
reach and maintain their optimal, physical, sensory, intellectual, psychiatric or socio-
functional levels. The Scheme is being implemented since 1999 with the objective of 
ensuring effective implementation of the Right of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
Activities/components admissible for grant under the scheme to the organisations 
include honorarium to staff, transportation of beneficiaries, stipend for 
beneficiaries/hostel maintenance, cost of raw materials and contingencies to meet office 
expenses, electricity, water charges and rent. 
4.2      The Grant-in-aid is provided to Implementing agencies (IAs) which are 
registered with NGO- Darpan Portal of NITI Aayog and have obtained unique ID of NITI 
Aayog. The Grant-in-Aid (GIA) is provided through e-Anudaan portal of the Department. 
All financial assistance is provided to the Implementing agencies through Public 
Financial Management System (PFMS). 
 4.3 The eligibility conditions for Grants under DDRS are as under:- 
Organizations registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (XXI of 1860), or 
any relevant Act of the State/Union Territory; or a Trust registered under the Indian 
Trust Act, 1882 or any other similar Act for the time being in force; or a Not-for-Profit 
company registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 or any relevant Act for 
the time being in force.    
a. Registration should have been in force for at least 2 years at the time of applying 
for grant under this scheme. 
b.  Must be registered in the NITI Aayog portal (NGO-Darpan) portal and obtain 
Unique  ID of NGO-Darpan before applying for Grant under the scheme. 
c. Must be registered either under erstwhile Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995 or 
Rights   of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.   

28 
 
d. An organization as specified above should have the following characteristics: 
(i) It should have a managing body with its powers, duties and responsibilities 
clearly defined and laid down in Memorandum of Association. 
(ii) It should have resources, facilities and experience for undertaking the 
programme. 
(iii) It should not be run for profit to any individual or a body of individuals.

District Disability Rehabilitation Centre (DDRC): 
4.14 DDRC Scheme is a sub component under the DDRS scheme from year 2019-20. 
Before that it was under SIPDA. DDRC is being implemented since 1999-2000. DDRCs 
are established for providing comprehensive rehabilitation services to Persons with 
Disabilities (PwDs). 325 districts were initially identified for establishing DDRCs, out of 
which, DDRCs were set up in 269 districts. Presently all districts of the country are 
authorized to establish DDRC. At present, there are total 74 DDRCs are functional. 
4.15 The Main functions of DDRCs are as under:- 
Early Identification and Intervention, awareness generation, assessment of 
need/provision/fitment of assistive devices, therapeutic services e.g. 
Physiotherapy, Occupational Therapy,  Speech Therapy, etc., referral and 
arrangement of surgical correction,  assistance in providing scholarships, skill 
training, arrangement of loans for self-employment, survey & identification of 
persons with disabilities through camp approach, assisting in the issue of UDID 
Cards, and to act as outreach centres for the services provided by the National 
Institutes and for promoting barrier free environment. The scheme has been 
revised with effect from 01.04.2023.  
4.16 Regarding the proposal for GIA of DDRC, it has been informed as under:- 
 “Proposals for Grant-in-aid for DDRCs under Deendayal Divyangjan Rehabilitation 
 Scheme (DDRS) were accepted through offline mode till the FY 2023-24. The 
 Ministry now aims at making the application process smoother and more efficient 
 by embracing the convenience of online application of proposals for Grant-in-aid 
 for DDRCs through the e-Anudaan Portal from the year 2024-25. Now some of 
 the DDRCs have also submitted their online proposals for the year 2024-25 on e-
 Anudaan Portal”.   
  

34 
 
4.17 The Committee recognize the crucial role of DDRS in providing 
rehabilitation services to Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) through NGOs and 
implementing agencies. An analysis of fund utilization trends over the past 
three years reveals significant fluctuations, with 2022-23 and 2023-24 
recording high fund utilization, while in 2024-25, actual expenditure stood at 
₹87.95 crore as of 03.03.2025, despite a Budget Estimate (BE) of ₹165 crore. 
The Committee note that the transition from the CNA Model to TSA Hybrid 
Model 1-A led to procedural delays in fund disbursement, impacting the pace 
of implementation. Additionally, as grants were previously processed on a 
reimbursement basis, NGOs were required to submit audited accounts by 
June 30 of the next financial year, further slowing down fund releases. 
However, with the revised DDRS guidelines effective from 01.10.2024, which 
allow Grant-in-Aid on an advance-cum-reimbursement basis, the Committee 
expect that fund flow will improve and implementation delays will be 
minimized. The Committee recommend that the Department ensure timely 
release of advances, particularly to NGOs with strong compliance records, 
while also strengthening the capacity of implementing agencies to meet 
documentation requirements on time, ensuring efficient utilization of 
allocated funds. The Committee also urge the Department to ensure a 
smoother transition in funding mechanisms by streamlining financial 
procedures and proactively addressing administrative bottlenecks to avoid 
such shortfalls in future fiscal years. 
4.18 The Committee note that physical targets under DDRS have witnessed 
a downward revision since 2024-25, with the target reduced from 40,000 in 
2023-24 to 32,000 in 2024-25 and 2025-26. The Department has attributed 
this to the number of projects supported remaining largely the same over the 
years, with new proposals being considered only after the release of funds to 
organizations. The Committee emphasize that rehabilitation services for 
PwDs should not be constrained due to procedural delays in fund 
disbursaland recommend that the Department take proactive steps to 
expedite approvals for new projects. The Committee urge the Department to 

35 
 
explore expanding the scope of DDRS to cover more PwDs by identifying 
underserved areas where rehabilitation services are limited or absent. 
4.19 The Committee appreciate the Department’s efforts in introducing 
monitoring mechanisms, including video inspections of NGOs and time-bound 
forwarding of proposals under the revised DDRS. The provision for automatic 
transmission of pending proposals from the district levels to the State 
Government and further to the DEPwD if no action is taken within a month of 
submission is a commendable measure aimed to streamline the approval 
process and minimize administrative delays.   However, the Committee 
recommend strict enforcement of these provisions to ensure that no proposal 
remains pending for an unreasonable duration. Further, the Committee 
support the decision that organizations running both DDRS and National 
Trust schemes should choose only one to avoid duplication of services, 
ensuring that funds reach the maximum number of  beneficiaries. 
4.20 The Committee note that DDRCs function as decentralized 
rehabilitation units, providing early identification and intervention, assistive 
device distribution, therapy services, and skill development for PwDs. While 
DDRCs were initially planned for 325 districts, only 269 DDRCs were set up, 
and currently, only 74 are functional. The Committee express concern over 
the low operational count of DDRCs and recommend that the Department 
prioritize the revival and expansion of DDRCs in districts lacking 
rehabilitation facilities. The Committee also welcome the shift to online 
applications for Grant-in-Aid (GIA) for DDRCs through the e-Anudaan Portal 
from 2024-25, which is expected to simplify and expedite the application 
process.

CHAPTER V 
 
SCHEMES ARISING OUT OF THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PERSONS WITH 
DISABILITIES ACT 2016 (SIPDA) 
The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities has been 
implementing a central sector scheme, the Scheme for Implementation of the Rights of 
Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (SIPDA) for providing financial assistance for 
undertaking various activities outlined in the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 
2016 (RPwD Act). The RPwD Act, 2016 endorses the rights of Persons with Disabilities 
for access to education, vocational training, employment, public transport, built-up 
environment, and information and communication ecosystems and upholds their 
independence and dignity.  
5.2 SIPDA is an umbrella scheme of the Department comprising of following 10 sub-
schemes: 
(i) Creation of Barrier Free Environment for Persons with Disabilities  
(ii) Accessible India Campaign (AIC)  
(iii) Divyang Samarth Yojana [National Action Plan (NAP) for Skill Training 
of Persons with Disabilities and Incentive to Private Employer].  
(iv) Unique Disability ID (UDID) Project  
(v) Awareness Generation and Publicity (AGP) with In-service Training and 
Sensitization of key functionaries of Central & State Governments, Local 
Bodies and Other Provider.  
(vi) Financial support to Study and  Research on priority areas of disability 
sector and to Research & Development of suitable product, aids & 
appliances for empowerment of  Persons with Disabilities  
(vii) Assistance to Spinal Injury Centres (State Spinal Injury Centre (SSIC) 
and Indian Spinal Injury Centre (ISIC))  
(viii) Cross-Disability Early Intervention Centre

(ix) Projects under SIPDA:  Financial Support for Development of Accessible 
Learning Materials and Financial Assistance for the existing Deaf 
Colleges in five regions of the Country 
(x) Central Project Management Unit (CPMU) cum Data Strategy Unit

5.13 The Committee observe significant inconsistencies in the Budget 
Estimates (BE), Revised Estimates (RE), and actual fund utilization under 
SIPDA over the past three years. Frequent downward revisions at the RE 
stage and low actual expenditure despite available allocations indicate 
systemic inefficiencies in fund absorption. In 2022-23, the BE was ₹240.39 
crore, which was reduced by 58.4 per cent at the RE stage to ₹100 crore, 
with actual expenditure at just ₹65.59 crore. Similarly, in 2023-24, the BE of 
₹150 crore was cut to ₹67 crore, yet actual expenditure exceeded the RE at 
₹76.79 crore (114.7 percent of RE). In 2024-25, despite an RE of ₹111 crore, 
only ₹43.90 crore (39.5 percent of RE) had been utilized as of 03.03.2025. 
These fluctuations indicate inconsistent fund planning and delays in fund 
utilization, leading to missed opportunities for enhancing accessibility and 
disability-related initiatives. The Committee strongly recommend that the 
Department strengthen its financial planning mechanisms by ensuring that 
BE allocations are realistic, demand-driven, and reflective of actual 
implementation capacity.  
5.14 In addition to financial inconsistencies, the Committee note a 
significant shortfall in meeting physical targets under SIPDA. In 2022-23, 
against a target of 44,520 beneficiaries, 44,162 were assisted, reflecting 99.2 
percent achievement. However, in 2023-24, the achievement dropped to 
29,374 beneficiaries against the same target (65.9 percent), and as of 
16.01.2025, only 11,933 beneficiaries (27.4per cent) had been covered out of 
the 43,520 target for 2024-25. This indicates delays in execution and 
ineffective implementation strategies. The Committee recommend that the 
Department enhance coordination with State Governments and 

42 
 
implementing agencies to ensure faster approval and processing of 
applications, preventing recurring lapses in achieving physical targets. 
Furthermore, a robust monitoring framework should be instituted to track 
real-time progress, ensuring better alignment between financial allocations 
and physical achievements. The Department must identify and address 
systemic bottlenecks to ensure that SIPDA meets its intended goals of 
accessibility, empowerment, and inclusion of Persons with Disabilities. 
5.15 The Committee also find that persistent challenges such as delays in 
fund disbursement, pending utilization certificates, and incomplete proposals 
have impacted the effective implementation of SIPDA. Given that SIPDA is 
the flagship scheme for PwDs, the Committee strongly recommend that the 
Department strengthen its monitoring and coordination mechanisms by 
ensuring regular follow-ups with State Governments and implementing 
agencies. The Central Project Monitoring Unit (CPMU) should be further 
empowered to enable real-time tracking of fund utilization, proposal 
approvals, and physical progress under various sub-schemes .Furthermore, 
timely clearance of compliance documents such as Utilization Certificates 
(UCs) and pending proposals should be ensured to prevent underutilization 
and last-minute fund surrender. 
 
Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) 
5.16 Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) was launched on 03rd 
December, 2015 as a nation-wide flagship campaign for achieving universal accessibility 
to enable Divyangjan (Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) to gain access for equal 
opportunity, independent living and full participation in all aspects of life in an inclusive 
society. The campaign was kick-started with three verticals - enhancing accessibility of 
already built environment/buildings and infrastructure, making all transport systems like 
buses, trains, etc. Divyangjan friendly; and Information & Communication eco-system 
accessible to all Divyangjans. The Campaign was scheduled to continue upto 31st 
March, 2024, nonetheless, it has now been subsumed under the Sub-Scheme – 

43 
 
“Creation of Barrier Free Environment Scheme (CBFE)” under the umbrella Scheme for 
Implementation of Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (SIPDA) as accessibility is a 
continuous and on-going process. 
5.17 In view of this the Department was asked to clarify how accessibility efforts will 
be sustained after the Accessible India Campaign is subsumed under the Sub-Scheme – 
“Creation of Barrier Free Environment Scheme (CBFE)” under the umbrella Scheme for 
Implementation of Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (SIPDA) and how would funds 
be allocated for its continuation. In reply, the Department has furnished as under  
“It is noteworthy that the Accessible India Campaign has, subsequent to 
31.03.2024, been subsumed under the “Creation of Barrier Free Environment 
(CBFE) Scheme”. Furthermore, there is no separate budgetary allocation under 
the CBFE Scheme and funds are disbursed directly under the Budgetary 
Allocation in the umbrella Scheme – SIPDA.  
Regarding the sustenance of accessibility efforts after subsumption of AIC into 
CBFE, the Department is promoting the same by providing for barrier free 
environment for persons with disabilities, which includes access to built 
environment in schools, colleges, educational and training institutions, offices 
and public buildings, recreational areas, health centres/hospitals etc. This will 
include ramps, rails, lifts, accessible toilets for wheelchair users, Braille signage 
and auditory signals, tactile flooring, slopes in pavements for easy access of 
wheelchair users, engraving on the surface of zebra crossings for persons with 
blind or low vision, engraving on the edges of railway platforms for persons with 
blind or low vision and appropriate symbols of disability etc. Under this sub-
scheme, since the subsumption of AIC into CBFE Sub scheme, Rs. 9.96 Cr has 
been released to State/UT Governments, autonomous organizations/NIs and 
statutory bodies for provisioning of Barrier Free Environment in public 
establishments and accessibility trainings”.

5.24 National Action Plan for Skill Training under SIPDA 
The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities launched 
the National Action Plan for Skill Development of Persons with Disabilities (NAP-
SDP) in March 2015 with the objective to enhance skills of Persons with 
Disabilities, enable them to have gainful employment/ become self-employed and 
to make them self-reliant and independent members of society. Training under 
the NAP-SDP scheme is being provided through various Government and Non-
Government Organizations. The scheme is being implemented on the common 
norms prescribed by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 
(MSDE). PwDs with at least 40per cent disability in the age group between the 
age of 15-59 years are eligible to avail skill training programme. This is being 
implemented through PM-DAKSH-DEPwD Portal which is providing opportunity to 
PwDs to apply for the skill training as per their choice of training partner, place

training centers as per his disability and locality. PwD also can enroll in area of 
interest on PM-DAKSH-DEPwD portal.  
NAP-SDP Scheme is a Central Sector Scheme, it is a demand driven scheme. 
Funds under the scheme are released to empanelled organizations from across 
the Country on the basis of their demands/proposals.  Since 2022, an amount of 
Rs.23.54 crore has been released for conducting skill training under NAP-SDP as 
till date.

5.34 Unique Disability ID Project (UDID) 
 
The UDID Card or Unique Disability Identity card is an initiative by 
Government of India with a view of creating a National Database for PwDs and 
to issue a Unique Disability Identity Card to each person with disabilities. The 
Department has instituted and online portal (www.swavalambancard.gov.in) 
where the medical authorities notified by the respective State Government have 
been on-boarded for issuance of disability certificate/Unique Disability Identity 
Card (UDID) to Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). The disability certificate/UDID 
card is issued by the notified medical authority of State/UT. 
 
The main objectives of UDID are :   
a. To create a National Database for PwDs by identifying and issuing a 
Unique Disability ID Card to every Person with Disability through the web-
portal. 
b. Uniformity in the form of disability certificate and UDID card across the 
country. 
c. Issue Disability Certificates not only to those who are still uncovered but 
also to persons with new types of disabilities under the RPwD Act 2016 
d. Encourage transparency, efficiency and ease of delivering government 
benefits to PwDs pertaining to  several Schemes, include Scholarship, Skill 
training, Inclusive Education, Rehabilitation, Pension, 

56 
 
e. Tracking of physical and financial progress of benefit delivery at all levels 
of hierarchy of implementation – from Village, Block, District, State and 
National levels. 
 
5.35 When asked about the benefits of UDID, the Committee have been informed as 
under:  
“Access to government schemes and benefits: The UDID card is 
recognized as a proof of disability by the government of India. This means 
that PwDs can use their UDID card to access various government schemes 
and benefits such as financial assistance, healthcare services, education, 
and employment. 
 
Easy identification: The UDID card provides a unique identification 
number to each PwD. This helps in easy identification of the person with 
disability and ensures that they receive the right kind of assistance and 
support. 
 
Accessibility: The UDID card contains information about the type and level 
of disability of the person. This information can be used to make public 
places and transportation more accessible for PwDs”.  
5.36 Asked to explain the mechanism of this scheme, the Department has submitted 
as under:- 
“The Department has instituted an online portal (www.swavalambancard.gov.in) 
where the medical authorities notified by the respective State Government have 
been on-boarded for issuance of disability certificate/Unique Disability Identity 
Card (UDID) to Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). Under Unique Disability Id 
project, disability certificates and UDID cards are issued to persons with 
disabilities mentioned in the RPwD Act, 2016. The persons in rural and far flung 
areas who don’t have internet coverage, may visit any CSC Centre for applying 
for Disability Certificate and UDID Card.   
At central level, the UDID Project is managed by the Department of 
Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), Ministry of Social Justice 
and Empowerment in the country. At state level, UDID project is managed by the 
State Social Welfare Departments in consultation with the State Health 
Departments. Also there is provision to appoint one state coordinator in each 
State/UT for smooth implementation of the UDID project in the country. The 
Grant is Aid for remuneration of these state coordinators is provided by the 
DEPwD”. 

57 
 
 
While no targets are set for this project, about 1.18 crore UDID has been 
generated so far through Swavalamban portal.

strengthen medical infrastructure, expedite the inclusion of private medical 
professionals in the certification process, and ensure the availability of well-

should facilitate specialized training programs for medical authorities to

5.40 Recognizing the UDID’s critical role in enabling PwDs to access various

structured and time-bound approach should be adopted to enhance 
accessibility and ensure that all eligible PwDs receive their UDID cards 
without unnecessary delays. 
5.41 The Committee further observe that PwDs in rural and remote areas 
face difficulties in accessing the UDID system due to limited internet

also like to recommend that awareness campaigns be conducted in 
collaboration with State Governments to ensure that all eligible PwDs are 
aware of the benefits of UDID and the process for obtaining it.

CHAPTER VI 
 
SCHOLARSHIPS  FOR STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES 
 
Section 31 (1) & (2) of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 mandates 
that every child with benchmark disability between the age of six to eighteen years shall 
have the right to free education in a neighborhood school, or in a special school, of his 
choice and the appropriate Government and local authorities shall ensure their access 
to free education in an appropriate environment till he attains the age of eighteen 
years. 
 To fulfill this mandate, the DEPwD is implementing Umbrella Scheme 
‘Scholarships for Students with Disabilities’ comprising following six components with 
the objective to empower students with disabilities to study further to earn their 
livelihood and to find a dignified place in the society - 
(i) Pre-matric Scholarship (For Classes IX  and X) 
(ii) Post-matric Scholarship (For Class XI to Post-Graduate Degree/Diploma 
(iii) Top Class Education (For Graduate and Post-Graduate Degree/Diploma in 
notified institutes of excellence in education) 
(iv) National Overseas Scholarship (For Master’s Degree/Ph.D. in 
Institutions/Colleges/Universities abroad) 
(v) National Fellowship for PwDs (For M. Phil and Ph.D. in Indian Universities)  
(vi) Free Coaching schemes (For recruitment examinations for Group A, B and C 
posts and entrance examinations for admission to various technical and 
professional courses) 
6.2 The Salient Features of various Scholarship schemes are as below:- 
(i) 50per cent of the total scholarship slots available each year in Pre-matric, 
Post-matric and Top Class Education and 30 percent slots in National 
Overseas Scholarship and Free Coaching Scholarship Scheme are reserved 
for girl candidates.  
(ii) Various assistance under the Scholarship Schemes include Maintenance 
Allowance, Tuition fees, Book allowance, Disability allowance among other 
financial assistance as applicable under various components.  

64 
 
(iii) Top Class Education also provides for Reimbursement of expenses for 
purchase of a computer/ laptop and requisite aids and assistive devices.  
(iv) National Overseas Scholarship also provides contingency and equipment 
allowance. Disbursement of scholarship and reimbursement of 
miscellaneous expenses is done by M/o External Affairs (MEA) through 
Indian Mission abroad. 
(v) National Fellowship scheme provides for award of fellowships to 200 
Fellows each year; 75per cent scholars based on National Eligibility Test-
Junior Research Fellowship (NET-JRF) of UGC and remaining 25per cent 
scholars based on UGC-Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (UGC-
CSIR) NET-JRF joint test. 
(vi) Free Coaching Scheme is implemented by the Department through National 
Institutes/ Composite Regional Centers and also through Central 
Universities/Institutes, State Universities under the purview of Central 
Government and State Governments and any other government institutes 
working in the field of education/special education.  
6.3 The General Conditions of Eligibility for Scholarship Scheme are as under: 
(i) The scholarships are open only to Indian nationals.  
(ii) All the components of scholarships are open to students with benchmark 
disability i.e. 40per cent or more disability as defined in ‘Rights of Persons 
with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
6.4 Further, the applicants should have/possess:       
a) Aadhaar based biometric authentication. 
b) UDID/UDID enrolment with valid certificate of disability issued by the 
competent authority 
c) Not more than two children with disabilities of the same parents will be 
entitled to receive benefits of the scheme. In case the second child is a twin, 
the scholarship under the schemes will be admissible to the twin. 
d) Scholarship for studying in any class will be available for only one year.  If 
a student has to repeat a class, she/he would not get scholarship for that class 
for a second (or a subsequent) year.   
e) A scholarship holder under this scheme will not avail any other 
scholarship/stipend. No scholarship will be paid to the students under this 
scheme from the date he/she accepts any other scholarship/stipend.

6.17 The Committee observe significant fluctuations in fund allocation, 
utilization, and target achievement under the Scholarship Scheme for 
Students with Disabilities. In 2022-23, the Revised Estimate (RE) was 
increased to ₹145.00 crore, with 97.9 percent utilization (₹142.00 crore).

crore, and as of 03.03.2025, only ₹58.38 crore (72.9 percent of RE) had been 
utilized. Similarly, physical target achievement dropped from 99.2 percent in 
2022-23 to just 27.4 percent in 2024-25(as of Jan, 2025). This 
underutilization, despite high demand in previous years, indicates the need 

72 
 
for better forecasting and planning. The Committee recommend that the 
Department adopt a more structured approach to fund allocation, ensuring 
that budgetary provisions align with actual demand. Additionally, efforts 
should be made to streamline the verification and disbursement process at 
the State Nodal Officer level to avoid delays and ensure timely financial 
assistance to beneficiaries. 
6.18 Given the low application numbers in certain years, the Committee 
emphasize the need for a more robust awareness campaign. While steps 
have been taken, such as newspaper advertisements and communication 
with State Governments, a more proactive strategy is required. The 
Department should leverage digital platforms, collaborate with educational 
institutions, and engage disability rights organizations to maximize outreach. 
Special efforts must be made to target students in remote and rural areas 
who may be unaware of their eligibility for these scholarships. 
6.19 To prevent recurring issues of low fund utilization, the Committee 
urges the Department to implement a real-time monitoring mechanism for 
tracking application processing and fund disbursement. Regular review 
meetings with State Nodal Officers should be mandated, and timelines 
should be fixed for application verification and fund release. Additionally, 
simplifying application procedures and integrating AI-based verification tools 
can significantly improve efficiency. The Committee stress that every effort 
must be made to ensure full utilization of the ₹145 crore allocated for 2025-
26, benefiting the maximum number of eligible students with disabilities.

Centre for Disability Sports  
Centre for Disability Sports now known as Atal Bihari Vajpayee Training Centre for 
Disability Sports (ABV-TCDS), Gwalior is an Autonomous body established by the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (Divyangjan), Ministry of 
Social Justice & Empowerment, Govt. of India. It is a premier facility dedicated to the 
development and promotion of para-sports in India and aims to provide world-class 
training, rehabilitation, and competition opportunities for athletes with disabilities. The 
main objectives of the centre are as under  
(i) To establish a state-of-the-art international level Centre of Excellence for sports 
for Divyang sports persons (PwDs) with full accessibility as per norms. 
(ii) To create specialized sports infrastructure so that the para-sports persons can 
undergo rigorous and specialized training in the Centre. 
(iii) To ensure the participation of Divyangjan in sports activities in greater numbers 
and enable them to effectively compete in international events. 
(iv) To help build confidence and develop a sense of belonging in Divyangjan to 
facilitate their integration into Society. 
7.2 The institute provides sports training with the latest facilities at par with the 
world to persons with disabilities to enable them to effectively compete and win medals 
in Paralympics, Deaflympics, Special Olympics and other International events for Sports 
persons with Disabilities. Sports facilities are available including outdoor activities like 
Archery, Athletics, Football and Tennis, and Indoor activities like Badminton, Wheelchair 
Basketball, Table Tennis, Sitting Volleyball, Judo, Taekwondo, Wheelchair Fencing, 
Wheelchair rugby, Boccia, Goalball, Football 5-a-Side, Para Dance Sport and Para 
Powerlifting as well as a hostel.

CHAPTER VIII 
NATIONAL UNIVERSITY FOR DIVYANGJAN 
In the budget announcement of Hon’ble Finance Minister in FY-2015-16, 
upgradation of National Institute of Speech and Hearing (NISH) into a National 
University of Disability Studies and Rehabilitation Sciences was included. The EFC in its 
meeting held on 30th March 2016 recommended the proposal for setting up of 
University at cost of ₹382 crore. Subsequently, a Cabinet Note was circulated on 
30.06.2017, which was returned by the Cabinet Secretariat in July 2018 for review. The 
proposal was reviewed and it was decided in the Ministry to set up the University in 
Kamrup district, Assam. 
8.2 Regarding the present statusof the University, it has been informed that:- 
“The Department engaged EdCIL (India) Limited, NOIDA, to prepare a 
Detailed Project Report (DPR) for establishing the National University of Disability 
Studies and Rehabilitation Sciences in Kamrup, Assam. The final DPR has been 
submitted in March 2023, and a Public Investment Board (PIB) note was 
prepared and circulated to stakeholder ministries/departments for comments in 
June 2023. The Department of Expenditure (DoE), vide OM dated 01.11.2023, 
11.12.2023 & 10.07.2024, had made some comments/observations regarding the 
establishment of NUDSRS and given the project cost it was advised to obtain 
Delegated Investment Board (DIB) approval for the project This Department is in 
process of compliance of DoE comments regarding the NUDSRS and the proposal 
is currently under process for appraisal of DIB note. 
A three-member team comprising officials from DEPwD and CRC Guwahati
, along with the Kamrup District Administration, conducted a site visit in Novemb
er 2024 to identify the allocated land. In this regard, a joint survey report from t
he District Commissioner, Kamrup, has been received.  
Upon receipt of the Joint Survey Report from the District Commissioner, 
Kamrup, it was confirmed that the initially allocated 150 Bighas of land at 
Bondapara, BekeliMouza, included 126 Bighas within the Khatajuli Reserve Forest 
and only 24 Bighas as Government Khas land. Given the non-availability of 
alternative land under Boko Revenue Circle, a D.O. letter dated 31.12.2024 was 
issued by the Hon’ble Minister of Social Justice & Empowerment (HMSJE) to the 
Hon’ble Chief Minister of Assam, seeking intervention either for forest land 
clearance or allocation of an alternate 50-acre land suitable for the university. 

77 
 
In response, the Hon’ble Chief Minister of Assam through a D.O. letter 
dated 03.02.2025 conveyed that an alternate land under Chaygaon Revenue 
Circle, Kamrup District, has been identified for the purpose. Accordingly, the 
Department is in the process of deputing a team of officials to visit Kamrup, 
Assam, to evaluate the suitability of the proposed site before proceeding with the 
necessary land allotment formalities. Further action will be initiated based on the 
findings of the site visit”. 
8.3 The Committee emphasize the urgent need to expedite the 
establishment of the National University of Disability Studies and 
Rehabilitation Sciences in Kamrup, Assam, given the prolonged delays since 
its announcement in 2015-16. Recognizing the critical role of the university 
in advancing education, research, and rehabilitation for Persons with 
Disabilities, the Committee urge the Department to swiftly resolve land 
allocation issues, ensure timely compliance with the Department of 
Expenditure’s observations, and secure necessary approvals without further 
delay.  The Committee recommend that a clear implementation roadmap 
with defined timelines be formulated to ensure the project progress 
efficiently, enabling the university to become operational at the earliest.
