1. 1.15 The Committee appreciate the proactive initiatives taken by various 
State Governments in establishing dedicated Department for disability 
affairs and significantly increasing budgetary allocations. They also 
acknowledge the innovative approach of community-based 
interventions, such as Karnataka’s village-level disability workers and 
the nationwide SugamyaYatra initiative, which fosters grassroots 
accessibility improvements. To build on this momentum, the 
Committee recommend that the Department actively collaborate with 
States to institutionalize similar models across the country, ensuring 
sustainable and community-driven disability inclusion. Additionally, a 
structured framework should be developed to document and monitor 
accessibility improvements under SugamyaYatra, enabling the 
replication of best practices nationwide. 
2. 2.15 From a thorough examination of the Demands for Grants (DFG) over 
the past three years, the Committee observe a persistent trend of 
underutilization of funds across key schemes such as ADIP, SIPDA, 
DDRS, and Scholarships, with actual expenditures consistently falling 
short of Revised Estimates (RE) and Budget Estimates (BE). The BE 
allocations were invariably reduced at the RE stage in 2022-23, 2023-
24, and 2024-25, yet the Department was unable to fully utilize even 
the reduced funds. The Department utilized 97.38per cent of RE in 
2022-23 and 93.39per cent in 2023-24. However, as of 03.03.2025, 
only ₹892.68 crore of ₹ 1167.27 crore (76.48per cent) has been spent. 
This shortfall was primarily due to disruptions from the introduction of 
the CNA and TSA models. Delays in receiving Utilization Certificates 
(UCs) from State Governments under SIPDA and a lack of adequate 
proposals from North-Eastern States further hindered funds 
utilization. While the Committee were assured by the Department’s 
representatives that the remaining 2024-25 funds would be fully 
utilized by 31.03.2025, the Committee strongly urge the Department 
to adopt targeted remedial measures and strategic interventions to 
ensure efficient fund utilization in 2025-26. Proactive engagement 
with State Governments, NGOs, and implementing agencies is 

84 
 
essential to streamline proposal submissions and disbursement 
process, particularly for skill training programs and capital 
expenditure. Furthermore, given the challenges in meeting fixed 
targets for schemes like SIPDA and DDRS, the Department should 
reassess target-setting methodologies to ensure that they are 
realistic, flexible, and aligned with performance trends. The 
Committee recommend decisive action to improve fund utilization and 
program execution in the remaining year of the 2024-26 financial 
cycle, ensuring that allocated resources effectively advance the 
welfare of persons with disabilities and that the Department 
successfully meets its commitments under various schemes. 
3. 3.20 The Committee recognize that the Assistance to Persons with 
Disabilities for Purchase/Fitting of Aids/Appliances (ADIP) Scheme is 
an important initiative aimed at enhancing mobility, independence, 
and economic empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). The 
Committee note that fund allocation and utilization under ADIP have 
shown a steady increase, with actual expenditure surpassing initial 
Budget Estimates (BE) in multiple years. In 2022-23, the BE was 
₹235.00 crore, which was revised to ₹230.00 crore, yet actual 
expenditure exceeded expectations at ₹242.29 crore. Similarly, in 
2023-24, the BE of ₹245.00 crore was significantly revised to ₹305.00 
crore, with actual spending at ₹290.60 crore. In 2024-25, the BE was 
further enhanced to ₹315.00 crore, and the Revised Estimate (RE) 
increased to ₹350.00 crore, with ₹346.27 crore utilized as of 
03.03.2025. The Committee also note that increased financial 
allocations has been ably matched by the physical 
performance/targets set under the Scheme. In 2022-23 and 2023-24, 
the target was exceeded, benefiting 2.89 lakh and 3.15 lakh 
beneficiaries, respectively. However, in 2024-25, only 2.10 lakh 
beneficiaries were assisted as of 14.02.2025, accounting for 67per 
cent of the target of 3.15 lakh beneficiaries. While the Department has 
cited the imposition of the Model Code of Conduct during General 
Elections and the transition to the TSA Model-I as reasons for the 
slower pace of the expenditure, the Committee urge the Department 
to learn from these experiences and establish contingency plans to 
ensure uninterrupted service delivery in the future. The Committee 
however express concern over the reduction of the physical targets for 

85 
 
2025-26 to 2.05 lakh beneficiaries and recommend that the 
Department continuously assess demand trends and explore 
possibilities for expanding beneficiary coverage. 
4. 3.21 The Committee appreciate the revisions in the ADIP Scheme, effective 
26.09.2024, which aim to enhance inclusivity and provide greater 
financial relief to Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). The modifications 
include higher income eligibility ceilings, increased financial support 
for assistive devices, and expanded coverage for advanced mobility 
aids and corrective surgeries. The enhancements in subsidies for 
motorized tricycles, wheelchairs, and high-end prostheses, along with 
greater financial assistance for cochlear implants and corrective 
surgeries, are expected to significantly improve accessibility and 
independence for PwDs. By reducing the financial burden on 
beneficiaries and ensuring access to better-quality assistive devices, 
these changes will promote greater social and economic inclusion. The 
Committee, however, emphasize the need for periodic impact 
assessments to evaluate whether these modifications are effectively 
improving the quality of life for PwDs, ensuring that the intended 
benefits reach the maximum number of eligible individuals. 
5. 3.22 The Committee appreciate the establishment of Pradhan Mantri 
Divyasha Kendras (PMDKs), which provide walk-in access to assistive 
aids and have benefitted 35,919 PwDs as of 2024-25. These centers 
play a crucial role in ensuring last-mile service delivery, and the 
Committee recommend their expansion to underserved regions, 
particularly in remote and tribal areas. The removal of the 
requirement for State Government recommendations in NGO 
proposals is also a welcome step toward reducing bureaucratic delays 
and ensuring the timely release of funds. However, the Committee 
stress the importance of strict monitoring mechanisms to prevent 
misuse of funds and maintain transparency in implementation. 
6. 3.23 The Committee commend the inclusion of Motorized Tricycles with Li-
Iron-Phosphate batteries and Folding Joystick Wheelchairs in the 
ADIP Scheme, with a subsidy of up to ₹50,000, as a significant step 
towards improving mobility and independence for PwDs. These 
modern assistive devices, along with enhanced financial support for 
high-end prostheses and cochlear implants, will broaden accessibility, 
lower maintenance costs, and provide financial relief to beneficiaries 

86 
 
and their families. The Committee strongly recommend that the 
Department undertake extensive outreach efforts to ensure that 
maximum eligible PwDs can avail these benefits and urge 
collaboration with research institutions and industry partners to 
continuously enhance and upgrade assistive devices, making them 
more cost-effective, durable, and efficient. 
7. 3.24 The Committee appreciate the Department’s efforts in enhancing 
accessibility and mobility for the elderly by distributing over 18,000 
assistive devices during the Kumbh Mela at Prayagraj under the 
Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana (RVY). Such initiatives play a vital role in 
reaching vulnerable populations in large public gatherings and 
ensuring their comfort and dignity. To further strengthen these 
efforts, the Committee recommend that similar outreach programs be 
integrated into other major national and regional events. Additionally, 
a structured mechanism for pre-event assessment and beneficiary 
registration should be developed to ensure the distribution of need-
specific assistive devices, maximizing the impact of such initiatives. 
8. 4.17 The Committee recognize the crucial role of DDRS in providing 
rehabilitation services to Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) through 
NGOs and implementing agencies. An analysis of fund utilization 
trends over the past three years reveals significant fluctuations, with 
2022-23 and 2023-24 recording high fund utilization, while in 2024-
25, actual expenditure stood at ₹87.95 crore as of 03.03.2025, despite 
a Budget Estimate (BE) of ₹165 crore. The Committee note that the 
transition from the CNA Model to TSA Hybrid Model 1-A led to 
procedural delays in fund disbursement, impacting the pace of 
implementation. Additionally, as grants were previously processed on 
a reimbursement basis, NGOs were required to submit audited 
accounts by June 30 of the next financial year, further slowing down 
fund releases. However, with the revised DDRS guidelines effective 
from 01.10.2024, which allow Grant-in-Aid on an advance-cum-
reimbursement basis, the Committee expect that fund flow will 
improve and implementation delays will be minimized. The Committee 
recommend that the Department ensure timely release of advances, 
particularly to NGOs with strong compliance records, while also 
strengthening the capacity of implementing agencies to meet 
documentation requirements on time, ensuring efficient utilization of 

87 
 
allocated funds. The Committee also urge the Department to ensure a 
smoother transition in funding mechanisms by streamlining financial 
procedures and proactively addressing administrative bottlenecks to 
avoid such shortfalls in future fiscal years. 
9. 4.18 The Committee note that physical targets under DDRS have witnessed 
a downward revision since 2024-25, with the target reduced from 
40,000 in 2023-24 to 32,000 in 2024-25 and 2025-26. The 
Department has attributed this to the number of projects supported 
remaining largely the same over the years, with new proposals being 
considered only after the release of funds to organizations. The 
Committee emphasize that rehabilitation services for PwDs should not 
be constrained due to procedural delays in fund disbursal and 
recommend that the Department take proactive steps to expedite 
approvals for new projects. The Committee urge the Department to 
explore expanding the scope of DDRS to cover more PwDs by 
identifying underserved areas where rehabilitation services are limited 
or absent. 
10. 4.19 The Committee appreciate the Department’s efforts in introducing 
monitoring mechanisms, including video inspections of NGOs and 
time-bound forwarding of proposals under the revised DDRS. The 
provision for automatic transmission of pending proposals from the 
district levels to the State Government and further to the DEPwD if no 
action is taken within a month of submission is a commendable 
measure aimed to streamline the approval process and minimize 
administrative delays.   However, the Committee recommend strict 
enforcement of these provisions to ensure that no proposal remains 
pending for an unreasonable duration. Further, the Committee support 
the decision that organizations running both DDRS and National Trust 
schemes should choose only one to avoid duplication of services, 
ensuring that funds reach the maximum number of beneficiaries. 
11. 4.20 The Committee note that DDRCs function as decentralized 
rehabilitation units, providing early identification and intervention, 
assistive device distribution, therapy services, and skill development 
for PwDs. While DDRCs were initially planned for 325 districts, only 
269 DDRCs were set up, and currently, only 74 are functional. The 
Committee express concern over the low operational count of DDRCs 
and recommend that the Department prioritize the revival and 

88 
 
expansion of DDRCs in districts lacking rehabilitation facilities. The 
Committee also welcome the shift to online applications for Grant-in-
Aid (GIA) for DDRCs through the e-Anudaan Portal from 2024-25, 
which is expected to simplify and expedite the application process. 
12. 5.13 The Committee observe significant inconsistencies in the Budget 
Estimates (BE), Revised Estimates (RE), and actual fund utilization 
under SIPDA over the past three years. Frequent downward revisions 
at the RE stage and low actual expenditure despite available 
allocations indicate systemic inefficiencies in fund absorption. In 
2022-23, the BE was ₹240.39 crore, which was reduced by 58.4 per 
cent at the RE stage to ₹100 crore, with actual expenditure at just 
₹65.59 crore. Similarly, in 2023-24, the BE of ₹150 crore was cut to 
₹67 crore, yet actual expenditure exceeded the RE at ₹76.79 crore 
(114.7 percent of RE). In 2024-25, despite an RE of ₹111 crore, only 
₹43.90 crore (39.5 percent of RE) had been utilized as of 03.03.2025. 
These fluctuations indicate inconsistent fund planning and delays in 
fund utilization, leading to missed opportunities for enhancing 
accessibility and disability-related initiatives. The Committee strongly 
recommend that the Department strengthen its financial planning 
mechanisms by ensuring that BE allocations are realistic, demand-
driven, and reflective of actual implementation capacity.  
13. 5.14 In addition to financial inconsistencies, the Committee note a 
significant shortfall in meeting physical targets under SIPDA. In 2022-
23, against a target of 44,520 beneficiaries, 44,162 were assisted, 
reflecting 99.2per cent achievement. However, in 2023-24, the 
achievement dropped to 29,374 beneficiaries against the same target 
(65.9per cent), and as of 16.01.2025, only 11,933 beneficiaries 
(27.4per cent) had been covered out of the 43,520 target for 2024-25. 
This indicates delays in execution and ineffective implementation 
strategies. The Committee recommend that the Department enhance 
coordination with State Governments and implementing agencies to 
ensure faster approval and processing of applications, preventing 
recurring lapses in achieving physical targets. Furthermore, a robust 
monitoring framework should be instituted to track real-time 
progress, ensuring better alignment between financial allocations and 
physical achievements. The Department must identify and address 
systemic bottlenecks to ensure that SIPDA meets its intended goals of 

89 
 
accessibility, empowerment and inclusion of Persons with Disabilities. 
14. 5.15 The Committee also find that persistent challenges such as delays in 
fund disbursement, pending utilization certificates, and incomplete 
proposals have impacted the effective implementation of SIPDA. Given 
that SIPDA is the flagship scheme for PwDs, the Committee strongly 
recommend that the Department strengthen its monitoring and 
coordination mechanisms by ensuring regular follow-ups with State 
Governments and implementing agencies. The Central Project 
Monitoring Unit (CPMU) should be further empowered to enable real-
time tracking of fund utilization, proposal approvals, and physical 
progress under various sub-schemes .Furthermore, timely clearance of 
compliance documents such as Utilization Certificates (UCs) and 
pending proposals should be ensured to prevent underutilization and 
last-minute fund surrender. 
15. 5.23 The Committee note with appreciation the initiatives undertaken 
under the Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) to 
enhance accessibility in built environments, transportation, and 
information & communication technology (ICT).However, with the 
campaign now subsumed under the “Creation of Barrier-Free 
Environment (CBFE)” sub-scheme under SIPDA, the Committee 
express concern over the absence of a dedicated budgetary allocation 
for CBFE and the continued financial support required for sustained 
accessibility initiatives. The Committee strongly recommend that the 
Department create a structured financial framework within SIPDA, 
ensuring that accessibility projects receive adequate funding without 
dependence on overall SIPDA allocations. Additionally, a long-term 
accessibility roadmap should be developed to maintain momentum 
and expand initiatives to underserved regions. 
16. 5.31 The Committee observe that the National Action Plan for Skill 
Development of PwDs (NAP-SDP) has consistently underperformed in 
meeting its physical targets, with achievements ranging from only 
12.62 per cent in 2022-23 to 32.25 per cent in 2024-25 (as of January 
2025). Given the demand-driven nature of the scheme, the Committee 
recommend that the Department strengthen its mobilization efforts, 
improve coordination with training partners, and ensure timely 
disbursal of funds. Further, efforts should be made to optimize the 
utilization of the budget allocation by addressing administrative 

90 
 
bottlenecks, improving the training infrastructure, and ensuring a 
greater alignment of courses with market demand to enhance 
employment prospects for PwDs. 
17. 5.32 The Committee however appreciate the Department's efforts in 
signing MoUs with private firms and job aggregators like Amazon, 
Youth4Jobs, and Zomato to facilitate employment opportunities for 
trained PwDs. However, with only 28,000 PwDs employed till date, the 
Committee recommend a robust strategy to strengthen employment 
linkages, including expanding industry partnerships, promoting 
entrepreneurship support programs, and ensuring sector-specific skill 
training tailored to high-demand job markets. A structured tracking 
mechanism should also be put in place to monitor the employment 
status of trained PwDs. 
18. 5.33 Noting the challenges in data tracking and monitoring of training and 
placements, the Committee welcome the introduction of the PM-
DAKSH-DEPwD Portal. However, the Committee recommend that the 
Department ensure its full operationalization with real-time data 
tracking, performance audits of training partners, and impact 
assessments of training programs. Further, a feedback mechanism 
should be established where trained PwDs can report challenges faced 
in employment, enabling timely interventions and policy adjustments 
to enhance the scheme’s effectiveness. 
19. 5.39 The Committee note that while the UDID project has successfully 
generated approximately 1.18 crore cards, its implementation 
continues to face challenges due to a shortage of medical 
professionals, inadequate hospital infrastructure, and a large backlog 
of pending applications at hospitals. To address these issues, the 
Committee recommend that the Department work in close 
coordination with State Governments to strengthen medical 
infrastructure, expedite the inclusion of private medical professionals 
in the certification process, and ensure the availability of well-
equipped facilities for disability assessment. Additionally, the 
Department should facilitate specialized training programs for medical 
authorities to improve efficiency in issuing disability certificates and 
reduce delays. 
20. 5.40 Recognizing the UDID’s critical role in enabling PwDs to access 

91 
 
various government benefits and services, the Committee underscore 
the importance of ensuring full utilization of the allocated budget for 
2025-26. This requires robust monitoring of fund disbursement, 
proactive engagement with State and UT authorities, and the timely 
clearance of pending UDID applications. A structured and time-bound 
approach should be adopted to enhance accessibility and ensure that 
all eligible PwDs receive their UDID cards without unnecessary delays. 
21. 5.41 The Committee further observe that PwDs in rural and remote areas 
face difficulties in accessing the UDID system due to limited internet 
coverage and therefore urge the Department to strengthen the role of 
Common Service Centres (CSCs) and explore the deployment of 
mobile service units for on-site registration and certification. The 
Committee would also like to recommend that awareness campaigns 
be conducted in collaboration with State Governments to ensure that 
all eligible PwDs are aware of the benefits of UDID and the process for 
obtaining it. 
22. 5.47 The Committee observe that the Scheme for Financial Assistance to 
Spinal Injury Centers (ASIC) is vital for providing treatment and 
rehabilitation to individuals with spinal cord injuries, especially those 
from economically weaker sections. However, with only eight State 
Spinal Injury Centers (SSICs) supported so far, the scheme's reach 
remains limited. To address this, the Committee recommend proactive 
engagement with State governments to expand SSICs in government 
hospitals and ensure better accessibility to specialized care. Given that 
ASIC operates under SIPDA without a separate budgetary allocation, 
the Department must prioritize its funding needs and streamline 
proposal approvals to ensure timely disbursal of grants. Strengthening 
monitoring mechanisms, expediting clearances, and raising awareness 
among stakeholders will be key to ensuring full utilization of funds and 
maximizing the scheme’s impact. 
23. 6.17 The Committee observe significant fluctuations in fund allocation, 
utilization, and target achievement under the Scholarship Scheme for 
Students with Disabilities. In 2022-23, the Revised Estimate (RE) was 
increased to ₹145.00 crore, with 97.9 per cent utilization (₹142.00 
crore). However, in 2024-25, the RE was sharply reduced by 43.9 per 
cent to ₹80.00 crore, and as of 03.03.2025, only ₹58.38 crore (72.9 
per cent of RE) had been utilized. Similarly, physical target 

92 
 
achievement dropped from 99.2per cent in 2022-23 to just 27.4 per 
cent in 2024-25(as of Jan,2025). This underutilization, despite high 
demand in previous years, indicates the need for better forecasting 
and planning. The Committee recommend that the Department adopt 
a more structured approach to fund allocation, ensuring that 
budgetary provisions align with actual demand. Additionally, efforts 
should be made to streamline the verification and disbursement 
process at the State Nodal Officer level to avoid delays and ensure 
timely financial assistance to beneficiaries. 
24. 6.18 Given the low application numbers in certain years, the Committee 
emphasize the need for a more robust awareness campaign. While 
steps have been taken, such as newspaper advertisements and 
communication with State Governments, a more proactive strategy is 
required. The Department should leverage digital platforms, 
collaborate with educational institutions, and engage disability rights 
organizations to maximize outreach. Special efforts must be made to 
target students in remote and rural areas who may be unaware of 
their eligibility for these scholarships. 
25. 6.19 To prevent recurring issues of low fund utilization, the Committee 
urges the Department to implement a real-time monitoring 
mechanism for tracking application processing and fund 
disbursement. Regular review meetings with State Nodal Officers 
should be mandated, and timelines should be fixed for application 
verification and fund release. Additionally, simplifying application 
procedures and integrating AI-based verification tools can 
significantly improve efficiency. The Committee stress that every 
effort must be made to ensure full utilization of the ₹145 crore 
allocated for 2025-26, benefiting the maximum number of eligible 
students with disabilities. 
26. 7.6 The Committee express satisfaction with the establishment and 
progress of the AtalBihari Vajpayee Training Centre for Disability 
Sports (ABV-TCDS), Gwalior, recognizing its vital role in promoting 
para-sports in India. The Centre’s state-of-the-art facilities, extensive 
sports infrastructure, and commitment to training Divyangjan athletes 
at par with international standards are commendable. The 
Committeeare pleased to note the Centre’s efforts in organizing 
national and State-level championships, talent identification 

93 
 
programs, and collaborations with reputed institutions and sports 
federations. While acknowledging the challenges in operationalizing 
the facility, the Committee are optimistic that with sustained efforts, 
ABV-TCDS will emerge as a premier institution, significantly enhancing 
India’s representation and success in international para-sporting 
events. 
27. 8.3 The Committee emphasize the urgent need to expedite the 
establishment of the National University of Disability Studies and 
Rehabilitation Sciences in Kamrup, Assam, given the prolonged delays 
since its announcement in 2015-16. Recognizing the critical role of the 
university in advancing education, research, and rehabilitation for 
Persons with Disabilities, the Committee urge the Department to 
swiftly resolve land allocation issues, ensure timely compliance with 
the Department of Expenditure’s observations, and secure necessary 
approvals without further delay.  The Committee recommend that a 
clear implementation roadmap with defined timelines be formulated 
to ensure the project progress efficiently, enabling the university to 
become operational at the earliest.

INTRODUCTION 
 
  I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment (2024-25) having been authorized by the Committee do 
present on their behalf this Seventh Report on 'Demands for Grants for the 
year 2025-26' pertaining to the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. 
2. The Committee considered the ‘Demands for Grants (2025-26)’ of the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs which were laid on the Table of the House on 13 
February, 2025. After obtaining the Budget Documents, Explanatory Notes, 
etc., the Committee took evidence of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs on 21 
February, 2025. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at the 
sitting held on 18.03.2025. 
3. The Committee wish to express their thanks to the Officers of the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs for tendering oral evidence and placing before them 
the detailed written notes and post evidence information as desired by the 
Committee in connection with the examination of the ‘Demands for Grants 
(2025-26)’. 
4. For ease of reference observations/ recommendations/ comments of 
the Committee have been printed in bold in the body of the Report.    
 
 
 
 
 
 
New Delhi 
 18   March, 2025 
 27   Phalguna, 1946 (Saka) 
 
SHRI P.C MOHAN 
Chairperson 
Standing Committee on Social Justice 
and Empowerment 
 

1 
 
REPORT 
CHAPTER-I 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs administers various Central Sector and Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes besides a Special Area Programme, viz. Grants-in-Aid under 
Article 275(1) of the Constitution to contribute the overall efforts for development of 
tribal people in the country.  
 
1.2 The programmes and schemes of the Ministry are intended to support and 
supplement, through financial assistance, the efforts primarily of other Central 
Ministries/Departments, the State Governments and partly of voluntary organizations, 
and to fill critical gaps in institutions and programmes, taking into account the situation 
of STs. While the primary responsibility for promoting the interests of Scheduled Tribes 
in implementation of sectoral schemes rests with all the Central 
Ministries/Departments, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs supplements their efforts by way 
of various developmental interventions in critical sectors through specially designed 
schemes. These schemes are administered by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and 
implemented mainly through the State Governments / Union Territory Administrations 
for social, economic and educational development and through institution building. 
 
1.3 The following Schemes are being implemented by the Ministry: 
 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) 
1. Pre-Matric Scholarship for Scheduled Tribes   
2. Post-Matric Scholarship for Scheduled Tribes 
3. Support to Tribal Research Institutes 
4. Development of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) / 
Pradhan Mantri  Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN) 
5. Pradhan Mantri Adi Adrash Gram Yojna –PMAAGY (previously known as 
Special Central Assistance to Tribal Sub-Scheme - SCA to TSS) 
6. Administrative Cost to States / UTs. 
 
 

2 
 
Central Sector Schemes (CS) 
 
1. Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) 
2. National Fellowship and Scholarship for Higher Education of ST Students 
3. Scholarship to the ST Students for studies abroad 
4. Aid to Voluntary Organizations working for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes 
5. Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM) 
6. Tribal Research Information, Education, Communication and Events (TRI-ECE) 
7. Monitoring, Evaluation, Survey and Social Audit (MESSA) 
8. Venture Capital Fund for Scheduled Tribes 
9. Marketing and Logistics Development for Promoting Tribal Products from North 
East ern Region 
 
1.4 The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes is a constitutional body under 
the Ministry. Other than this, National Schedule Tribes Finance and Development 
Corporation (NSTFDC), National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS) and 
Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation of India Limited (TRIFED) are 
also set up under the administrative control of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. 
 
National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) 
 
1.5 The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) was set up with effect 
from 19th February, 2004 by amending Article 338 and inserting a new Article 338A in 
the Constitution, through the Constitution of India (Eighty-ninth Amendment) Act, 2003.  
The main duties of the Commission are to investigate and monitor all matters relating 
to the safeguards provided for the Scheduled Tribes and to evaluate the working of 
such safeguards, and to inquire into specific complaints with respect to the deprivation 
of rights and safeguards of the Scheduled Tribes. The Commission is vested with all 
the powers of a civil court trying a suit while investigating any matter or inquiring into 
any complaint relating to deprivation of rights and safeguards of the Scheduled Tribes.  
 
National Scheduled Tribes Finance and Development Corporation (NSTFDC) 
 
1.6 National Scheduled Tribes Finance and Development Corporation (NSTFDC) is 
an apex organisation set up on 10.04.2001, exclusively for the economic development 

3 
 
of Scheduled Tribes. This Corporation was incorporated as a Government company 
under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and granted license under Section 25 of the 
Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013). It is managed by a 
Board of Directors with representation from Central Govt., State Channelising 
Agencies, Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI), Tribal Co-operative Marketing 
Development Federation of India Ltd. (TRIFED) and eminent persons representing 
Scheduled Tribes, etc. The Corporation plays a significant role in providing credit 
support for economic upliftment of Scheduled Tribes at concessional rates of interest.  
 
National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS) 
 
1.7 The National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS), an autonomous

CHAPTER-III 
TRIBAL RESEARCH INSTITUTES (TRIs) 
 
  
 The Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs) are engaged in the work of conducting 
research and evaluation studies, collection of data, identification of challenges in the 
field of social-economic development of tribals and in understanding, promoting and 
preserving their culture through various studies and other kind of interventions. The 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs has taken various steps to preserve tribal traditions, culture and 
customs through the Centrally Sponsored Scheme- of ‘Support to Tribal Research 
Institutes’ under which various activities are undertaken to conserve and promote tribal 
culture, archives, artifacts, customs and traditions of the tribal communities. As part of 
the research activities of the TRIs, the Ministry also supports construction of tribal 
museums within the premises of the TRIs to preserve the tribal art, craft and culture.

2022 at the rented building of Indian Institute of Public Administration Campus in 
Indraprastha Estate, New Delhi. NTRI is a coordinating agency to provide guidance and 
assistance for conducting evidence-based research projects, workshops, seminars, and 
capacity-building activities addressing tribal concerns, issues, and matters of 28 TRIs.”

3.13  The Committee are happy to note that 28 Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs) set 
up in various States in the country are administrated by the State Governments and 
supported by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs in their infrastructural needs, research and 
documentation activities, training & capacity building programmes, organization of 
tribal festivals/ yatras for promotion of unique cultural heritage and in promotion of 
tourism and organization of exchange visits by tribals so that the tribal cultural 
practices, languages and rituals are preserved and disseminated. The Committee find 
that budgeted estimates for 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 were revised downward at 
RE stage from ₹121.00 crore to ₹58.50 crore, ₹118.64 crore to ₹50.00 crore and ₹111.00 
crore to ₹90.00 crore respectively. However, the revised estimate could not be spent 
fully during these years. The Committee believe that mere allocations of funds would 
not ensure effective implementation of TRI Scheme. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs 
should pursue with the State/UT Governments  and other Implementing Agencies so 
that annual Action Plan from State/UT Governments are timely received to achieve  the 
purpose for which the Scheme came into existence. They would also like the Ministry 
to immediately resolve other issues such as delay in submission of Utilization 
Certificates (UCs), clearance of SNA balances, submission of progress report and DPR 
etc by the State Authorities. Thus, the Committee, recommend that the Ministry should 
take requisite measures to remove technical and procedural bottlenecks, 
administrative delays and address capacity building issues, etc. The Committee also 
desire that regular review meetings with State Governments at periodic intervals are 
held with the objective of augmenting the usage of funds. The Committee would like to 
be informed of the action taken by the Ministry in this regard.   
  
3.14  The Committee appreciate the initiative of Ministry of Tribal Affairs for 
establishing of ‘Tribal Freedom Fighters’ Museums’ as they acknowledge the heroic 

16 
 
and patriotic deeds of tribal idols who are otherwise often under-represented in the 
mainstream history. The Committee note that the Ministry have so far supported 11 
Tribal Freedom Fighters’ museums in 10 States to celebrate the lives and deeds of 
tribal heroes and inculcate a spirit of pride in the minds of tribal communities. 
However, the Committee note that out of 11 sanctioned Tribal Freedom Fighters’ 
Museums  by the Ministry, only 3, namely, ‘Bhagwan Birsa Munda Memorial Freedom 
Fighter Museum’ at Ranchi, Jharkhand, ‘Badal Bhoi State Tribal Freedom Fighters 
Museum, Chhindwara and ‘Raja Shankar Shah and Kunwar Raghunath Shah Freedom 
Fighter Museum’, Jabalpur, have been inaugurated. The Committee would like to 
underline the slow progress in construction of remaining 8 museums, as they were 
sanctioned far back in 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20 and mention about Tribal 
Freedom Fighter Museums in Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Telengana, Gujarat and 
Mizoram, which are yet to be completed. The Committee are also concerned for the 
Tribal Freedom Fighters’ Museums sanctioned for Kerala, Manipur and Goa in 2017-
2018, 2018-19 and 2020-21 respectively as they are still at DPR stage even after the 
lapse of several years. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs may evolve a strategy for timely completion of these Museums. The 
Committee would like the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to ensure that the four Tribal 
Freedom Fighters’ Museums scheduled to be completed by November, 2025 and one 
by May, 2026, are completed by the stipulated date.

Ministry is implementing the Central Sector Scheme of Eklavya Model 
Residential School (EMRS) to provide quality education to the tribal children (from class 
VI to XII) in their own environment from the year 2018-19 in remote areas to enable 
them access to the best opportunities in education and to bring them at par with the 
general population. Earlier EMRS was a component under Article 275(1) of the 
Constitution. Under the new scheme, Government decided to establish one EMRS in 
every block having more than 50% ST population and at least 20,000 tribal persons (as 
per census 2011).

4.19 The Committee note that an expenditure of ₹1,09,000/- per student per 
annum was specified in the EMRS guidelines,2020. The Committee were informed 
that this amount was not sufficient since revision in dearness allowance, 
implementation of pay revision, revision in labour cost,  inflation in food and 
other commodities have increased significantly and could not be met in the 
amount fixed in the guidelines.  The Committee were informed that the amount

Navodaya Vidyalayas as per the approval of Cabinet.  The Committee, however, 
note that the revision of recurring expenditure in NVS on mess, uniform and other 
direct expenditure on students is done from time to time and total average 
expenditure for a student in NVS is ₹1,56,000/- for 9 months of functioning of 
NVS. The Committee feel that since the modeling of EMRS is based on NVS, 
hence, the expenditure of EMRS should also be in comparison with the NVS. The 
Committee are also not convinced with the idea of including expenditure on 
salary head while calculating the expenditure per student per annum.  They 
desire that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs should examine and calculate average 
expenditure for each student in EMRS by excluding salary head expenditure as 
the average recurring expenditure would be adversely affected as the salary 
expenditure would keep on increasing annually due to   increase in dearness 
allowance and annual Increment. The Committee would like the Ministry to 
consider the above suggestions while calculating average expenditure for EMRS 
student and ensure that at least the average expenditure is not in any case less 
than provided under NVS.

5.8 The Committee note that Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha 
Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN) was launched by discontinuing erstwhile Scheme of 
Development of PVTGs from 2024-25 for the socio-economic development of  
45,56,773 people  belonging to Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)  
across 18 States and one UT with a financial outlay of ₹24,000 crore.  The 
Scheme proposes to improve socio-economic status of PVTGs by bridging the 
gaps in health, education, livelihoods by improving basic infrastructure, 
habitations and families by aligning with existing Schemes of Nine Ministries/ 
Departments.  The Committee also note that 29,000 villages were proposed to be 
saturated by 2025-26 but only 4,288 villages have been saturated as per the

32 
 
the launch of the Abhiyan, 8 aligning Ministries/ Department spent ₹ 1367.30

Odisha, Tamil Nadu & Uttarakhand and funds are proposed to be released to 
Gujarat, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and 
Tripura. On the glance of expenditure incurred and the number of villages 
saturated out of the targeted 29,000 villages, the Committee opine that the 
progress of work is slow and requires to be expedited to complete the given 
task within the stipulated period.  The Committee appreciate the involvement of 
various Ministries/ Department as it would enhance the speed of the Abhiyan 
but are also apprehensive about the coordination between the 
Ministries/Departments.  The Committee would, therefore, like to recommend 
that the necessary mechanism may be established to ensure proper 
coordination between the Ministries/Departments and there is no dispute in the 
execution of work so that the work envisaged is executed cordially without any 
delay. The Committee would also like the Ministry to develop a monitoring 
mechanism to keep a check on the progress of work so that the work is 
completed as envisaged.

CHAPTER-VI 
PRADHAN  MANTRI JANJATIYA VIKAS MISSION (PMJVM) 
 
Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM) has been formulated with the 
merger of the two earlier schemes for promotion of tribal livelihood, i.e., “Mechanism for 
Marketing of Minor Forest Produce (MFP) through “Minimum Support Price (MSP) and 
Development of Value Chain for MFP” and “Institutional Support for Development and 
Marketing of Tribal Products/Produce”.  PMJVM has the vision to strengthen tribal 
entrepreneurship initiatives and seeks to support the theme of “Vocal for Local by 
Tribal” by promoting more efficient, equitable, self-managed, optimum use of natural 
resources, MFPs/non-MFPs, tribal product-based enterprises. A budget provision of 
Rs.1612.27 Crore has been kept for implementing PMJVM from 2021-22 to 2025-26.

central implementing agency of this scheme. The major activities supported under the 
scheme are as under: 
 
(i) MSP Fixation and Procurement of non-nationalized, non-timber MFPs 
(ii) Infrastructure development / creation viz. Haat Bazars, Storage Godowns and

(iii) Value addition to various MFPs, non-MFPs and other produce / products 
(iv) Setting up of Van Dhan Vikas Kendra (VDVK) and Van Dhan Producer 
Enterprises (VDPE) 
(v) Sale & purchase of products made by VDVKs/VDPEs and other tribal products 
(ex. handloom, handicrafts etc.)  
(vi)  Advertisement, Branding and Promotion of various tribal produces / products in 
the market through Organizing/Participation in various festivals / exhibitions / 
tribal artisan melas / Mahotsavas etc.

advertise tribal products through on-line and off-line advertising strategies to

an in-house e-commence platform featuring an advanced user inter-face and user-
experience and they are in the process of formalizing a strategic partnership with

TRIFED should immediately enhance their efforts to build a robust e-commerce 
ecosystem for their products and scale up advertising through both conventional 
and online channels to expand their customer base within and outside the country to 
provide better marketing scope and remunerative pricing to tribal communities.

CHAPTER-VIII 
 
THE SCHEDULED TRIBES AND OTHER TRADITIONAL FOREST DWELLERS 
(RECOGNITION OF FOREST RIGHTS) ACT, 2006 
`The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of 
Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was enacted to recognize and vest the forest rights and 
occupation in forest land in Forest Dwelling Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional 
Forest Dwellers who have been residing in such forests for generations. Act also 
provides a statutory framework for recording the forest rights so vested and the 
nature of evidence required for such recognition and vesting in respect of forest 
land. The Act also empowers the forest rights holders, Gram Sabha and village 
level institutions to protect the wildlife, forest and biodiversity. 
 
Status of Implementation of the Act  
 
8.2 The implementation of the Act has been carried out since its inception as 
an ongoing process by various State Governments / UT Administrations. Progress 
in implementation of FRA in different States/UTs is furnished by the States/UTs on 
a monthly basis indicating the claims received, titles distributed and the extent of 
forest land for which titles have been distributed. Reports received from the 
States/UTs are compiled and put in public domain. As per the latest information 
reported by States and collated under MPR- FRA is being implemented in States -
20 states 1 UT covering 386 districts. 
 
8.3 On being asked about the details of latest status of implementation of the 
Act with regard to different States/UTs and the number of habitat rights given to 
tribal communities in different States/UTs, the Committee was informed as under. 
 
“FRA is being implemented in States -20 states 1 UT covering 386 
districts.As per the information received from States/ UTs upto 31.01.2025,a 
total of 51,03,764 claims (49,02,427 individual and 2,01,337 community) 
have been filed and 24,98,185 titles (23,80,502 individual and 1,17,683 
community) have been distributed to the extent of 1,91,91,086.66 acres 
(50,89,284.80 acres for individual and 1,41,01,801.87 acres for community) 
of forest land. For recognition of habitat rights for PVTGs, State 
Governments have started the process of vesting rights under Section 3 (1) 

47 
 
(e) of FRA. So far, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh have initiated 
and vested Habitat Rights for 10 PVTGs in 14 districts.”  
 
8.4 On being enquired about effectiveness of the Act in empowering and 
strengthening Tribals including PVTGs, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs inter-alia 
submitted vide their written reply that:- 
“Recently the Government has approved 'Dharti Aaba Janajatiya Gram 
Utkarsh Abhiyan' (DA-JGUA) with the aim of improving the socio-economic 
condition of tribal communities by adopting saturation coverage for tribal 
families in tribal majority villages and Aspirational Districts covering about 
63000 villages. Under DA-JGUA, MoTA is taking various initiatives like the 
Development of State and National FRA Portal and Digitisation of record 
and claim process, Mapping of Potential Forest Rights, Setting up of FRA 
Cells in States, and Support to States for CFR Management. DA-JGUA 
adopts a holistic approach aimed at providing sustainable livelihood to 
Forest-dwelling tribal families who have been vested with Individual and 
Community Forest Rights. Under DA-JGUA, there is a multi-sectoral 
livelihood support component for FRA patta holders in convergence with 
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmer’s Welfare, Department of Fisheries, 
Department of Animal Husbandry. Further, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs 
(MoTA) and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj (MoPR) have collaborated to 
conduct a special capacity-building campaign for the effective 
implementation of FRA and strengthening PESA Gram Sabha under 'Dharti 
Aaba Janajatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan”. 
 
8.5  On being asked about the complaints received in implementing the 
Scheme along with the actions taken, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs submitted vide 
written reply that: 
“the Ministry receive the complaints / grievances through online Centralized 
Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) portal 
wherein a complainant can lodge grievance. Since, January 2020 to 14 
February, 2025, 629 grievances were received by States/UTs out of which 
120 have been disposed of.” 
 
 8.6    With regard to the role of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs in the 
implementation of Forest Rights Act, the Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, 
deposed before the Committee during oral evidence that : 
 
“we have done three interventions off late.  The first major intervention is to 
try and digitize the process.  Once a person has given a petition, it should be 
visible to all.  Where it is lying and for how many days?  What is the 
disposal?  So, that process is on.  I am happy to say that three States have 
finished the process.  We are giving the money and the technology to help 

48 
 
them do it.  We have also helped the States to have a GIS digitization of 
potential area.  What is happening is this.  Normally there is a conflict 
between the Forest Department and the Tribal Welfare Department.  The 
Forest Department will say, no they do not deserve any patta out of this 
area, etc.  So, we said that we will create FRA atlases.  We have paid 
money and hired technical expertise and NGOs.  So, all the forest area near 
these villages is being mapped. In fact, that process is mostly over and many 
States have published the atlas also. So, that becomes the potential FRA 
area eligible for tribal community. So, at least, the Forest Department in this 
area will not harass. We are formally getting these digital FRA atlases 
published by a State Government. Fortunately, we have a good cooperation. 
In another three months’ time, we will finish the entire FRA in 17 States.”  
 
8.7 The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition 
of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was enacted to recognize and vest the forest rights 
and occupation in forest land on forest dwelling schedules tribes and other 
traditional forest dwellers. The Committee find that out of the 51,03,764 claims 
filed by Tribals,  24,98,185 titles have been distributed by 31 January, 2025. The 
Committee also find from January, 2020 to February, 2025, out of total number 
of 629 grievances related to FRA received by the States/UTs, only 120 have been 
disposed off.  The Committee strongly feel that there is an urgent need to set up 
an effective grievance redressal mechanism so that the claims filed by Tribals 
are settled within a time frame as State/UT Governments are taking time in 
resolving grievances filed by Tribals.  The Committee also feel that vesting of 
habitat rights to PVTGs is also getting delayed as only three States/UT viz. 
Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Chattisgarh have initiated the process till date.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs are 
required to take suitable measures and direct all the State Governments/UT 
Administrations to vigorously implement the various provisions of the Act.    
 
8.8 The Committee find that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs  has recently 
launched 'Dharti Aaba Janajatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan' (DA-JGUA). Under the 
Abhiyan, various steps are being taken as regards to implementation of FRA Act 
such as Development of State and National FRA Portal,  digitization of record 
and claim process, mapping of Potential Forest Rights, setting up of FRA Cells 
in States, and support to States for CFR Management. The Committee also find 
that under DA-JGUA, there is a multi-sectoral livelihood support component for 

49 
 
FRA patta holders in convergence with Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ 
Welfare, Department of Fisheries and Department of Animal Husbandry. Further, 
the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj have 
collaborated to conduct a special capacity-building campaign for the effective 
implementation of FRA provisions.  The Committee appreciate the efforts made 
by the Ministry and expect that various initiatives taken under DA-JUGA should 
be implemented in a time bound manner so that livelihood support with the 
coordination of various Ministries/Departments are provided to FRA patta 
holders.

should step into newer markets, expand their customer

TRIFED should immediately enhance their efforts to build a 
robust e-commerce ecosystem for their products and scale 
up advertising through both conventional and online 
channels to expand their customer base within and outside 
the country to provide better marketing scope and 
remunerative pricing to tribal communities.    

65 
 
12. 7.6 The Ministry of Tribal Affairs awards 750 National Fellowship 
& Scholarship Scheme for pursuing higher studies and 20 
National Overseas Scholarship for pursuing studies abroad to 
tribal students.  The Committee, however, find that during the 
year 2024-25, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs were not able to 
spend single rupee under National Fellowship Scheme and a 
token amount has been allocated under National Fellowship 
and Scholarship Scheme and National Overseas Scholarship 
during 2025-26. The Committee find that the Ministry has 
proposed an additional allocation of ₹220 crore for National 
fellowship for 2025-26.  The Committee also  find that on the 
requests from ST students, the Ministry is proposing EFC for 
the next Finance Commission cycle (2026-27 to 2030-31) to 
increase the number of slots from 20 to 50 under National 
Overseas Scholarship Scheme and 750 to 1000 slots under 
National Fellowship & Scholarship Scheme.  The Committee 
appreciate the efforts being made by the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs for getting additional provision of ₹220 crore and ₹ 
9.25 crore for 2025-26 under both the Schemes and also 
appreciate for considering the requests for Tribal students to 
enhance the number of slots under both the Schemes.  The 
Committee would like the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to also 
consider the request of Tribal students to increase the 
sanctioned amount and incorporate in the proposal to EFC as 
the amount has not been increased for many years.  The 
Committee recommend that the sanctioned amount should 
have inbuilt mechanism to absorb the inflation and also 
desire that the Ministry should pursue with EFC in getting 
proposed additional provision for both the Schemes for 2025-
26 and also ensure that the slots are enhanced for next 
Finance Commission cycle. The Committee would like to be 
apprised on the status of proposal made by the Ministry of 

66 
 
Tribal Affairs to EFC. 
13. 8.7 The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers 
(Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 was enacted to 
recognize and vest the forest rights and occupation in forest 
land on forest dwelling schedules tribes and other traditional 
forest dwellers. The Committee find that out of the 51,03,764 
claims filed by Tribals,  24,98,185 titles have been distributed 
by 31 January, 2025. The Committee also find from January, 
2020 to February, 2025, out of total number of 629 grievances 
related to FRS received by the States/UTs, only 120 have been 
disposed off.  The Committee strongly feel that there is an 
urgent need to set up an effective grievance redressal 
mechanism so that the claims filed by Tribals are settled 
within a time frame as State/UT Governments are taking time 
in resolving grievances filed by Tribals.  The Committee also 
feel that vesting of habitual rights to PVTGs is also getting 
delayed as only three States/UT viz. Odisha, Madhya Pradesh 
and Chattisgarh have initiated the process till date.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs are required to take suitable measures and direct all 
the State Governments/UT Administrations to vigorously 
implement the various provisions of the Act.    
14. 8.8 The Committee find that the Ministry of Tribal Affairs  has 
recently launched 'Dharti Aaba Janajatiya Gram Utkarsh 
Abhiyan' (DA-JGUA). Under the Abhiyan various steps are 
being taken as regards to implementation of FRA Act such as 
Development of State and National FRA Portal,  digitization of 
record and claim process, mapping of Potential Forest Rights, 
setting up of FRA Cells in States, and support to States for 
CFR Management. The Committee also find that under DA-
JGUA, there is a multi-sectoral livelihood support component 
for FRA patta holders in convergence with Ministry of 

67 
 
Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Department of Fisheries, 
Department of Animal Husbandry. Further, the Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj have 
collaborated to conduct a special capacity-building campaign 
for the effective implementation of FRA provisions.  The 
Committee appreciate the efforts made by the Ministry and 
expect that various initiatives taken under DA-JUGA should 
be implemented in a time bound manner so that livelihood 
support with the coordination of various 
Ministries/Departments are provided to FRA patta holders.

REPORT 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
 
 The mandate of the Ministry of Minority Affairs includes formulation of overall 
policy and planning, coordination, evaluation and review of the regulatory and 
development programmes for the benefit of the minority communities namely Jains, 
Parsis, Buddhists, Sikhs, Christians and Muslims.  
1.2 The vision of the Ministry is to create an enabling environment for strengthening 
the multi-facial, multi-cultural, multi-lingual and multi-religious character of the nation. 
The mission of the Ministry is to improve the socio-economic condition of the Minority 
communities through an affirmative action and inclusive development so that every 
citizen has equal opportunity and to participate accordingly in building a dynamic 
nation, to facilitate equitable share for Minority communities in education, employment, 
economic activities and to ensure their upliftment.  
1.3 T he following Schemes are being implemented by the Ministry for the welfare 
of Minority Communities: 
 
 
 
I. Pradhan Mantri Jan Vikas Karyakram (PMJVK), a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme of the Ministry provides for development of infrastructure projects in 
Education, Health, Skill Development Sectors and Women-centric projects, for 
improving the socio-economic conditions of people in the identified areas. 
 
II. The Ministry has designed Pradhan Mantri Virasat Ka Samvardhan (PM 
VIKAS), an umbrella scheme by converging five of the existing schemes of the 
Ministry namely –Seekho Aur Kamao, Upgrading the Skills and Training in 
Traditional Arts / Crafts for Development (USTTAD), Hamari Dharohar, Nai 
Roshni and Nai Manzil.  
 
III. The Ministry of Minority Affairs implements three scholarship schemes namely 
Pre-Matric, Post-Matric and Merit-cum-Means based Scholarship Schemes for 
the educational empowerment of notified minority communities. The schemes 
intend to lower the financial burden of financially weaker sections of religious 
minority communities. As part of an overall exercise to harmonize all the 
scholarship schemes of various Ministries/ Departments, the schemes will be 
brought under the ambit of an umbrella scheme. 
  

2 
 
IV. Jiyo Parsi is a Central Sector Scheme concerning the decline of Parsi 
population in India. The scheme has three components, Medical Assistance, 
Advocacy and Health of Community. Since inception, the scheme has enabled 
birth of more than 400 Parsi children till 31.03.2024. 
 
V. The National Minorities Development & Finance Corporation (NMDFC) was 
incorporated on 30.09.1994 as a ‘Not for Profit’ company under Section 25 of the 
Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 8 of Companies Act, 2013). NMDFC provides 
concessional credit viz., Term Loan, Education Loan, Micro Finance & Virasat 
implemented through the State Channelizing Agencies (SCAs) for self-
employment and income generating activities for the socio-economic 
development of the ‘backward sections’ amongst the notified Minorities. 
 
1.4 The Ministry of Minority Affairs had proposed for the Budgetary Allocation of 
₹4381.28 crore for the year 2025-26 for different Schemes. The Ministry of Finance has, 
however, allocated ₹3350.00 crore. The Scheme-wise proposal made by the Ministry

“(i) With the approval of competent authority, 02 schemes namely (a) Free 
Coaching & Allied Scheme, and (b) Nai Udaan, were discontinued from beginning 
of FY 2022-23. Under the Free Coaching and Allied Schemes (Naya Savera) 
wherein coaching was provided to minority youth was discontinued as the New 
Education Policy 2020, does not support coaching programs. Under the Nai 
Udaan scheme financial support was provided to candidates who qualify in the 
preliminary examinations conducted by Union Public Service Commission 
(UPSC), Staff Selection Commission (SSC), State Public Service Commissions 
(SPSCs). As no other Ministry / Department was providing such support to their 
beneficiaries, thus, in order to attain uniformity, the Ministry, decided to 
discontinue the Scheme w.e.f. 2022-23. 
 
(ii) From year 2022-23 onwards, the Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme is being 
harmonized with the Schemes of other line ministries, Ministry of Social Justice & 
Empowerment, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, etc. Accordingly, the coverage under the 
Pre-Matric Scheme has been restricted to class IX-X, whereas Schemes like 
Padho Pardesh and Maulana Azad National Fellowship have been discontinued 
since 2022-23 due to the fact that there was an overlap of these two schemes 
with the schemes of other Ministries/ Departments. 
 
(iii) The Scheme of Providing Education in Madarsas/Minorities (SPEMM), 
comprising 2 sub-components namely (i) SPQEM, and (ii) IDMI, was under 
implementation of Department of School Education & Literacy, Ministry of 
Education from 1993-94 to 2020-21. Thereafter, the scheme was transferred to 
the Ministry of Minority Affairs in 2021-22. As the Scheme was approved upto FY 
2021-22, thus, the Ministry of Minority Affairs implemented the scheme upto 2021-
22 only.”

2.5 As regards to policy changes likely to be introduced in 2025-26 for the effective 
implementation of the Schemes and Programmes of the Ministry so that the welfare of 
the notified Minority communities is not compromised, the Committee were informed 
vide written reply that: 
(i) “As per the felt needs on the basis of experience gained during 
implementation and execution of PMJVK and also based on the 
recommendations given by different independent Evaluations Studies during the 
years 2008-09 to 2022, from time to time necessary modifications have been 
carried out in the scheme’ guidelines.  The latest amendments in the PMJVK’ 
Guidelines were carried out in April 2022 inter-alia making it implementable 
across the country irrespective of the declared Minority Concentration Areas 
along with some more changes.  In future also the scheme would be subject to 
modifications as per the requirements. 
(ii) In respect of Scholarship Schemes, as of now, Ministry is making efforts to 
get the schemes approved for implementation at the earliest. 
 (iii) The Ministry has designed and constructed the PM VIKAS scheme 
 considering the specific requirements of the notified minority communities. The 
 scheme aims at providing comprehensive skill development, traditional training, 
 leadership and entrepreneurship promotion and education support to the notified 
 minority communities.”  
 
 
 

8 
 
2.6. The Committee note that the actual expenditure of the Ministry of 
Minority Affairs has gone down considerably during previous years. The 
Ministry could spend only ₹837.68 crore and ₹1,032.65 crore out of 
₹2,612.66 (RE) crore and ₹2,608.93 (RE) crore during the year 2022-23 and 
2023-24 respectively. The situation did not improve in 2024-25 as the 
Ministry were able to spend only ₹919.10 crore out of budgetary allocation 
of ₹3,183.24 crore (BE) by 31 December, 2024. The Committee have been 
apprised that the Ministry have not been able to spend the budgetary 
allocation as several Schemes such as ‘Free Coaching and Allied Scheme’, 
‘Nai Udaan’, ‘Scheme of Providing Education in Madrasas/ Minorities 
(SPEMM)’, etc, have been discontinued and PM-VIKAS launched in 2023-24 
did not initiate. Further, the amount allocated during 2022-23 to 2024-25 
under various  Scholarship Schemes of the Ministry could not be spent 
because these Schemes are under consideration for approval since 2022-
23 as they are being harmonised with the Schemes of other line Ministries, 
viz. Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment and Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs. The Committee strongly believe that the Ministry of Minority Affairs 
are making all efforts to achieve the mission of the Ministry by streamlining 
and strengthening the  prevailing System so that the deserving Minorities 
can avail the benefits of the Schemes and  the funds are not misused. The 
Committee feel that the steps taken by the Ministry were necessary in order 
to harmonize the system with the welfare Schemes of Ministry of Social 
Justice & Empowerment and Ministry of Tribal Affairs and hope that these 
steps will improve the implementation of the Schemes and enhance the  
socio-economic condition of six notified minority communities in the 
country. Since the Ministry of Minority Affairs are in process of 
streamlining/strengthening the prevailing System,  the Committee expect 
that  the necessary approvals will be obtained by the Ministry at the earliest 
so that the allocated Budget of ₹3,350.00 crore for 2025-26 is fruitfully 
utilised. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry of Minority 

9 
 
Affairs to vigorously pursue with the concerned Ministries/ Departments for 
the pending approvals and keep the administrative machinery of the 
Ministry ready for immediate implementation of the Schemes as soon as 
they are approved.

CHAPTER-V 
PRADHAN MANTRI JAN VIKAS KARYAKRAM (PMJVK) 
 
  The Pradhan Mantri Jan Vikas Karyakram (PMJVK), erstwhile Multi Sectoral 
Development Programme (MsDP) initiated in the year 2008-09, is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme(CSS) being implemented from financial year 2017-18 with the objective to 
develop community infrastructure and basic amenities in the identified areas for 
improving the quality of life of the people in these areas. The Minority Concentrated 
Areas (MCAs) were identified on the basis of concentration of minority population and 
backwardness in terms of identified indicators. The areas covered under PMJVK were 
increased from 90 Districts originally, to 308 Districts in 33 States/ UTs w.e.f. May, 2018. 
The scheme has been revised with the approval of the Cabinet in the year 2022 for 
continuation over the 15th Finance Commission Cycle i.e. upto 2025-26. The Scheme is 
now implementable in all Districts across the Country including all the Aspirational 
Districts subject to fulfilling of crieteria that the place of infra-development under the 
scheme should have more than 25% Minority Population within the catchment area of 15 
kms.  
  
5.2 As per procedure the proposals under PMJVK are recommended by the State 
Level Committee (SLC) headed by the Chief Secretary of the respective States/Union 
Territories (UTs) based on demand for infrastructure development in the identified areas. 
The proposals recommended by the SLC are considered by the Screening 
Committee(SC) chaired by JS(PMJVK) and then considered and approved by 
Empowered Committee(EC) chaired by Secretary, Ministry of Minority Affairs after due 
consultation with the concerned Central Ministries, projects under PMJVK are 
implemented and managed by concerned State/UT Government/CGOs. 
  
5.3 Education, health, skill development and women-oriented projects are the priority 
sector under PMJVK. The type of works undertaken under PMJVK include construction of 
schools, additional classrooms, hostels, computer labs/digital classrooms, science 
laboratories in schools, drinking water facilities and toilets in schools, colleges, 
dispensaries, hospitals, Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), Polytechnics, working women 
hostels, sports facilities, public/ community toilets etc. The projects are implemented on a 
fund sharing arrangement between the Centre and the State Government/UT 
Administration in the ratio of 90:10 for North East States, Hilly States (J&K, Himachal 
Pradesh, Uttarakhand)/ UTs without Legislation, 100% for UTs without Legislature and 
60:40 for all other States/ UTs/ UTs with Legislation.   Proposals received from Central 
Government Organisations are supported 100%.

focused remedial actions. The Committee are also of the opinion that 
proactive engagement with stakeholders is essential to address delays in 
proposal submissions from State Governments, NGOs, and implementing 
agencies, ensuring timely and complete proposals to facilitate smooth fund

Department should take decisive actions to improve fund utilization and 
achieve the intended outcomes of all the schemes in the remaining years 
of the current financial cycle (2023-2026). This will ensure that the 
resources allocated for the welfare of persons with disabilities are utilized 
effectively, enabling the Department to meet the targets set under various

Recommendation (Para No. 6.18) 
The Committee find that while the Central Sector Umbrella Scheme of Scholarship for 
Students with Disabilities has made commendable efforts in empowering students with 
disabilities, several challenges persist in achieving its full potential. The Committee note 
that, despite an increase in budgetary allocations over the years, utilization rates have 
been inconsistent, and physical achievements have fallen short. Challenges such as 
delays in application verifications, insufficient awareness, and technical issues with 
UDID and Aadhaar-based systems have hampered effective implementation. The 
Committee would like to recommend strengthening the verification process at the State 
Nodal Officer level, enhancing the capacity of the National Scholarship Portal to address 
technical bottlenecks, and expanding the scope of outreach programs through targeted 
awareness campaigns. The Committee emphasize the need for timely disbursal of 
funds, regular monitoring through physical inspections, and improved coordination with 
State/UT Governments to reduce pendency and duplication. The Committee further 
recommend revising the scholarship guidelines to ensure adequate flexibility for 
addressing emerging needs and streamlining the documentation process for applicants.

These measures will enhance the effectiveness of the scheme and better serve the 
educational aspirations of students with disabilities. 
  
Reply of the Government 
  
Under the Scholarship Umbrella Scheme, applications are received on NSP online portal 
for the Pre-matric, Post-matric and Top Class Education Scholarship Scheme. Aadhaar 
and UDID have been made mandatory to get the benefits of Scholarships. The Aadhaar 
details of beneficiaries are collected through the National Scholarship 
Portal and Fellowship Management Portal. UDID has also been integrated and 
beneficiary’s information is  fetched through API without any manual intervention for 
correct and accurate data. 
  
The applications are verified at various levels such as from the school or institute level 
to the domicile State or UT level. The State Nodal Officer verifies the application form 
and uploaded documents. The Nodal Officer can verify, defect, reject, or mark the 
application as fake. Once the application is verified at these levels, the National 
Scholarship Portal runs the Sanity checks and generates Red Flags. The doubtful 
applications are again sent to the State Nodal Officers for re-validation. The Department 
releases the scholarship amount only for those applications which are duly verified and 
approved by all verification authorities. The scholarship is disbursed only to the 
Aadhaar-seeded bank account of the beneficiary. Beside of this, the data verification 
works are assigned to the CPMU team for the Post Matric/Top Class Education 
applications and National Fellowship Scholarship Schemes on regular basis. The 
Department has revised the scholarship guideline for the year 2024-25 to ensure 
adequate flexibility for addressing emerging needs and streamlining the documentation 
process for applicants.

Recommendation (Para No. 2.18) 
 
The Committee observe that from 2021-22 to 2023-24, there has been a consistent

Estimates (BE), with actual expenditures falling short across various schemes of the

urge the Department to conduct a thorough review of the factors contributing to the 
underutilization of funds and take immediate and focused remedial actions. The

essential to address delays in proposal submissions from State Governments, NGOs, 
and implementing agencies, ensuring timely and complete proposals to facilitate 
smooth fund release. Streamlining fund disbursement processes, particularly for skill 
training programs and capital expenditure, is crucial to mitigating delays and enhancing 
program delivery. Furthermore, given the challenges in meeting the fixed targets for 
schemes like SIPDA and DDRS, the Department should reassess the targets setting to 
ensure they are realistic and achievable while maintaining flexibility in adjustments 
based on performance trends. Therefore, the Committee recommend that the 
Department should take decisive actions to improve fund utilization and achieve the 
intended outcomes of all the schemes in the remaining years of the current financial 
cycle (2023-2026). This will ensure that the resources allocated for the welfare of 
persons with disabilities are utilized effectively, enabling the Department to meet the 
targets set under various Schemes.
